#### D199 Order of the blocks of several rules and rewriters on one block
Question: Architecture 5.5 orders the blocks of one rule: @SAVE, requires, pre, the block, post, @RESTORE. Code-guidelines 5 (row 'Chain of rewriters') says the expander runs the rules and the plugin rewriters 'in a fixed order over each block' but does not say which order. Case: TOOL=2 COOLANT:THROUGH=ON with [tool_change] pre = ["HOME Z"] and the clutch rule. The order shows in trace, in the compiled program, and in which saved value each @RESTORE pops. Main nests them. The rule of the first triggering word in canonical order stands outermost. The rewriters follow in their order, each inside the previous one, next to the block, and limits = "clamp" runs last over all of them. Generated blocks trigger no rule and go to no rewriter.
Recommendation: Keep the nesting as coded and write it into architecture 5.5. Rules come in the canonical order of their triggering words (language 5 rule 6), each table's rule once. The rewriters follow in plugin load order (P7-01, PluginSet), each later one inside the earlier ones. The clamp comes last. Nesting has two advantages. It pairs each @RESTORE with its own @SAVE when two rules save the same variable, since the VM pops the newest entry of that variable. And it keeps an outer rule's required state in force while the inner blocks run. The canonical order makes the result independent of the order the author wrote the words in. Generated blocks are not expanded again, because the expander runs once over the parsed program (architecture 5.5). This also rules out endless expansion. Alternative: sequential order, where each rule's before blocks and after blocks stand in the same order on both sides. It is simpler to read. But with two restores of one variable, the first pops the other rule's saved value, so the blocks between them run in the wrong state.
Where: architecture 5.5 (one paragraph after the flowchart); code-guidelines 5 (Chain of rewriters row). Code: src/Ncx.Core/Expander/ExpansionRules.cs Of (TODO(question) at line 22), Expander.cs ExpandBlock, BlockExpansion.Surround; tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/Expander/ExpansionRuleTests.cs Architecture55_TwoRulesOnOneBlock_NestInTheCanonicalOrderOfTheirWords.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: Keep the nesting and write it into architecture 5.5: what is switched on last must be cancelled first. Mori Seiki prescribes exactly this for the NTX1000 — the 3D coordinate conversion G68.1/G69.1 and the tool offset G43/G49 must be given in one of two patterns, and each pattern's cancel sequence is the exact reverse of its switch-on sequence (pattern 1: G68.1 then G43, cancelled G49 then G69.1; pattern 2: G43 then G68.1, cancelled G69.1 then G49), block by block. Where order matters between functions of one block, controls do not resolve it inside the block either: Brother states that several M codes of one block with the same timing are output simultaneously and must be split into separate blocks if their order matters, and Hermle classifies each M code as acting at block start or block end. So the nesting is right and each rule's words belong in generated blocks of their own. Caveats: The manuals settle nesting versus sequential order for paired states; they say nothing about which of two independent rules stands outermost (the canonical order of language 5 rule 6), about plugin load order, or about the clamp running last — those stay NCX design choices. The Mori Seiki case is a pair of modal G functions, not an expansion rule, but it is the same save/restore structure. The manual does not say a wrong order is unrecoverable: it says that if the coordinates cannot be restored because of an error in the designation order of the cancel commands, the X, Y and Z axes must be returned to the zero point manually.
Evidence: `Mori-Seiki_NT-NTX-Serie_Programmierung_Programmieranleitung-NTX1000SZM_PX-NT_4-K0DEEN_2011`, p. 176-178 (G68.1 3D-Koordinatenumwandlung) (A CAUTION requires the G68.1/G69.1 on/off commands to be given together with the G43/G49 tool-offset commands in the order of pattern 1 or pattern 2; the listed cancel sequences mirror them (pattern 1: G49 then G69.1; pattern 2: G69.1 then G49), the commands must be executed block by block, the G68.1 block may contain no other G code and G69.1 must stand in a block of its own, and if the coordinates cannot be restored after an order error the axes must be returned to zero manually.); `Brother_CNC-C00_Programmierung-DIN-ISO_DE_2013`; same text in `Brother_S500X1-S700X1-M140X1_Programmierhandbuch_DE_2014`, p. 277 (section 12.2.1 Mehrfach M-Kode-Befehle in einem Satz) (Up to three M codes may stand in one block; codes with the same timing are output simultaneously, and if attention must be paid to the order of the M codes they have to be split over several blocks.); `Hermle_Allgemein_Programmierung_M-Funktionen-C400-C12-C60_DE_2015`, p. 1-2 (Kopf der M-Funktionstabelle) (The table's last two columns mark, per M code, whether it takes effect at 'Satzanfang' or 'Satzende' - the only ordering the builder documents inside one block.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep the nesting: rules in canonical order of their triggering words (each table's rule once), outermost first; plugin rewriters in load order, each inside the previous; limits clamp last. Generated blocks are not expanded again. Write into architecture 5.5.
Basis: manual
Source: Mori NTX1000 G68.1/G43 patterns: cancel sequence is the exact reverse of switch-on; Brother/Hermle: order inside one block is not defined, so each rule's words go in their own blocks.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none (docs).

#### D200 The line of a generated block in a diagnostic
Question: D98 and VM 2.9 render a diagnostic on a generated block as file(line, from 12), with the origin in OriginLine. Code-guidelines 6 says every diagnostic carries the line of an NCX block or a source block and, for a generated block, the originating line. None of them says what `line` is for a block that stands on no line of the file. Implementation 16 (phase 6) gives a moved word the line of its destination block, which exists; a block the expander inserts has none. Main gives a generated block the line of its origin (GeneratedText.Parse), so a diagnostic reads test.ncx(4, from 4): WARNING VM060. P1-07's trace writes that line followed by the origin.
Recommendation: Keep what the code does: a generated block has the line of the block it was generated for, and 'from' marks it as generated. D98 gets a Clarified line, and VM 2.9 gets one sentence: 'A block the expander generates has the line of its origin; a diagnostic on it reads file(12, from 12).' This keeps D98's form, and both numbers point at the one line an editor can open. Alternative: a generated block has no line of its own (Line null, the 'no line' value that the open D110 proposes for command-line diagnostics), rendered file(from 12). Option, whichever way this is answered: a VM diagnostic on a generated block starts its message with the rule or rewriter and the reason, as the expander's parse diagnostics already do ([tool_change] pre "HOME Z": ...). Two generated blocks of one origin can then be told apart.
Where: D98 (Clarified line in decisions.md and rationale.md); VM 2.9; code-guidelines 6; language 4.15; D110 for the alternative. Code: src/Ncx.Core/Expander/GeneratedText.cs Parse (TODO(question) at line 149); src/Ncx.Core/Model/Diagnostic.cs ToText; for the option, where the VM reports diagnostics on generated blocks; tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/Expander/GeneratedBlockTests.cs D98_DiagnosticOnAGeneratedBlock_NamesTheOriginatingLine.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. No manual says what `line` is for a generated block, but Siemens answers the closest question the same way the code does, so keeping GeneratedText.Parse (a generated block carries the line of the block it was generated for, rendered file(12, from 12)) is the reading the manuals point to. With DISPLOF the block display shows the cycle or subprogram call instead of the current block, and on an alarm the block number reported is that of the cycle or subprogram call from the last program level not marked DISPLOF; only the additional attribute ACTBLOCNO makes the alarm name the block in which it actually occurred. Siemens' own measuring cycles are declared SAVE ACTBLOCNO DISPLOF, i.e. they use both at once — which is what NCX's file(12, from 12) gives in one string. What is left for the maintainer: Siemens is deciding what an operator sees for code that lives in a separate cycle file, while an NCX generated block has no file of its own, so the analogy fixes the direction, not the rendering. Caveats: Downgraded from 'answered': the cited pages are a display convention with no machine consequence, and nothing in the library constrains an NCX diagnostic. They do settle the direction — the default is the origin's line in the user's program, with the inner line as the option. Note also that controller-mapping 6 already lists SBLOF/DISPLOF as RAW for Siemens, so this is an analogy only, not a mapping.
Evidence: `Siemens_Sinumerik-840D-sl_Programmierung_BS.000504-DE-000-00_DE`, p. 175 (section 2.24.2.6 DISPLOF, DISPLON, ACTBLOCNO) (In a cycle or subprogram DISPLOF suppresses the display of the current block and the call of the cycle or subprogram is shown instead; with DISPLOF and no ACTBLOCNO an alarm reports the block number of the cycle or subprogram call from the last program level not marked DISPLOF, while ACTBLOCNO makes it report the block in which the alarm occurred.); `Siemens_Sinumerik-840D-sl_Programmierung_BS.000504-DE-000-00_DE`, p. 176 (Beispiel 2, Satzanzeige bei der Alarmausgabe) (Two subprograms are contrasted, SUBPROG1 with DISPLOF ACTBLOCNO and SUBPROG2 with DISPLOF alone, to show which block number an alarm raised inside them puts on the screen (the example output names the inner block N9040).); `Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl-828D_Programming-Manual-Measuring-Cycles_SW44_EN_2011`, p. 217, 226, 228, 231 (parameter lists CYCLE973, CYCLE976, CYCLE978, CYCLE998) (Every measuring cycle's PROC line ends in SAVE ACTBLOCNO DISPLOF - Siemens' own cycles show the call in the block display and still report the internal block on an alarm.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

A generated block has the line of its origin and renders `file(12, from 12)` (GeneratedText.Parse as coded). D98 gets a Clarified line, VM 2.9 one sentence. Adopt the option: a VM diagnostic on a generated block starts its message with the rule or rewriter and its reason.
Basis: manual
Source: Siemens DISPLOF/ACTBLOCNO: alarms report the calling block by default, the inner one only on request (840D sl programming manual); an analogy for the direction.
Differs from the recommendation: no (takes the message-prefix option)
Confidence: medium
Code impact: VM diagnostic message prefix for generated blocks.

#### D201 SKIP of the origin on its generated blocks
Question: Language 4.1 skips a SKIP block when its switch is on, and D53 runs SKIP blocks unless the run option skip_blocks says otherwise. Language 4.15 and VM 3.10 make generated blocks ordinary blocks, 'executed in both modes' and written by ncx compile. No document says whether the blocks generated for a SKIP block are skipped with it. Case: [tool_change] pre = ["HOME Z"] on SKIP=2 TOOL=1 under skip_blocks = [2]. Either HOME Z is skipped too, or the machine homes Z for a tool change that does not happen. Likewise, the compiler writes the generated lines either with or without /2. Main copies the origin's SKIP, bare or numbered, onto every generated block whose text does not write one (GeneratedText.Mark).
Recommendation: Keep what the code does. A generated block carries the SKIP of its origin unless its own text writes one. skip_blocks then skips or runs the block together with everything a rule or rewriter put around it, and the compiler writes the skip mark on each generated line. Reason: pre, requires and restore exist only for their block. With the block skipped, they would move an axis, or stop and restart the spindle, for nothing. Language 4.15 gets the sentence. Alternative: generated blocks carry no SKIP and always run.
Where: language 4.15 (one sentence); VM 3.10. Code: src/Ncx.Core/Expander/GeneratedText.cs Mark (TODO(question) at line 102); tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/Expander/ExpansionRuleTests.cs D53_GeneratedBlocks_CarryTheSkipOfTheirOrigin; the compilers (P3-03) write the skip mark on generated lines.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals settle the compiler half and leave the semantic half open. Block skip is strictly per block on every control: on Fanuc the slash must stand at the beginning of the block and everything from /n to the end of block is ignored while BDTn is 1 (several switches /1 /3 /5 may stand on one block, and setting any one of them skips it), and Heidenhain hides NC blocks one at a time by inserting one / character into the selected block. No control can mark a group of blocks, so whichever way this is answered the compiler must write the mark on every generated line, as the recommendation says. Whether the generated blocks are skipped together with their origin is not addressed anywhere; the nearest documented support is that a skipped block is ignored in full, so a skipped M98 or cycle call never triggers what it would have triggered — which is the reading the recommendation takes. Caveats: The 'skipped block triggers nothing' point is my inference from the rule that the data from / to end of block are ignored, not a sentence in the manual; mark it as such. Fanuc's timing diagrams show the skip is decided as the CNC starts reading the block, so origin and generated blocks, being read one after another, see the same switch state. A side note from the same page that may matter elsewhere: a block containing /M02, /M30 or /M99 is not treated as program end.
Evidence: `Fanuc_30i-B_Bedienung-Drehen-Fraesen_B-64484EN_EN`, p. 327-328 (ch. 13 Programmkonfiguration, wahlweise Satzausblendung) (When /n stands at the start of a block and signal BDTn is 1, the information from /n to the end of block is ignored; several skip switches may stand in one block (/1 /3 /5) and setting any one of them makes the block ignored; the timing diagrams show whether it is skipped depends on the signal when the CNC starts reading the block.); `Fanuc_30i-B_Bedienung-Drehen-Fraesen_B-64484EN_EN`, p. 328-329 (Anmerkung 2, Position des Schrägstrichs) (The slash for block skip must stand at the beginning of the block; if it stands anywhere else, the data between the slash and the end-of-block code are read over - the mark belongs to exactly one block. A CAUTION adds that a block with /M02, /M30 or /M99 is not treated as program end.); `Heidenhain_TNC640_Programmierung-Klartext_892903-18_NC-SW-34059x-10_DE_2019`, p. 195 (section 6.5 NC-Sätze überspringen) (NC blocks are hidden one at a time: select the wanted NC block and press EINFÜGEN, and the control inserts the / character into it; ENTFERNEN removes the character and un-hides it.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

A generated block carries its origin's SKIP unless its own text writes one (GeneratedText.Mark as coded); skip_blocks skips or runs the group together, and the compiler writes the skip mark on every generated line. Sentence in language 4.15.
Basis: manual
Source: Block skip is strictly per block (Fanuc B-64484EN: / at block start, several /n allowed; Heidenhain one / per block), so the compiler must mark every line; a skipped block triggers nothing it would have triggered.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none.

#### D202 State variables that @SAVE and @RESTORE may name
Question: VM 3.10 lets the state key of @SAVE and @RESTORE name 'a state variable of the channel by the key that sets it' and gives only SPINDLE:MAIN, COOLANT and F as examples. Machine-config 5a says only that restore lists 'the state variables to put back'. Read literally, TOOL, CYCLE, ORIGIN or a variable would qualify. But @RESTORE 're-applies it as if the program had written the word again', which one word cannot do for the transform chain, a cycle's parameters or a tool change. Main (RestoreRules.Resolve) keeps SPINDLE (with its RPM), RPM, SPINDLE_MODE, CSS, VC, RPM_MAX, COOLANT, FUNC, F, FEED_MODE, COMP and DIAMETER. Any other key is ERROR VM681, so restore = ["TCPM"] around a five-axis tool change, or ["WORKPLANE"], stops the run.
Recommendation: The restore stack keeps the modal state (VM 4) that one word sets again from one value. That is the coded list plus WORKPLANE, TCPM, POLAR, CYLINDER, ROTARY_PATH, ROTARY_FEED and TOLERANCE. TOLERANCE comes back with TOLERANCE:ROTARY and TOLERANCE_MODE, as SPINDLE comes back with its RPM. A restored POLAR or CYLINDER does to the position what the written word does (VM 3.4). These stay out, VM681 as now: TOOL, PRELOAD and OFFSET, because putting them back is a tool change; CYCLE, because a new CYCLE replaces all parameters (VM 2.6); ORIGIN, SETPOS and the chain words, because they form a chain, not one value, and ORIGIN empties it; SPINDLE_SYNC and PHASE, because they involve two spindles; ORIENT, because it is an action; WORKPIECE, because it switches the holder whose frame and rotary axis the following words use, and it leaves the position unknown (VM 3.4, 3.8 rule 3); UNITS, because it sets the unit of every stored coordinate and feed, including the values already on the restore stack; and variables and positions. VM 3.10 gives the list, and the restore bullet of machine-config 5a refers to it. Reason: a tool change that needs TCPM=OFF is the common case the coded list cannot express, and every added key is written back by one word, like the coded ones. Alternative: keep the coded list and add keys when a machine needs them.
Where: VM 3.10 (the list); machine-config 5a (restore bullet). Code: src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/RestoreRules.cs Resolve, Save, PutBack (TODO(question) at line 35) and the VM681 message; tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/VirtualMachine/RestoreStackTests.cs; docs/spec/generated/diagnostics.md (VM681 row).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The controls have this mechanism and this criterion, but they draw the line wider than the draft. Sinumerik's PROC <name> SAVE restores the modal G commands active before the subprogram call; the DMG training volume spells out that this puts back the settable zero offset (modal G group 8 = NCX ORIGIN) plus the programmable zero offset and the base offset, and the F value when the feed-type group changed, while the frame behaviour under SAVE is machine-data dependent. Because G70/G71/G700/G710 (group 13, inch/metric) are marked modal in the same manual's G-group tables, inch/metric (NCX UNITS) comes back with them. Fanuc puts the whole "Modalinformation" back when an interrupt macro returns with M99. Every key the draft adds is one value of one modal group: WORKPLANE is Siemens group 6, COMP 7, FEED_MODE/CSS 15 (G93-G97), DIAMETER 29, and TCPM is Fanuc G-code group 08 beside G43, G44 and G49. TOLERANCE really is a triple, since cycle 32 takes T, HSC-MODE and TA - the mapping recorded D85 already makes. What the manuals cannot judge is NCX's reason for excluding ORIGIN and UNITS, since no control has NCX's transform chain and no restore stack there holds values that carry a unit; what they do show is that the nearest control mechanism restores both. Caveats: This proposal contradicts the recommendation. Sinumerik SAVE is scoped to a subprogram call, not to the expander's @SAVE/@RESTORE pair, so the wider line is a fact about the control mechanism, not about NCX's stack. That UNITS is restored is an inference from two pages (SAVE restores the modal G commands; group 13 is modal), not from one sentence. The mapping of NCX keys onto Siemens G groups and Fanuc groups is mine; the manuals name the groups, not the NCX keys.
Evidence: `Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl_Programmierhandbuch-NC-Programmierung_SW492_DE_2019`, p. 510-511 (section 3.2.2.4), constraint note on 512 (The SAVE attribute on PROC saves the modal G commands active before the subprogram call and reactivates them after the subprogram end. The warning about the path-control mode being broken at the return stands on 511 itself; page 512 adds only that frame behaviour under SAVE depends on the frame type and is set by machine data.); `DMG-MORI_GMX-CTX-TC_Trainingshandbuch-Sinumerik840D_DE_2010`, p. 166 (Spells out what SAVE puts back: the modal G functions to their value at subprogram start, and in addition to the settable zero offset (modal G function group 8) the programmable zero offset and the base offset; if the feed-type group (15) changed, e.g. G94 to G95, the matching F value is restored too.); `Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl_Programmierhandbuch-NC-Programmierung_SW492_DE_2019`, p. 19-20 (contents of section 4.3, G-Befehle) (Enumerates the modal G groups by name: 6 plane selection, 7 tool radius compensation, 8 settable zero offset, 13 workpiece dimensioning inch/metric, 15 feed type, 29 radius/diameter programming.); `Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl_Programmierhandbuch-NC-Programmierung_SW492_DE_2019`, p. 1230-1232 (sections 4.3.13 and 4.3.15) (The group tables themselves: group 13 holds G70, G71, G700 and G710, each marked "m" for modal, so inch/metric is one of the modal G commands SAVE restores. Group 15 (feed type) holds G93 to G97 and G931 to G952, so constant cutting speed is a value of the feed-type group, which is the NCX pair FEED_MODE/CSS.); `Fanuc_30i-B_Bedienung-Drehen-Fraesen_B-64484EN_EN`, p. 64-65, table 3.1 (a) G-Code-Liste (Group 07 holds G40/G41/G42 (with the three-dimensional forms), and group 08 holds G43, G44, G43.1, G43.3, G43.4, G43.5 and G49 - so tool-centre-point control is one value of one modal G-code group, exactly like compensation.); `Fanuc_16i-18i-MA_Benutzerhandbuch_B-63014GE-02_DE`, p. 458, custom-macro interrupt (An interrupt macro must not disturb the interrupted program, so the modal information valid before the interrupt takes effect again when the control returns with M99; only with M99 Pxxxx are the interrupt program's modal changes handed on. The unit saved and put back is the whole modal information, not a chosen list.); `Heidenhain_TNC640_Zyklen_892905-18_NC-SW-34059x-10_DE_2019`, p. 373 (cycle 32 TOLERANZ, cycle parameters) (Cycle 32 has three parameters: the contour tolerance T, HSC-MODE (0 finishing, 1 roughing) and TA, the permitted position deviation of the rotary axes in degrees under active M128 (FUNCTION TCPM). One control object carries all three, which is the NCX triple of recorded D85.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

As recommended. The restorable keys are the coded list plus WORKPLANE, TCPM, POLAR, CYLINDER, ROTARY_PATH, ROTARY_FEED and TOLERANCE (with TOLERANCE:ROTARY and TOLERANCE_MODE). TOOL, PRELOAD, OFFSET, CYCLE, ORIGIN, SETPOS, the chain words, SPINDLE_SYNC, PHASE, ORIENT, WORKPIECE, UNITS, variables and positions stay VM681. ORIGIN and UNITS stay out on purpose. Re-writing ORIGIN=n empties the chain, so it would not bring back the frames that Siemens SAVE restores, and the machine would then move in a different frame without a word of warning. A restored UNITS would change the unit of values already on the stack. VM 3.10 notes that the controls restore a wider set on a subprogram return (Siemens PROC SAVE, the Fanuc interrupt M99), and that NCX restores a narrower one on purpose.
Basis: logical
Source: The manual facts are Siemens PGH SW4.92 p. 510-512, DMG Training p. 166 and Fanuc 16i p. 458. They describe subprogram scope, not @SAVE/@RESTORE. Logical: NCX re-applies one word per key. ORIGIN and UNITS cannot be faithfully re-applied by one word, and a wrong frame or unit moves the machine wrongly, so the ERROR is the safe choice.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: medium
Code impact: RestoreRules.Resolve/Save/PutBack (add the seven keys); VM681 text.

#### D203 Which targets limits = "clamp" rewrites
Question: VM 5 compares 'a target beyond the axis limits' in the MACHINE frame, 'not checked while the machine position is unknown'. It also says that 'with limits = "clamp" in the configuration the expander rewrites the value' (D64; machine-config 1: 'RPM, F and targets'). Architecture 5.5 says the expander 'never sees VM state', and the machine position of a target in the workpiece frame (ORIGIN, the frame chain, a SETPOS shift; D100, D101) is VM state. The code rewrites only absolute axis words of RAPID, LINE and ARC blocks under FRAME=MACHINE, and leaves `RAPID X=700` in the workpiece frame as written (LimitClampTests.D64_WorkpieceTargetAndRotaryTarget_AreNotRewritten, which runs only the expander). The VM compares such a target (VM442) only when it knows the machine position through a SETPOS recorded against it (FrameRules.MachineCoordinate; MotionValidationTests.Target_BeyondTheLimitThroughTheSetposShift_Warns). After ORIGIN alone, neither side checks it. Rewriting the end point of a CENTER-form ARC can also make its centre inconsistent, which VM 5 makes an ERROR.
Recommendation: Keep what the code does, minus ARC, and write it into VM 5 and machine-config 1. Under "clamp" the expander rewrites only the absolute axis words of RAPID and LINE blocks under FRAME=MACHINE, which are machine coordinates as written. Every other target keeps VM442 under both policies wherever the VM knows its machine position (VM 5, D100). That covers an ARC target or an incremental word under FRAME=MACHINE, and a workpiece target through a SETPOS recorded against the machine position (D101). A target known only in the workpiece frame is not checked, as VM 5 and the travel-limit analytic of VM 8 already say. ARC comes out of the clamped verbs because a moved end point changes the arc (R form) or makes its centre inconsistent (CENTER form, an ERROR). An ARC target is reported, not rewritten. Reason: this is the only reading possible without VM state (architecture 5.5), and an arc end point cannot move without its centre. Alternative: keep ARC among the clamped verbs, as on main. Whether the X of a machine-frame target on a diameter axis is a diameter is D137.
Where: VM 5 (the limits item and its clamp clause); machine-config 1 (the limits comment). Code: src/Ncx.Core/Expander/LimitClamp.cs ClampTarget (TODO(question) at line 151; the verb test that names ARC); src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/FrameRules.cs MachineCoordinate (what VM442 can see); tests LimitClampTests.D64_MachineFrameTargetBeyondTheLimits_IsClamped and D64_WorkpieceTargetAndRotaryTarget_AreNotRewritten, MotionValidationTests.Target_BeyondTheLimitThroughTheSetposShift_Warns and Target_WithTheMachinePositionUnknown_IsNotCompared.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals say plainly that no control rewrites a target: Sinumerik states the working-area limits in the base coordinate system and stops the program run when the tool reference point leaves the area, and the one function that computes a clamped value, CALCPOSI, hands the maximum possible travel back to the program as a number instead of moving anything. Both Siemens and Fanuc make the check conditional on the axes being referenced — CALCPOSI returns status -6 when a machine axis needed for the check is not referenced, and Fanuc's safety chapter says a travel-range check is possible only after manual reference-point return — which is the same condition as VM 5's "not checked while the machine position is unknown". That supports the draft: keep VM442 as the reporting path, confine the rewrite to the absolute machine-frame axis words of RAPID and LINE, and report an ARC target rather than move it. The contrast machine-config 1 rolls into one "RPM, F and targets" clause is documented for speed: under G96 a spindle speed above the value set with G92 S is clamped to that maximum. What is left to the maintainer is the NCX side, since no control does the rewrite at all; note also that Sinumerik's WALCS variant does limit in the workpiece coordinate system, but only with the full frame and transformation state that architecture 5.5 denies the expander. Caveats: The library documents position limits as an alarm or a stop, never as a silent clamp; I found no manual that describes a control rewriting a programmed position. The Fanuc referencing condition is a safety warning about the machine, not a statement about a program analyser.
Evidence: `Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl_Programmierhandbuch-NC-Programmierung_SW492_DE_2019`, p. 355-356 (Arbeitsfeldbegrenzung im BKS, G25/G26, WALIMON/WALIMOF) (The working-area limits are assigned per channel axis and the coordinates apply in the Basiskoordinatensystem, a machine-side frame, not in the workpiece frame.); `Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl_Programmierhandbuch-NC-Programmierung_SW492_DE_2019`, p. 357-358 (If the tool reference point stands outside the working area or leaves it, the program run is stopped. Nothing is rewritten. The same page points at CALCPOSI as the way to test a planned path before moving.); `Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl_Programmierhandbuch-NC-Programmierung_SW492_DE_2019`, p. 595-596 (CALCPOSI) (CALCPOSI checks in the workpiece coordinate system whether the geometry axes can travel a given path without violating software limit switches, working-area limits or protected zones; when they cannot it returns a status code and the maximum possible travel path, and status -6 means at least one machine axis needed for the check is not referenced.); `Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl_Programmierhandbuch-NC-Programmierung_SW492_DE_2019`, p. 358-359 (WALCS0 ... WALCS10) (There is a second form that limits travel in the workpiece coordinate system or the settable zero system, and its stated precondition is that the channel axes must be referenced.); `Fanuc_30i-B_Bedienung-Drehen-Fraesen_B-64484EN_EN`, p. 6, safety warning 6 "Verfahrbereichskontrolle" (A travel-range check is only possible after a manual reference-point return, and with the check switched off no alarm is raised even when the travel is exceeded.); `Fanuc_16i-18i-MA_Benutzerhandbuch_B-63014GE-02_DE`, p. 168, 9.3 constant surface speed control (Under constant surface speed control a spindle speed that exceeds the maximum spindle speed set with G92 S is clamped to that maximum; after power-on the limit is not yet active and the speed is not limited. Speeds are clamped by the control; positions are not.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Under "clamp" the expander rewrites only absolute axis words of RAPID and LINE under FRAME=MACHINE; ARC is removed from the clamped verbs. Every other target keeps VM442 wherever the VM knows its machine position; a target known only in the workpiece frame is not checked. Write into VM 5 and machine-config 1.
Basis: manual
Source: No control rewrites a target: Sinumerik working-area limit stops the program, CALCPOSI only returns the possible travel; checks need referenced axes (Siemens CALCPOSI status -6, Fanuc safety chapter).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: Ncx.Core expander limit clamp (drop ARC); LimitClampTests.

#### D205 Output of trace, annotate, convert and compile after an ERROR
Question: VM 2.9 and code-guidelines 6 say an ERROR stops the run, and D97 gives exit 1. Architecture 7 ends convert with a STATIC pass that 'reports its diagnostics together with the reader's'. No document says whether a command still writes its output. The P0-06 task log reads it for format: nothing is written after a parser ERROR. P1-07 writes the trace rows of the blocks executed before the ERROR, and the whole annotate copy with those blocks' values. Both write nothing after a parser or expander ERROR. P3-02c writes the whole converted text, because the reader always completes the program with RAW (D5). It does so also after a reader ERROR such as RDR101 (M6 without preload), which keeps the check from starting (VM 2.9). Every command writes nothing when an input cannot be read (exit 2), or when ncx.toml, the machine file or its catalog loads with an ERROR. compile is next (P3-03), and its plan names only where the NC file goes.
Recommendation: Keep what the code does and state it once in architecture 10, after the exit codes. trace writes the rows of the blocks executed before the ERROR. annotate writes the whole copy, where blocks not executed carry no values. convert writes the whole text. Each exits 1. format writes nothing after a parser ERROR. compile writes no NC file after any ERROR, because that file goes to a control. Nothing is written when the run does not start: an input that cannot be read (exit 2); an ncx.toml, machine file or catalog with an ERROR; a controller without a reader; and for trace and annotate a parser or expander ERROR. Reason: the rows before the ERROR are what the user needs to find it, and the converted text is what the user corrects. The exit code and the standard error tell a script not to use it. A compiled program with an ERROR must never reach the machine. Alternative: no output after any ERROR, as format does, so that a pipe never receives a partial result.
Where: Architecture 10 (a sentence after the exit codes; the convert row); VM 6; implementation 13 P3-03 (compile). Code: src/Ncx.Cli/Commands/TraceCommand.cs and AnnotateCommand.cs Run, ConvertCommand.cs Run (TODO(question) at TraceCommand.cs line 93, AnnotateCommand.cs line 46, ConvertCommand.cs line 152). Tests: ConvertCommandTests.Convert_ErrorOfTheReader_WritesTheTextAndStopsTheCheck; TraceCommandTests.Trace_UnknownKey_WritesNothingAndExitsOne and AnnotateCommandTests.Annotate_UnknownKey_WritesNothingAndExitsOne pin the parser case. No test yet pins the rows written before a VM ERROR.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. No control manual bears on this, but the library does hold documentation of a program generator for these machines, and it is worth reading before architecture 10 is written. Mori Seiki's own ESPRIT post-processor manual states about a dozen times that a bad setting does not stop the post: "you will get an error message in your NC code" — the NC output is produced and carries the diagnostic. The same manual shows the other behaviour for a different class of fault: when the tool inclination does not match the operation, a message is displayed and the run cannot be executed at all. So the practice in this shop's own toolchain is: a data error still produces output with the message in it, an impossible geometry produces none. That cuts against the recommendation's line that compile writes no NC file after any ERROR, and supports the rest of it (trace, annotate and convert write what they got). It does not settle the question — a CAM post is not NCXchange, and a program that alarms on the control is a different safety design from one that never reaches it. The evidence is from a CAM post-processor, not a control, so it binds nothing; it is a precedent the maintainer should weigh for the compile row. Note also that Hermle's sheet is not the one document in the library that states requirements on a program generator: the library also holds the Mori Seiki ESPRIT post manual (135 pages), six WFL Millturn post-processor notes, Grob's G750T post-processor description and Correa's post-processor requirements (a scan with no text). I searched all of them for Fehler/Warnung/Protokoll/Abbruch; only the ESPRIT manual says anything, and none of them mentions exit codes or partial output.
Evidence: `Mori-Seiki_Allgemein_Software-Tools_ESPRIT-Postprozessor_IX-ESPRITPOSTNL12-D0DEEN_2012`, p. 20 (If the station number specified is out of range, "you will get an error message in your NC code" — the post writes the NC code and puts the diagnostic inside it. The same sentence is repeated for other settings on pages 23, 31, 32, 46, 53, 62, 63, 72 and 113.); `Mori-Seiki_Allgemein_Software-Tools_ESPRIT-Postprozessor_IX-ESPRITPOSTNL12-D0DEEN_2012`, p. 79 (Two behaviours side by side: a forgotten work-coordinate setting for a tilted tool gives "an error message in your NC code", whereas an inclination the machine cannot reach displays the message "Can't reach this position (needs another axis of rotation)" and the simulation cannot be executed.); `Mori-Seiki_Allgemein_Software-Tools_ESPRIT-Postprozessor_IX-ESPRITPOSTNL12-D0DEEN_2012`, p. 95 ("When Free is set there, the error message will be output in the NC code" — the message is part of the written program, not of a separate report.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

As coded, stated in architecture 10: trace writes rows of blocks executed before the ERROR; annotate the whole copy (unexecuted blocks without values); convert the whole text; each exits 1. format writes nothing after a parser ERROR; compile writes no NC file after any ERROR. Nothing is written when the run does not start (exit 2, config load ERROR, no reader, parser/expander ERROR for trace and annotate).
Basis: logical
Source: Mori's ESPRIT post writes output with error text, but a program that alarms on a control is a weaker safety design than one that never reaches it; NCX prefers no NC file.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: compile command (P3-03) must suppress the file on ERROR.

#### D207 Where ncx looks for the cycle catalog of a machine
Question: Machine-config 6 writes [cycles] catalog = "heidenhain-cycles.toml", a catalog 'shipped with NCXchange, user-extendable'. Machine-config 10 puts it in the project's cycles/, and architecture 10 lets ncx.toml name the cycle folder. No document says which folders are searched and in which order, whether the value may be a path (and counted from where), or what a catalog that cannot be found means. Case: before the P2-04 review fix, the --machine path rules loaded a machine file siemens.toml in the working directory, with catalog = "siemens.toml", as its own catalog. The code now searches the cycle folders alone: the one ncx.toml names, then cycles/ of the working directory, then cycles/ of the tool's own folder. A value with a folder in it counts from each of them, and a full path, or one that climbs out with '..', names no file. A catalog found nowhere or unreadable is CLI202, exit 2; one that loads with an ERROR exits 1.
Recommendation: Keep what the code does and write it into machine-config 6 and 10. Reason: the project folder before the tool's own folder lets a shop replace a shipped catalog in its project without touching the installation. It is the same order implementation 12 P2-04 gives the machine folders. A machine file is shared between PCs, so a full path would tie it to one PC. A catalog that the machine names but ncx cannot read is an unreadable input (D97). Answer this together with D156 (the names of the shipped catalogs). Alternative: first resolve the value from the folder of the machine file, so that a machine file and its own catalog travel together, and accept a full path. Only then try the cycle folders.
Where: Machine-config 6 ([cycles] catalog) and 10 (layout); architecture 10 (the ncx.toml paragraph); D156. Code: src/Ncx.Cli/RunMachine.cs WithCatalog (TODO(question) at line 132) and ProjectFolders.cs FindCatalog; tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Cli/RunMachineTests.cs (the CycleCatalog_ tests).

ANSWER: (Peter, 2026-10-07, drafted by Claude in project_spike) Accept as recommended: keep the code's order (the folder ncx.toml names, the project's cycles/, the tool's own folder) and write it into machine-config 6 and 10, extended by D371's built-in copy as the fourth and last place. A shop's own catalog may override a shipped one on purpose; the CAM's bundle is protected by the schema version of D348.
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. No manual can settle where ncx looks for its own catalog files; this is an NCX layout decision. What the library does give is a precedent worth citing in machine-config 6: the SINUMERIK resolves a subprogram or cycle called without a path by walking a fixed search path — the current directory in which the program was selected first, then the subprogram directories of the NC and global program memory, then a CALLPATH extension, then the user cycle directory, then the manufacturer cycle directory, then the Siemens standard cycle directory — so the project's own copy wins over the manufacturer's and the manufacturer's over the shipped installation, which is exactly the order the recommendation argues for. Two details of that rule also match the code: a directory is never searched recursively, and the search path is walked afresh for each single call regardless of where the calling program sits.
Evidence: SINUMERIK 840D sl NC-Programmierung, Programmierhandbuch 06/2019 (CNC-SW 4.92), p. 572-573 (Section 3.4.1.4: for a subprogram call without a path the absolute path is found by walking a fixed search path in eight steps: the current directory (where the program was selected), the same name with _SPF and with _MPF, the _N_SPF_DIR of the NC and of the global part-program memory, any CALLPATH extension, then _N_CUS_DIR (user cycles), _N_CMA_DIR (manufacturer cycles) and _N_CST_DIR (standard cycles). Page 573 adds the rules: the path is walked for each single call, so where the calling program sits is irrelevant, and nested directories inside a directory are not searched.).
Confidence: low.

#### D213 A JUMP out of a running REPEAT
Question: VM 2.7 keeps a repeatStack next to the callStack, and VM 3.6 says REPEAT with TIMES 're-executes the section from the label to the current block'. Neither says what happens to a repeat that still has passes when a JUMP or JUMP=END takes the flow out of those blocks. A Heidenhain source can do this: an FN 9 GOTO LBL out of a CALL LBL REP part, whose label heidenhain.md 7 rule 3 makes a LABEL. Case: LABEL=1, VAR:Q1={$Q1+1}, JUMP=9 IF={$Q1==2}, REPEAT=1 TIMES=5, LABEL=9, and later flow that reaches REPEAT=1 again. Does the repeat end, keep its remaining passes, or is the jump an ERROR? On main the repeat ends (EndRepeatsOutside), and the next arrival at the REPEAT block starts a new repeat with all its passes. A jump to a block inside the section keeps the repeat.
Recommendation: Keep what the code does. A JUMP or JUMP=END whose target lies outside the blocks from the label to the REPEAT block ends the repeat. A later arrival at the REPEAT block starts a new repeat with TIMES passes. Reason: the repeatStack is flow state like the callStack, which leaving a section already unwinds (Leave in the code). The number of passes then depends only on the flow between the label and the REPEAT block, never on a count left over from an earlier visit. The compilers must write the same behaviour. The Fanuc counter of controller-mapping 6 starts at the REPEAT block and is cleared by every JUMP that leaves the section. Whether the TNC restarts its REP counter after an FN 9 out of the part is a control fact for P3-04 to confirm; heidenhain.md 1 does not say. Alternative: the repeat keeps its remaining passes and continues when the flow reaches its REPEAT block again. Each REPEAT block then keeps a counter, reset only when it is used up.
Where: VM 3.6 (REPEAT bullet), VM 2.7 (repeatStack row); controller-mapping 6 (REPEAT + TIMES row, Fanuc column); heidenhain.md 1 once confirmed. Code: src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/VirtualMachine.Interpreted.cs EndRepeatsOutside (TODO(question) at line 309) and the JUMP branches of RunSection; tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/VirtualMachine/InterpretedFlowTests.cs Repeat_LeftByAJump_Ends; P3-04 (HeidenhainFlow), P3-06 (Fanuc flow).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, corrected 2026-10-26 after the manual audit, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The earlier answer read the one Siemens page as ruling against the recommendation; after the audit that verdict is withdrawn. The Sinumerik manual says that when jumps and program-part repeats are mixed the blocks are processed purely sequentially, and that after a jump out of a repeat the control machines on until the programmed end of the part is found. Its example jumps with GOTOF from inside the repeated region to a label that still lies before the REPEAT line, and the pass ends at that label's ENDLABEL. The case of D213, a jump past the REPEAT block itself, is not covered, so "the remaining passes stand" would be an extrapolation. The same list says that M17 or RET during a repeat aborts it and continues after the REPEAT line, and a level abort does the same; a jump is not named. The Heidenhain manuals are silent: jumps do not take the LBL 0 return marks of subprograms and part repeats into account, which says only that a jump does not resume anything, not that it clears the REP counter, and searches in other Heidenhain manuals found no rule for the counter. Fanuc has no program-part repeat of this shape. So the manuals neither confirm nor contradict the recommendation; the maintainer decides, and VM 3.6 should state the rule either way.
Evidence: SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D, Programmierhandbuch NC-Programmierung (06/2019, CNC-SW 4.92), p. 482 (When jumps and program-part repeats are mixed the blocks run purely sequentially; after a jump out of a repeat the control machines on until the programmed end of the part is found. The example jumps with GOTOF BEGIN2 from the region of BEGIN1 to BEGIN2, which with its ENDLABEL stands before N130 REPEAT BEGIN1 P=2.); same manual, p. 481 (A program-part repeat occupies a subprogram level; M17 or RET during a repeat aborts it and the program continues after the REPEAT line; after a level abort the program continues after the call of the repeat.); HEIDENHAIN TNC 640, Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung (892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10), p. 277-278 (Jumps need no closed regions ending with LBL 0 and do not take those return marks into account.).
Corrected: Softened "the one control that documents the case rules against the recommendation" to not settled, because the Siemens example jumps to a label before the REPEAT line, not past it, so the manual does not cover the NCX case.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

As recommended in NCX: a JUMP or JUMP=END to a target outside the label..REPEAT section ends the repeat, and a later arrival at the REPEAT starts it fresh with TIMES passes. Compilers must reproduce this. Fanuc uses its counter, cleared by every JUMP that leaves the section. When a JUMP leaves the section, the Heidenhain compiler writes the repeat as a Q-parameter counter loop instead of CALL LBL REP, because the TNC keeps REP counters as block state that is reset only by GOTO 0 or a new program selection. The Heidenhain reader writes a WARNING when an FN 9 jump leaves a CALL LBL REP part: "the control may keep the remaining REP count; NCX ends the repeat".
Basis: web + logical
Source: HEIDENHAIN TNC 406 user manual, program section repeats (https://www.manualsdir.com/manuals/798522/heidenhain-tnc-406.html?page=197). REP n/m shows the remaining repeats, the counters are reset only on a new program or GOTO 0, and GOTO > 0 resets none. Siemens PGH SW4.92 p. 481-482 does not cover a jump past REPEAT. Logical: the pass count then depends only on the current flow, which is predictable.
Differs from the recommendation: yes: adds the Heidenhain reader WARNING and the Heidenhain compiler's Q-counter form for sections that a jump leaves.
Confidence: low
Code impact: none in the VM (EndRepeatsOutside stays); P3-04 HeidenhainFlow warning; Heidenhain compiler REPEAT emission.

#### D215 File name in CALL="name"
Question: Language 4.9 calls an external program 'by file name (CALL="O9010")', VM 3.6 searches the working directory, and D74 gives NCX files the extension .ncx. No document says whether the name carries .ncx or a directory, or which file the VM opens. On main, Pipeline.LoadExternalProgram opens the file named exactly as written, and tries name + .ncx only when no such file exists. A Fanuc source O9010 without extension that stands next to its converted O9010.ncx is therefore parsed as NCX, and the call fails. The Fanuc reader already writes the bare name: FanucMacro.External writes 'O' plus four digits for M198. Controller-mapping 6 reads EXTCALL("path/name") as CALL="name", and heidenhain.md 1 says a program's name is its file name without .h. HeidenhainFlow.ReadProgramCall, however, keeps a CALL PGM name as written, extension and path included.
Recommendation: The name is the program's file name without directory and extension. The VM opens `<name>.ncx` in the working directory and no other file. This follows the 4.9 example, controller-mapping 6 and heidenhain.md 1. It also leaves every compiler the bare name it needs for M98 P9010, CALL PGM and EXTCALL. The missing-target ERROR of VM 3.6 names the file it looked for. Code changes: LoadExternalProgram tries only name + ".ncx". The Heidenhain reader drops a path and a .h or .H from CALL PGM, a P3-05 follow-up. VM 3.6 then reads 'loads `<name>.ncx` from the working directory'. For a CALL to find a converted program, convert must write that program as `<name>.ncx`. Where and under which name convert writes is D209 (main writes to stdout or to the --output file only). Alternative: a name that ends in .ncx is taken as written, any other name gets .ncx appended, and a file of the bare name is never read.
Where: Language 4.9 (CALL row); VM 3.6 (CALL bullet); controller-mapping 6 (CALL rows); architecture 10 (convert row, D209). Code: src/Ncx.Cli/Pipeline.cs LoadExternalProgram (TODO(question) at line 158); src/Ncx.Readers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainFlow.cs ReadProgramCall; tests/Ncx.Readers.Tests/Heidenhain/HeidenhainFlowTests.cs (a test to add: CALL PGM with a path and .h; the existing test reads CALL PGM DRILL); P3-04, P3-06, P5-02 (the call written per target).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. All three controls treat the bare name plus the target's own extension as the normal form, which supports the recommendation that the VM opens `<name>.ncx` in the working directory and no other file. The iTNC 530 manual says that if only the program name is entered the called program must be in the same directory as the calling one, that otherwise the full path is entered, and that a DIN/ISO program is called by appending the file type .I — so .H is the implicit default and the extension appears only when it is not the default. Siemens EXTCALL takes the name without the _N_ prefix with the extension MPF or SPF optional, and the path optional. Fanuc M198 calls by program or file number, with the file-name form written in angle brackets. What is left for the maintainer is the NCX rule itself, and one detail: the Heidenhain reader must not drop just any extension, because a `CALL PGM NAME.I` names a DIN/ISO program and dropping the .I loses that.
Evidence: HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Programmierung (NC-SW 340490-05, 2008), p. 269-270 (Section 10.4, calling any program as a subprogram: the full path name is entered; if only the program name is entered, the called program must be in the same directory as the calling program; if it is elsewhere, the full path is given, with the example TNC:\ZW35\SCHRUPP\PGM1.H; and to call a DIN/ISO program the file type .I is appended after the program name); SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D, Programmierhandbuch NC-Programmierung (06/2019, CNC-SW 4.92), p. 548 (EXTCALL takes a string of the form path plus program name; the path is optional and the program name is given without the _N_ prefix, with the file extension MPF or SPF optionally appended by an underscore or a dot. The three spellings of the same call are shown as "WELLE", "WELLE_SPF" and "WELLE.SPF"); SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D, Programmierhandbuch NC-Programmierung (06/2019, CNC-SW 4.92), p. 549 (With a relative path or none, the control searches from the preset external program directory first and then the user memory, stops at the first hit, and aborts the program at the EXTCALL line when nothing is found — a missing-target error at the call, as VM 3.6 has); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 1144-1145 (M198 takes either P with a program or file number, or the file name written immediately after M198 in angle brackets. File names may use upper- and lower-case letters, digits and the four symbols hyphen, plus, underscore and dot, with a length limit per device, and a name that is not registered raises alarm SR1079). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

The name is the file name without directory and extension; the VM opens `<name>.ncx` in the working directory and no other file; the missing-target ERROR names that file. LoadExternalProgram tries only name + ".ncx". The Heidenhain reader drops a path and a `.h`/`.H` from CALL PGM; any other extension (e.g. `.I`, a DIN/ISO program) keeps the block RAW with a WARNING.
Basis: manual
Source: iTNC 530: bare name = same directory, .H implicit, DIN/ISO called with .I; Siemens EXTCALL extension optional; Fanuc M198 by number.
Differs from the recommendation: no (narrows the Heidenhain extension drop)
Confidence: high
Code impact: Ncx.Core Pipeline.LoadExternalProgram; Heidenhain reader ReadProgramCall (P3-05).

#### D216 $SYS_POS_X and $SYS_MPOS_X under DIAMETER=ON
Question: D28 and language 4.2 have the VM store radii. The DIAMETER row says 'X values are diameters (the program says X=20, the axis stands at radius 10 ...)'. It 'affects exactly' the X words it lists: X, IX, the absolute CENTER:X and the X words of an AXIS=X cycle. A $SYS_ read is none of these words. VM 2.7 and VM 3.6 read the SYS_ names 'from the VM state' through the configuration's mapping, and that state holds the radius. Language 4.12 only reserves the names. Case: DIAMETER=ON, RAPID X=40 Z=0, VAR:Q1={$SYS_POS_X}. Q1 is 40 in the program's view and 20 in the store. The answer decides whether LINE X={$SYS_POS_X} leaves the axis where it is. With what the controls read (D240), it also decides whether readers and compilers convert Fanuc #5041 and #5021 and Siemens $AA_IW[X] and $AA_IM[X]. On main both names read the diameter: VariableStore.PositionOf doubles X under DIAMETER=ON.
Recommendation: Keep what the code does. Under DIAMETER=ON, $SYS_POS_X and $SYS_MPOS_X read the diameter, the value an X word of that frame would carry. A value read back into an X word, or into X with FRAME=MACHINE, therefore lands where it was: MotionRules.ValueOf halves every X word, the one of a FRAME=MACHINE block included. Under DIAMETER=OFF they read the radius. The DIAMETER row and the system variables paragraph of 4.12 name the X reads among what DIAMETER affects. This fits D137 as recommended there, where the machine-frame X values of a diameter axis are written as diameters, and D125 as recommended there, where every X word is a diameter. Whether #5041, #5021, $AA_IW[X] and $AA_IM[X] read diameters is a controller fact of its own (D240). Where one reads radii, its reader and compiler convert, since machine-config 7 carries no factor. Alternative: the radius, the unit of D28. A program under DIAMETER=ON then writes {2 * $SYS_POS_X} to reuse the value.
Where: Language 4.2 (DIAMETER row), 4.12 (system variables paragraph); VM 2.7 (system variables row), VM 3.6 ($SYS_* bullet); D60 log line; related D125, D137. Code: src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/State/VariableStore.cs PositionOf (TODO(question) at line 260); tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/VirtualMachine/InterpretedExpressionTests.cs SystemVariable_PositionOfXUnderDiameterOn_ReadsTheDiameter; machine-config 7; P3-06, P5-01 and P5-02 for the controller conversion.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, corrected 2026-10-26 after the manual audit, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals settle the work-frame half, and the machine-frame half is now partly settled. Siemens states the recommended behaviour outright for the work frame: with DIAMON or DIAM90 the facing-axis actual values are always shown as diameters, and that expressly holds for reading actual values in the workpiece coordinate system with MEAS, MEAW, $P_EP[X] and $AA_IW[X]; so $SYS_POS_X reading the diameter matches the control that documents it, and $AA_IW[X] needs no conversion. For the machine frame the function manual lists the data that stay radius values on a facing axis whatever DIAMON says, among them the display data in the machine coordinate system, and MD20360 bits 6 and 7 are what switch actual values and their display to diameter. So on a standard Siemens setup a machine-frame value of a facing axis is a radius, and $AA_IM[X] very likely reads a radius. That is an inference: the page names display data, not the variable, and the variable list gives no unit beyond a linear position. One page points the other way: PRESETONS, which sets a machine-frame actual value, takes an active DIAMON into account. If $AA_IM reads a radius, $SYS_MPOS_X can still read the diameter as recommended, but the Siemens reader and compiler need a factor 2 for $AA_IM[X] under DIAMETER=ON unless MD20360 is set; that factor is D240's. Fanuc says nothing either way: #5021 and #5041 are defined only as the current position in the machine and in the workpiece coordinate system, and the diameter table does not mention the macro position variables. So the proposal now supports the recommendation, with a conversion for $AA_IM. Left for the maintainer: whether $SYS_MPOS_X follows $SYS_POS_X on that basis, and whether the Fanuc reader and compiler must convert #5021/#5041, which needs a test on the machine.
Evidence: SINUMERIK 840D sl/828D Programmierhandbuch Grundlagen (03/2013), p. 169-170, section 8.3.6 (Note on p. 169: with DIAMON or DIAM90 the actual values of the facing axis are always shown as diameters, also when read in the WCS with MEAS, MEAW, $P_EP[x] and $AA_IW[x]. The list on p. 170 names the WCS display, JOG increments, end positions with I, J, K under AC, and actual values read in the WCS; no machine-coordinate read.); SINUMERIK 840D sl/828D Funktionshandbuch Grundfunktionen (2012), p. 900-901 (diameter data under DIAMON and DIAM90, actual values read in the WCS: $AA_MW, $P_EP, $AA_IW.); same manual, p. 901-902 ("Fest Radius-bezogene Daten": for facing axes always radius are offsets and frames, limits, feed and the display data in the machine coordinate system.); same manual, p. 902-903 (MD20360 bit 6: actual values of the facing axis as diameter; bit 7: their display as diameter.); SINUMERIK 840D sl Programmierung BS.000504, p. 310-311 (PRESETONS sets a new actual value in the machine coordinate system; an active DIAMON is taken into account.); SINUMERIK 840D sl Listenhandbuch Systemvariable (SW 4.5, 2012), p. 477 ($AA_IW[ax], setpoint in the WCS) and 479 ($AA_IM[ax], setpoint in the MCS; neither entry mentions diameter or radius.); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-MODEL B Operator's Manual B-64484EN, p. 488-489 (position information #5001 to #5080: #5021ff [#_ABSMT] current position in the machine coordinate system, #5041ff [#_ABSOT] in the workpiece coordinate system; no diameter or radius column.); FANUC B-64484EN, p. 230-231, Table 8.4 (a) (diameter values under diameter programming; the macro position variables are not listed.).
Corrected: Replaced "the machine-frame read is not in that list, so the Siemens rule does not reach it": Grundfunktionen p. 901-902 makes machine-frame data of a facing axis radius values by default, so $AA_IM[X] likely needs a factor 2, with PRESETONS (BS.000504 p. 310-311) noted as a counter-hint. The proposal now supports the recommendation instead of only warning; the Fanuc pages now cite the English B-64484EN.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Siemens: $AA_IW[X] needs no conversion; $AA_IM[X] reads a radius on a standard setup, so the Siemens reader/compiler apply factor 2 under DIAMETER=ON unless the machine sets MD20360 bits 6/7 (D240). Fanuc #5021/#5041: no conversion until a machine test says otherwise; record as open in D240.

Source: Siemens Grundfunktionen p. 901-902 (machine-frame data radius on facing axis; MD20360 bits 6/7); $AA_IW under DIAMON reads diameter. Fanuc unsettled by manuals and web (search found nothing definitive).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: medium

#### D217 What the two readings of 2.5D_FRAESEN must share (M6)
Question: Several documents require 2.5D_FRAESEN to read from both sources to the same canonical text: phases.md row 3, the phase-3 status line and exit checklist, the acceptance paragraph of architecture 11 (line 1100) and sources/README.md. The M4 row of architecture 12 also wants the Fanuc reading to equal the example, and P3-02 and P3-05 want each reading to equal the example block for block. But recorded rules give the two readings different blocks: the example's note 2 (offsets where G43 H and D stand, D7) and note 4 (HOME for G28, against the M91 moves); controller-mapping 1 with D92 (a Fanuc comment-only line is trivia) against P3-01 (a Klartext * - line is SECTION); heidenhain 7 rule 2 (TOOL CALL 1 Z S1592 puts RPM on the TOOL block) against fanuc 9 rule 2 (S belongs to its M3, in N60); the R0 of Klartext block 9 against the Fanuc G40, which stands in the header; NUMBER=1, which only O0001 carries (language 4.1, controller-mapping 1: Klartext has no program number); and BLK FORM, which heidenhain 1 and 7 rule 9 make RAW with a WARNING while the example keeps a comment line. Today the Fanuc reader writes the example's blocks with these differences: no SECTION; TOOL=1 alone; SPINDLE=CW RPM=1592; RAPID X=50.4 Y=-7.025 without COMP=OFF; RAPID Z=2 OFFSET:LEN=1; LINE Y=2 OFFSET:RAD=1 COMP=LEFT; HOME Z and HOME X Y. It reports no diagnostics (FanucReaderTests.s_fanucReading). The Heidenhain reader writes the example's blocks except PROGRAM=BEGIN without NUMBER and two RAW:HEIDENHAIN blocks for BLK FORM after ORIGIN=1. It reports WARNINGs for the two RAW blocks and RDR010 for the missing M30 (HeidenhainReaderTests.s_heidenhainReading). The two readings therefore differ in thirteen blocks: eight are written differently, and five stand only in the Heidenhain reading (three SECTION blocks, two RAW blocks). Each difference follows a recorded rule, and one common text would need D7 and D92 reopened. No document says whether the phase 3 criterion is met.
Recommendation: Amend the criterion, not the readers. M6 means that each reader reproduces the example except the differences the example's notes list, each tied to its rule, and that both readings format to themselves and check without ERROR. The following places read 'into the blocks of examples/2.5D_FRAESEN.ncx, except the reader differences its notes list': phases.md row 3, architecture 11 (line 1100), the M4 row of architecture 12, the status line and exit checklist of the phase-3 file, sources/README.md, and the acceptance of P3-02, P3-05 and P3-07. The example stays as it is, NUMBER=1 included, and its notes become the complete list, each difference with its rule: offsets (note 2, D7); RPM with TOOL CALL S (heidenhain 7 rule 2) against RPM with M3 (fanuc 9 rule 2), added to note 2; SECTION from * - against trivia from a Fanuc comment line (controller-mapping 1, D92); COMP=OFF from R0 against G40 in the Fanuc header; HOME against the M91 moves (note 4); NUMBER only from O0001; and BLK FORM, RAW:HEIDENHAIN in the Heidenhain reading, which the example leaves out so that it still compiles to Fanuc (language 4.1, RAW row). The line comments on example lines 9, 10 and 15 stop attributing those blocks to the Fanuc source, and the comment of line 7 points to the BLK FORM note. P3-06 checks the Fanuc output through its Fanuc-to-NCX-to-Fanuc round trip instead of compiling the example itself. The TODO(question) markers of the two acceptance tests become comments citing the notes. No reader changes. Reason: every difference follows a recorded decision or a documented reader rule, and the example already accepts two of them. Making the readers converge would move offset words out of their source block, against D7, or turn a Fanuc comment line into a SECTION word, against D92. The two acceptance tests already implement exactly these lists. Alternative 1: keep one expected text and give the P3-07 comparer a normalization for these differences: SECTION against trivia; OFFSET and RPM moved to the TOOL block; a COMP=OFF that only repeats the state, dropped; HOME against an M91 move to the reference point. That puts reader rules into the comparer. Alternative 2: drop NUMBER=1 from the example, so the Heidenhain header matches exactly and the Fanuc reading lists NUMBER instead.
Where: docs/plan/phases.md row 3; docs/implementation/13-phase-3-readers-compilers.md (status line, P3-02, P3-05, P3-06 and P3-07 acceptance, exit checklist); docs/architecture/architecture.md (acceptance paragraph at line 1100, M4 and M6 rows of section 12); docs/spec/examples/sources/README.md (first paragraph); docs/spec/examples/2.5D_FRAESEN.ncx (first comment, line comments on lines 7, 9, 10 and 15, notes 2 to 4, new notes); the 'Done when' of the P3-02 and P3-05 task files; tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Examples/FanucReaderTests.cs s_fanucReading (TODO(question) at line 28) and HeidenhainReaderTests.cs s_heidenhainReading (TODO(question) at line 29).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals cannot decide the criterion, which is an NCX process question, but they do confirm that most of the thirteen differences are genuine language differences and not reader defects, which is the load-bearing part of the recommendation. Heidenhain enters the spindle speed in the TOOL CALL block, so `TOOL CALL 1 Z S1592` really is where the RPM belongs; a Klartext program is identified by its file name in BEGIN PGM, with no program number on any of the pages that open a program; radius compensation is a word of the motion block (RL, RR, R0), not a modal G code in a header, so the R0 of Klartext block 9 against the Fanuc G40 is a real language difference; and BLK FORM is the blank definition the TNC needs only for the graphic simulation, which the dialogue lets you cancel outright — so leaving it out of the example changes nothing about the machining and keeping it RAW in the Heidenhain reading is right. On HOME the manuals are weaker than the draft claims: M91 is a per-block machine-datum reference, and section 7.3 names no command that sends a named axis to a reference point, but the manual does have M140 MB MAX, a tool-axis retract to the edge of the traverse range, so an M91 move is the only documented form for HOME X Y rather than something the control forces outright. Making the two readings converge would still mean writing something no control says, which is the reason to amend M6 rather than the readers.
Evidence: HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Programmierung (NC-SW 340490-05, 2008), p. 161 (Section 5.1: the spindle speed S in rpm is entered in a TOOL CALL block, and a later speed change is again a TOOL CALL block. The speed has no block of its own on a TNC, unlike a Fanuc S beside its M3); HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Programmierung (NC-SW 340490-05, 2008), p. 99, 100, 101 (Opening a program asks for a file name (the prompt shows DATEI-NAME = ALT.H) and a unit, and the TNC generates the BEGIN and END blocks with that name; no program number appears. The blank definition BLK FORM is needed only to test the program graphically, and the dialogue can be cancelled with DEL if no blank is wanted); HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Zyklenprogrammierung (670 388-12, NC-SW 340490-07), p. 53 (The list of what must be programmed before a cycle call names BLK FORM with the qualification "zur grafischen Darstellung (nur für Testgrafik erforderlich)", while the tool call, the spindle direction and the cycle definition are unqualified); HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Programmierung (NC-SW 340490-05, 2008), p. 349, 350 (Section 7.3: M91 in a positioning block makes that block's coordinates refer to the machine datum, M92 to a second machine reference point, and both are effective only in the block in which they stand, at the block start. The section names no command that sends an axis to a reference point); HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Programmierung (NC-SW 340490-05, 2008), p. 362 (Section 7.4, "Rückzug von der Kontur in Werkzeugachsen-Richtung: M140": M140 MB retracts a programmed distance along the tool axis, and the softkey MB MAX retracts to the edge of the traverse range, at rapid unless a feed is given. This is the machine-referenced retract the library does have; it is already the Heidenhain mapping of the NCX RETRACT verb in the recorded D83); HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Programmierung (NC-SW 340490-05, 2008), p. 188 (Radius compensation on a TNC is a word of the motion block itself: the block for a tool movement contains RL or RR for compensation, R+ or R- for an axis-parallel move, and R0 for none. It is not a modal G code standing in a header, as the Fanuc G40 of the example is). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Amend the criterion, not the readers: each reader reproduces examples/2.5D_FRAESEN.ncx except the differences its notes list, each tied to its rule, and both readings format to themselves and check without ERROR. Update phases.md row 3, architecture 11 and 12 (M4), the phase-3 status line and checklist, sources/README.md, P3-02/P3-05/P3-07 acceptance; complete the notes (offsets D7, RPM placement, SECTION vs trivia, R0 vs G40, HOME vs M91, NUMBER, BLK FORM RAW). P3-06 checks Fanuc output by round trip.
Basis: manual
Source: TNC 640 Klartext: S in TOOL CALL, no program number, RL/RR/R0 in the motion block, BLK FORM only for simulation. The differences are genuine language differences, not reader defects.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none (acceptance-test TODO markers become comments).

#### D218 Where the F of a Fanuc cycle block stands as the program feed
Question: The F of a Fanuc G8x block is the cycle feed and also the control's modal F. In BOHREN.fanuc.nc, G73 and G83 have no F and drill at the 565 of N90 G81, and N330 G1 Z3.8 moves at it too. D29 and language 4.7 keep CYCLE_F apart ('the program's F is never touched by a cycle definition'). The Fanuc cell of controller-mapping 5 (CYCLE_F row) says the cycle's feed never touches the modal F, which is not what the control does. No document says where the reader writes the F that the control carries on. The Siemens cell ('turns into CYCLE_F and restores afterwards') leaves this open too. Main writes F on the next LINE or ARC that moves with it (Expected/BOHREN.ncx line 43: LINE Z=3.8 F=565; FanucMotion.AddModalFeed).
Recommendation: Keep main's behaviour, which follows design rule 4 (a reader fills in what the source controller implies). When a new CYCLE block has no F, the reader writes the control's feed as CYCLE_F (language 4.7: a new CYCLE replaces all parameters). The reader writes F on the first feed motion afterwards whose NCX F differs from the control's, and never in the CYCLE block (D29). The Siemens reader handles the F before an MCALL the same way, and controller-mapping 5 says so in place of 'restores afterwards'. The Fanuc compiler (P3-06) counts a G8x F as the control's feed and writes F on the next G1 only where the NCX F differs, which gives back N330 without F. Alternative: write F=565 in the CYCLE block next to CYCLE_F. That states the change where the control makes it, but it puts F in a cycle definition, against D29.
Where: controller-mapping 5 (CYCLE_F row, Fanuc and Siemens cells); fanuc 6 or 9 rule 5; src/Ncx.Readers/Fanuc/FanucMotion.cs AddModalFeed (TODO(question) at lines 454-455); FanucCycles.Start and ReadDrilling (ControlFeed); tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Expected/BOHREN.ncx line 43; P3-06 FanucMotion; P5-01.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, corrected 2026-10-26 after the manual audit, not confirmed by the maintainer: Keep main's behaviour; the manuals settle the point. On Fanuc there is one modal feed: the F of G01 stays in effect until a new value is specified; the F_ of a drilling cycle is the cutting feedrate, the same address; drilling data stay in force until changed or cancelled; and the macro variables carry one modal F (#4109, the current block #4309). G80 clears R, Z and the other drilling data, but the feedrate given at F is retained after the drilling cycle is cancelled, as both the 30i-B turning manual and the Nakamura WY-250L manual state. So the F written on a cycle block is the control's feed afterwards, after G80 too: the reader writes it on the first following feed motion whose NCX F differs (BOHREN.ncx line 43) and never in the CYCLE block, and the Fanuc compiler gives back N330 without an F. The Fanuc cell of controller-mapping 5 ('the cycle's own feed never touches the modal F of the program') does not describe the control and should say instead that the cycle takes the control's feed and the reader carries it on the next feed motion.
Evidence: FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 76 (G01: the feedrate specified in F is effective until a new value is specified and need not be given in each block); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual Milling (B-64484EN-2), p. 58 (drilling data are retained until modified or cancelled; only modifications are specified while cycles run), p. 63 (G76 format: F_ the cutting feedrate) and p. 84 (G80: point R, point Z and the other drilling data are cleared; the feedrate is not named); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual Turning (B-64484EN-1), p. 93 (the feedrate specified at F is retained also after the drilling cycle is cancelled); Nakamura-Tome Programming Manual WY-250L (4810004EEE, 2020), p. 283 (the designated feedrate is retained if the drilling cycle is cancelled); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 458-460 (modal information #4109 [#_BUFF], the F code, and #4309 for the current block); FANUC 21i-TB Operator's Manual (B-63604EN-01), p. 359-361 (the B-axis operation program counts F codes and the P, Q and F codes of a canned cycle among its own modal data, apart from the normal program).
Corrected: the turning-manual page (EN-1 p. 93) and the Nakamura page (p. 283) settle that the F stays in force after G80, which the earlier answer had left open from the G80 page alone; the German citations are replaced by the English editions.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main. The F of a G8x block is the control's modal feed, and it stays in force after G80. If a new CYCLE block has no F, the reader writes the control's feed as CYCLE_F. It writes F on the first later feed motion whose NCX F differs, never in the CYCLE block (D29). The Fanuc compiler counts a G8x F as the modal feed and writes F on the next G1 only where it differs (N330 comes back without F). Correct the Fanuc cell of controller-mapping 5: the cycle takes the control's feed, and the reader carries it on the next feed motion. The Siemens MCALL cell says the same in place of 'restores afterwards'.
Basis: manual
Source: FANUC B-64484EN p. 76, 458-460; B-64484EN-2 p. 58, 84; B-64484EN-1 p. 93 (F kept after cancel); Nakamura WY-250L 4810004EEE p. 283 (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none in code (FanucMotion.AddModalFeed stays); docs: controller-mapping 5, fanuc 6/9.
