#### D223 Channel of a Fanuc file without a Nakamura path suffix
Question: Controller-mapping 7 (CHANNEL row) takes the path 'from the file name or a TOML rule', but machine-config names no such rule. The only documented file-name form is Nakamura's: O1000 is path 1, O1000.P-2 is path 2 (fanuc 1). Language 4.1 makes CHANNEL a header word with default 1, and language 4.14 and D15 let the job bind files to channels. The repository samples are named .path1.nc and .path2.nc, so path 2 reads without CHANNEL and runs on channel 1. There its M96 ([spindle_sync] channel = 2) is a word bound to another channel, which a single-channel compile reports as an ERROR (VM 3.8 rule 2a, D56). D155's recommendation, which drops the states of a table bound to another channel, needs the channel as well. Mori Seiki HEAD 1 and HEAD 2 programs have no documented name form at all. FanucReader.ChannelOfFile writes CHANNEL=n only for a .P-n file on a machine of the builder nakamura.
Recommendation: Keep the suffix rule as coded and add an explicit option. The reader writes CHANNEL=n for the Nakamura suffix .P-n, with or without an extension, on a machine of the builder nakamura. It also writes CHANNEL=n for `ncx convert --channel n` on any file, and the option wins over the suffix. Otherwise it writes no CHANNEL, and the program runs on channel 1 (language 4.1) unless a job names another (D15). Controller-mapping 7 replaces 'or a TOML rule' with this rule. Rename the samples to the documented form, NAKAMURA_WY250L_O1000.nc and NAKAMURA_WY250L_O1000.P-2.nc, so that path 2 reads CHANNEL=2. These are the names the files had when rationale B2 cited them (O1000.NC, O1000.P-2). Reason: the option covers the Mori Seiki, whose T words depend on the holder of the channel (D219), without a TOML rule that nobody has specified. Alternative: no option. Files without the suffix are converted for channel 1, and only a job binds them to another channel.
Where: controller-mapping 7 (CHANNEL row); fanuc 1; architecture 10 (ncx convert row of the CLI table) and 12 (M9 row, which names the files); docs/spec/examples/sources/NAKAMURA_WY250L_O1000.path1.nc and .path2.nc (file names); docs/spec/examples/sources/README.md; controller-mapping 8 (paragraph after the table); docs/controllers/sample-corpus.md (table row); tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Examples/FanucReaderTests.cs (InlineData names), ConvertExampleTests.cs and tests/Ncx.Config.Tests/Templates/TemplateNakamuraLinesTests.cs; src/Ncx.Readers/Fanuc/FanucReader.cs ChannelOfFile (TODO(question) at line 202); src/Ncx.Readers/ReadOptions.cs; the convert command in src/Ncx.Cli/Commands.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, corrected 2026-10-26 after the manual audit, not confirmed by the maintainer: The `.P-n` suffix is Fanuc's own channel convention, not a Nakamura rule. With bit 0 (MDP) of parameter 138 set, the control names the part program of path 1 without an extension and that of path n with `.P-n` (O0001, O0001.P-2 ... O0001.P10), both for program input and output and for the external subprogram call M198 (O0123.P-2); the suffix is not added when a file name is given explicitly. Nakamura's list of program file names on the memory card follows the same form (O△△△△ for the first turret, .P-2 and .P-3 for the others, the turret-to-number mapping depending on the machine type). So reading `.P-n` as CHANNEL=n rests on a control convention, and restricting it to builder `nakamura`, as the Recommendation does, has no basis in the manuals: the rule can apply to any Fanuc machine. A file without a suffix still needs `ncx convert --channel n` or a job binding, since nothing in a Fanuc file names the channel and the paths keep separate program memories that routinely hold the same O number (both Nakamura turrets run `O1000`). Channel 1 is written plain in the program tables; `.P-1` occurs only for a data file whose default name has no extension, so the reader must still accept `.P-1` and must not read it as "no channel".
Evidence: FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 1424-1425 (§8.8: with 138#0 (MDP) = 1 the path number is added to the extension of default file names; Tables 8.8 (c) and (d): the part program of path 1 has no extension, paths 2 to 10 get .P-2 to .P10, O0001 and O0001.P-2; not applied when a file name is specified; offset data TOOLOFST.TXT for path 1 and TOOLOFST.P-2 for path 2); p. 1146-1147 (Tables 4.5 (b) and (c): with MDP = 1, M198 P0123 calls O0123 on path 1 and O0123.P-2 on path 2); p. 2023 (storage file names with MDP = 1: TOOLOFST.P-1 for path 1, TOOLOFST.P-2 for path 2); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch 1 (4810004ECL-1), p. 152-153 (list of program file names on the memory card per machine and turret: O△△△△, O△△△△.P-2, O△△△△.P-3); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch 1 (4810004ECL-1), p. 25 (§2-4-6: each unit's program is stored in its own unit's memory, and the same program may serve both units); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch (Walter Meier), Fanuc 0iTF/31iB/32iA, p. 110-111 (two-channel example: the upper and the lower turret program are both numbered O1000).
Corrected: dropped "the only documented program-name table is a builder's"; Fanuc's own manual gives the .P-n tables for part programs and M198 under parameter 138#0 (EN p. 1146-1147, p. 1424-1425), so the proposal now rejects the Recommendation's restriction to builder nakamura. The German parameter-manual and operator's-manual citations are replaced by the English pages.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

The Fanuc reader writes CHANNEL=n for a file whose name ends in `.P-n` (n = 1..10, with or without a further extension) on any Fanuc machine, without the nakamura restriction. `.P-1` is read as CHANNEL=1, not as "no channel". If the machine file has fewer channels than n, the result is an ERROR. `ncx convert --channel n` sets CHANNEL=n on any file and wins over the suffix. Without either, no CHANNEL is written (channel 1 per language 4.1, unless a job binds it, D15). Controller-mapping 7 replaces "or a TOML rule" with this rule. The samples are renamed to NAKAMURA_WY250L_O1000.nc and NAKAMURA_WY250L_O1000.P-2.nc.
Basis: manual
Source: FANUC 30i-B B-64484EN, connector p. 1424-1425 (138#0 MDP: path 1 without an extension, path n `.P-n`) and p. 1146-1147 (M198), p. 2023 (`.P-1` for data files). Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch 1 p. 152-153.
Differs from the recommendation: yes: the builder restriction is dropped, `.P-1` is accepted, and a suffix beyond the channel count is an ERROR.
Confidence: high
Code impact: FanucReader.ChannelOfFile; ReadOptions and the convert command (--channel); sample renames and the tests that name them.

#### D224 CYCLE=OFF after a one-shot cycle
Question: machine-config 6 makes an entry with modal = false a native block that 'runs once where it stands' (Fanuc G70..G76), and controller-mapping 5 has a direct Siemens CYCLE81(...) call 'once at the current position'. In NCX every cycle stays active until CYCLE=OFF, the next CYCLE, TOOL or PROGRAM=END (language 4.7, VM 2.6, 4), and a TOOL while a cycle is active is a WARNING (VM 3.5, 5). No document says whether the reader closes such a cycle. Main writes `CYCLE=<entry> CONTOUR=<name>` and one bare CYCLE_CALL, without CYCLE=OFF (FanucCycles.ReadContourCycle). So the next tool change after a G71 gets the WARNING, and trace shows ROUGH_TURN active where the control has no cycle.
Recommendation: The reader writes CYCLE=OFF directly after the CYCLE_CALL of a one-shot entry, and the Siemens reader does the same after a direct cycle call. This matches the Heidenhain reader, which emits CYCLE=OFF where the source has no cancel word (controller-mapping 5, CYCLE=OFF row). A compiler writes nothing for a CYCLE=OFF that ends a one-shot cycle (no G80 after G70..G76), because it only cancels what the target keeps active. The VM stays as it is, so an NCX cycle means the same on every machine: a second CYCLE_CALL of ROUGH_TURN compiles to a second G71. Alternative: the VM ends a cycle whose catalog entry has modal = false after its CYCLE_CALL. That would give the same text different meanings on machines whose catalogs differ. It also needs the machine's catalog in the VM, which D114 (open) would add for other reasons.
Where: machine-config 6 (modal); controller-mapping 5 (CYCLE_CALL and CYCLE=OFF rows, Fanuc and Siemens cells); language 4.7.1; src/Ncx.Readers/Fanuc/FanucCycles.cs ReadContourCycle (TODO(question) at lines 240-243); P3-06 FanucCycles (no G80 for it); P5-01 Siemens reader.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals settle the premise, not the NCX form. A Fanuc G70..G76 is a group-00 code, and such a code is "nur in dem Satz wirksam, in dem er spezifiziert ist": it is over at the end of its own block and there is no cancel word for it (G80 belongs to group 10 and ends the drilling canned cycles only). On Siemens, modality is the separate `MCALL <Zyklus>`, which does not call at once but after every traverse block until a bare `MCALL` switches it off, so a plain `CYCLE81(...)` call runs where it stands. The recommendation's rule — reader writes `CYCLE=OFF` right after the `CYCLE_CALL` of a `modal = false` entry, compiler writes nothing for it — therefore matches both controls; where the boundary is drawn (reader vs VM) is still NCX's choice.
Evidence: FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 62-63 (Chapter 3 splits G codes into one-shot codes, effective only in the block where they stand, and modal codes that stay effective until another code of the same group appears; note 2 adds that G codes other than G10 and G11 are one-shot); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 70-71, table 3.2 (b) (The lathe G-code list puts G70 to G76 (finishing, stock removal, pattern repeat, peck drilling, grooving, threading) in group 00, while G80 sits in group 10 as the end of the drilling canned cycles); SINUMERIK ONE Programmierhandbuch NC-Programmierung, SW 6.14, p. PDF 527-528 (section 3.2.3.4) ("Modaler Unterprogrammaufruf (MCALL)": with MCALL <ProgName> the subprogram is not called at once, the call happens automatically after every traverse block with path motion from then on; MCALL without a program name switches the function off, and only the last MCALL is effective); SINUMERIK 840D Zyklen, Programmierhandbuch (Index edition LY4401.10092, 2004), p. 32-33 (A worked example writes MCALL CYCLE82(...) commented "modaler Bohrzyklusaufruf" and later a bare MCALL commented "modalen Aufruf abwählen"). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

The reader writes CYCLE=OFF directly after the CYCLE_CALL of a catalog entry with modal = false (Fanuc G70..G76). The Siemens reader does the same after a plain CYCLEnn(...) call; only MCALL is modal. A compiler writes nothing for a CYCLE=OFF that ends a one-shot cycle. The VM stays unchanged.
Basis: manual
Source: FANUC B-64484EN p. 62-63, 70-71 (G70..G76 are group 00 and one-shot; G80 is group 10); SINUMERIK ONE NC-Programmierung SW 6.14 p. 527-528 (MCALL) (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: FanucCycles.ReadContourCycle and the Siemens cycle reader emit CYCLE=OFF; compilers suppress G80 for it.

#### D225 Reading a subprogram whose blocks depend on its callers
Question: VM 3.9 walks a subprogram at every CALL with that caller's state, but a reader reads it once and writes one SUB. No document says what a reader writes for a block whose meaning depends on the caller. There are three cases: the callers leave different states, a call stands after the subprogram, or nothing in the file calls it. The Fanuc cases are the verb of X10., G90/G91, an active G81, the spindle of a bare S, and the chain a G52 or G69 acts on. The Heidenhain cases are the CC pole of a C, the cycle an M99 calls, and the plane of an arc. Architecture 7 and controller-mapping 2 say only that the source-side state resolves what the controller leaves implicit, and heidenhain 7 rule 1 names the state the Klartext reader keeps (modal feed, compensation, cycle definition, CC pole).
Recommendation: Keep what both readers do on main, and write it down once. The reader starts a subprogram from the facts that every call of the file agrees on, fact by fact, including the passes of a CALL with TIMES. A fact is unknown in three cases: the calls disagree on it, a call the reader has not reached yet leaves it open, or no call fixes it (a subprogram nothing calls). A block whose NCX words depend on an unknown fact stays RAW with its WARNING (D5), and a bare M6 stays a bare TOOL (D27, D47). A caller continues with the facts the subprogram may change marked unknown. Reasons: this is the reader side of D99, which writes each SUB once and makes walks that would write different lines an ERROR. One SUB text must mean the same at every call, and RAW keeps the source. A call after its subprogram is rare, since controller-mapping 1 places Fanuc and Klartext subprograms after the caller's M30. The cost: a RAW block compiles only to its own family (D5, VM 5), so such a subprogram does not convert to the other family. Alternatives: (a) Start the subprogram from the state of its first call. That gives fewer RAW blocks, but the text is wrong for every other caller and nothing reports it. (b) Write one SUB per distinct entry state (NAME=100, NAME=100_2, each CALL naming its copy). There is no RAW and every call is right, but the NCX file and the compiled program have sections the source does not have.
Where: controller-mapping 6 (a paragraph after the M99 paragraph) and architecture 7 (source-side state); fanuc 9 (new rule); heidenhain 7 rules 1 and 3. Code: src/Ncx.Readers/Fanuc/FanucReader.cs BeginSection (TODO(question) at line 256), FanucCalls.EntryOf, FanucCallerState (Agreed, After), FanucUnknowns; src/Ncx.Readers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainCalls.cs Enter (TODO(question) at line 30); the FanucSubprogramTests.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals bear on the premise only. A Fanuc modal G stays effective "bis ein anderer G-Code derselben Gruppe programmiert wird", and the subprogram chapter describes M98/M99 purely as call and return — call forms, nesting depth, the P return, and the note that neither M98 nor M99 sends a code or strobe signal — with nothing said to be initialised on entry or restored on return. A subprogram is therefore executed in whatever state the caller left, which is exactly why one SUB text can mean different things at different calls. No manual says what a translator should write for such a block, so the reader rule (start from the facts every call agrees on, keep a block that depends on an unknown fact as RAW with its WARNING) remains an NCX choice, and the recommendation is consistent with the controls.
Evidence: FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 62 (A modal G code stays effective until another G code of the same group is programmed; the rule is stated for the program as a whole, with no exception for subprograms); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 329-331, section 13.3 (The subprogram section gives only the call forms M98 P/L, the file-name form, ten levels of nesting and the return M99 (with M99 P for a return to another block), and notes that neither M98 nor M99 sends a code or strobe signal to the machine; nothing is said to be initialised on entry or restored on return); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch Band 1, 4810004ECL-1, p. PDF 25 (section 2-4-6) (Context only: the two units have separate program memories and the same program text may be loaded into both, so one body of blocks is expected to run under two different machine contexts. It is two copies of a program, not one subprogram entered from several callers, so it illustrates the problem rather than evidencing the inheritance rule). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main. A subprogram starts from the facts that every call agrees on, fact by fact, TIMES passes included. A fact is unknown when calls disagree, when a call is not reached yet, or when nothing calls the subprogram. A block that depends on an unknown fact stays RAW with its WARNING (D5), and a bare M6 stays a bare TOOL. After the call, the caller continues with the facts the subprogram may change marked unknown.
Basis: manual (premise) + logical
Source: FANUC B-64484EN p. 62, 329-331 (M98/M99 initialise and restore nothing, so the subprogram inherits the caller's state). Writing one SUB text that means the same at every call is the only form consistent with D99.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none (document in controller-mapping 6, fanuc 9, heidenhain 7).

#### D229 Encoding of a controller program
Question: Language 3 gives UTF-8 for NCX files only. No document gives the encoding of a Fanuc, Heidenhain or Siemens source. fanuc.md 1 says only that 'some controls restrict the character set to ASCII capitals', and the comment_charset of machine-config 2 applies to the compiler's output. Older controls and editors write ISO 8859-1 or Windows-1252 umlauts in comments. The maintainer's corpus comes from German and Swiss shops of every family (sample-corpus 2). It holds 415 files in the first pass, with 151 Heidenhain programs from Hermle, Fehlmann and DMU, and 62 Siemens programs in the second pass with MSG(...) texts before every operation. ConvertCommand reads strict UTF-8. So a single Latin-1 comment such as (ÄNDERUNG) makes the whole program CLI002, exit 2, and convert reads nothing of it. The same holds for the corpus test that P3-02c runs through the command.
Recommendation: Read the program as UTF-8 when its bytes are valid UTF-8, skipping a byte order mark. Otherwise read it as Windows-1252 and report a WARNING that names the code page assumed. The NCX text is written in UTF-8, as language 3 requires, and the compiler's output stays governed by comment_charset. Reason: an ASCII program reads the same either way, and bytes that are not valid UTF-8 reliably mark a single-byte code page. Windows-1252 holds every ISO 8859-1 letter, and nothing is assumed silently. Alternative: a machine-file key (for example [format] encoding, default UTF-8) that names the code page of the control's files, for the reader and the compiler alike. It is explicit, but a file saved by another editor still stops with CLI002.
Where: Language 3 (Encoding row) or controller-mapping 1; architecture 10 (convert row); machine-config 2 (for the alternative); P3-07 (the batch run over the corpus). Code: src/Ncx.Cli/Commands/ConvertCommand.cs Run (TODO(question) at line 95) and InputFile.cs; tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Cli/ConvertCommandTests.cs Convert_ProgramThatIsNoUtf8_ExitsTwoWithCli002.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals do not give the byte encoding of a program file, so the UTF-8-then-Windows-1252 fallback stays an NCXchange choice. What they do establish bounds the problem, and now for all three families. A Fanuc control reads a program against a fixed ISO/EIA code table and silently drops any code that is not in it, comments included. A Siemens 840D sl either converts a character outside the ASCII set into a blank or raises alarm 12080, according to a machine datum. Heidenhain names no encoding for .h files; it only fixes the allowed characters for file names and tool names and states that an FN 16 format file must not be UTF-8. Together: the control side is a single-byte, largely ASCII world, so a Latin-1 umlaut never reaches the control and only ever comes from an editor or CAM system on the PC side — which is evidence for reading defensively, not for Windows-1252 being the right guess.
Evidence: FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 322 (When a program is read in for memory operation, comment sections are not ignored but read in with it; codes not listed in the code table of Appendix A are "überlesen und nicht gespeichert". The control's own character set is the ISO/EIA table, and anything outside it is discarded on read-in); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 322-323 (The EOB / % restriction the earlier pass put on the previous page is here, one page later: "Folgende Codes können im Kommentarabschnitt nicht verwendet werden: - EOB - % (ER für EIA)". Page slip corrected); SINUMERIK 840D sl Parameter / Alarme (BS.000503-DE-000-00), p. 169 (Alarm 12080 "Syntaxfehler bei Text": one cause is the use of Unicode characters, recognizable by characters outside the ASCII set in the alarm text, and MD 10280 $MN_PROG_FUNCTION_MASK bit 3 decides whether a character outside the ASCII set is turned into a blank or raises the alarm. The Siemens parser is ASCII; a non-ASCII byte in a program is either swallowed or fatal); Heidenhain TNC 640 — Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung (892903-18, 10/2019), p. 293 (In the FN 16: F-PRINT notes: "Wenn Sie FN 16 verwenden, dann darf die Datei nicht UTF-8 kodiert sein." The only explicit encoding statement in the Heidenhain books, and it points away from UTF-8 on the control side. Verified); Heidenhain iTNC 530 — Benutzer-Handbuch HEIDENHAIN-Klartext-Dialog (NC-SW 606420-01, 2010), p. 166 (The tool table's NAME column allows at most 16 characters, capitals only, no space. Page 108 does the same for file names, by listing forbidden characters plus space (HEX 20) and delete (HEX 7F). Character sets are constrained per field, never per file encoding. Verified). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Read the program as UTF-8 (BOM skipped) when its bytes are valid UTF-8. Otherwise decode it as Windows-1252 with a WARNING that names the code page. NCX output is UTF-8, and compiler output follows comment_charset. CLI002 stays only for unreadable files.
Basis: manual + logical
Source: FANUC B-64484EN p. 322-323 (ISO/EIA table, other codes dropped); 840D sl alarms BS.000503 p. 169 (alarm 12080, non-ASCII); TNC 640 892903-18 p. 293 (cnc-manuals). Controls are single-byte, so non-UTF-8 bytes come from PC editors, and Windows-1252 is a superset of Latin-1.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: ConvertCommand.Run / InputFile decoding; the test Convert_ProgramThatIsNoUtf8 becomes a WARNING case.

### Seventh round: later

#### D230 Machine position of a rotary axis moved under a tilt
Question: D101 records a setpos shift against the machine position. Main keeps that machine position known through a motion only when the motion moved the machine by as much as the workpiece coordinate (FrameRules.FollowMotion, MovesAsItsWorkpieceCoordinate). Language 4.2 turns the frame by spatial angles (TILT) or by rotary axis positions (TILT_AXIS) and says nothing of a rotary axis word under an active tilt. Without the kinematics module, VM 3.4 marks the position unknown in the new frame at a TILT, TILT_AXIS, ROTATE or MIRROR change. Yet main lets a C motion under a ROTATE keep its machine position, and not one under a tilt. Case, on a machine whose C has home: HOME C, SETPOS C=0, TILT B=45, RAPID C=45, TILT=RESET, SETPOS C=0. At TILT B=45, C returns to the MACHINE frame through the record (SetposTests.FrameChange_AfterSetposAgainstTheMachinePosition_ReturnsTheAxisToItsMachinePosition shows this for X). After RAPID C=45, main leaves the machine position of C unknown. So at the RESET, C becomes unknown in every frame instead of returning to the MACHINE frame at its machine position. The last SETPOS C=0 is then the ERROR of VM 5 (D101), and so is an IC on C (VM 3.1), until the next absolute motion of C. Main compares no rotary limits yet (MotionValidation.CheckLimits, D193), so today the lost machine position costs no limit check. Since RR-P1-03 the marker sits in FrameRules.Turns, and the same workaround also covers a linear axis other than X, Y and Z under a tilt.
Recommendation: Keep what the code does: while a TILT or TILT_AXIS stands in the chain, a motion of a rotary axis leaves its recorded machine position unknown (it still couples no linear axis). VM 3.4 says so in one sentence. Reasons: VM 3.4 and 10 give the relation between a tilted frame and the machine to the kinematics module, and whether a control applies its tilt to rotary coordinates is control-specific. The case is rare: a 3+2 program positions its rotary axes through the tilt (MOVE=TURN) and does not move them while the tilt stands. The cost: after the tilt is reset, the axis is unknown in every frame until its next absolute motion. A SETPOS or an incremental word on it before then is an ERROR, and once rotary limits are compared (D193) its limit check is skipped until then. Alternative: a tilt turns only the linear frame, so a rotary axis word under it moves the machine axis by as much as its workpiece coordinate, as under ROTATE. Answer this together with D126 (the frame of the rotary positions TILT_AXIS gives) and with D183, which uses the same relation test: under this alternative, an IC after a TILT_AXIS would add in the MACHINE frame if D183 is answered as it recommends.
Where: VM 3.4 (one sentence after the rule for TILT and TILT_AXIS changes); language 4.2 (TILT and TILT_AXIS rows). Code: src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/FrameRules.cs Turns (TODO(question) at line 480), used by MovesAsItsWorkpieceCoordinate; tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/VirtualMachine/SetposTests.cs and SetposMotionTests.cs (no test covers the machine position of a rotary axis moved under a tilt yet; Tilt_AMotionOfARotaryAxis_KeepsTheMachinePositionOfALinearAxis checks X only); src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/Validation/MotionValidation.cs CheckLimits (rotary limits, D193).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals speak against the recommendation's premise that "whether a control applies its tilt to rotary coordinates is control-specific". On the Sinumerik this is settled outright: at most three geometry axes are used to program the frames and the workpiece geometry, and a rotary axis can never be made a geometry axis, so no frame — the swivel frame of CYCLE800 included — can turn a C coordinate; a C word under an active swivel frame is a plain channel-axis position. Heidenhain is not stated but points the same way: PLANE AXIAL is defined as giving the setpoint coordinates of the rotary axes, a rotary word is an axis angle (M94's own example: from 538 degrees to a programmed 180 degrees the actual travel is -358 degrees), and with the plane tilted the axis coordinates handed to the PLC refer to the un-tilted system. So the draft's alternative is the documented Siemens behaviour: a tilt turns the linear frame only, and a rotary axis word under it moves the machine axis by as much as its coordinate, exactly as under ROTATE. What is left for the maintainer is whether NCX wants that without the kinematics module (D24), and D126 and D183 should be answered together with it, since PLANE AXIAL settles the frame of TILT_AXIAL positions the same way. Caveats: This proposal contradicts the recommendation. No manual discusses NCX's recorded machine position or a setpos shift; the conclusion is drawn from what a rotary axis word means under an active tilt, not from a sentence about position bookkeeping. The Siemens sentence about rotary axes stands among the constraints of the GEOAX geometry-axis switching function, and "frames act on the geometry axes, so no frame turns a rotary coordinate" is my step, not the page's. Heidenhain is inferred from three separate passages, one of them about what the PLC reads.
Evidence: SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D, NC-Programmierung, Programmierhandbuch (CNC-SW 4.92, 06/2019), p. 376 (2.15.1.1 Hauptachsen/Geometrieachsen) (At most three geometry axes are used for programming the frames and the workpiece geometry (contour); on a milling machine these are X, Y and Z.); SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D, NC-Programmierung, Programmierhandbuch (CNC-SW 4.92, 06/2019), p. 900 (3.15 Achsfunktionen, geometry-axis switching, constraints, "Rundachsen") (Rotary axes cannot be made geometry axes. The same page notes that switching the geometry axes clears all frames, protected zones and working-area limits.); HEIDENHAIN TNC 640, Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung 892903-18 (NC-SW 34059x-10, 10/2019), p. 426-427 (PLANE AXIAL) (PLANE AXIAL defines both the tilt and orientation of the working plane and the setpoint coordinates of the rotary axes; the axis angles must correspond to the axes actually present on the machine, otherwise the control gives an error message, and an incremental axis angle is added to the axis angle currently in effect.); HEIDENHAIN TNC 640, Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung 892903-18 (NC-SW 34059x-10, 10/2019), p. 443 (M94) (By default the control moves from the current angle value to the programmed angle value: from 538 degrees to a programmed 180 degrees the actual travel is -358 degrees. A rotary axis word is an axis coordinate and the machine moves by the coordinate difference.); HEIDENHAIN Technisches Handbuch TNC 640 (NC-SW 34059x-10, 11/2019), p. 931 (PLC module 9041, constraints) (With the working plane tilted, the axis coordinates the PLC reads refer to the un-tilted system, and an axis whose reference point has not been crossed has an undefined coordinate value.).

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Take the draft's alternative. A TILT or TILT_AXIS turns the linear frame only. A rotary axis word under it moves the machine axis by its workpiece-coordinate difference, as under ROTATE, so its recorded machine position stays known (it still couples no linear axis). VM 3.4 says so in one sentence. FrameRules.Turns no longer treats a tilt as turning rotary axes. The question of a linear axis other than X Y Z under a tilt stays as coded. Answer D126 and D183 consistently with this: TILT_AXIS positions are machine-axis setpoints, like PLANE AXIAL.
Basis: manual
Source: Siemens PGH SW4.92 connector p. 376 (frames act on at most three geometry axes) and p. 900 (a rotary axis cannot be a geometry axis). Heidenhain TNC 640 Klartext p. 426-427 (PLANE AXIAL gives the rotary setpoints) and p. 443 (M94).
Differs from the recommendation: yes: the alternative is chosen, so a rotary motion under a tilt keeps the machine position.
Confidence: medium
Code impact: FrameRules.Turns / MovesAsItsWorkpieceCoordinate; a new SetposTests case for C under TILT.

#### D231 Reader rules against the configuration tables
Question: Which comes first for a source block, the configuration tables or a plugin's reader rule? Architecture 9 (ISourceRule row) and VM 7 give folding M5, M51, M3 S1500 back into COOLANT:THROUGH=ON to a reader rule, and the maintainer's D66 answer gives it to the AddIn. 17-phase-7 plans the sample samples/plugins/ThroughCoolantSourceRule for this fold (P7-02). Machine-config 5a says 'Readers use the same rules backwards' for the same sequence. The D66 row ('a reader rule (plugin or configuration)') and architecture 13 ('ISourceRule from a plugin, or the configuration tables') let the configuration do it as well. But these try the tables first: D40 (the [workpiece] table first, the chuck function rule second, a plugin's reader rule for the rest), the [func_meta] comment of machine-config 5, controller-mapping 4 (WORKPIECE row, 'the tables first'), architecture 9, VM 7 and 13-phase-3 P3-01. The tables name M5, M51 and M3, so ReaderBase.ReadSourceBlock never offers those blocks to a rule, and ReaderRulesTests pins that order. How a rule claims more than one block is D232.
Recommendation: The reader offers every source block to the plugins' reader rules first, in the order the plugins are loaded. A block that no rule claims is read as today: the tables, then the family's own words. Without a plugin nothing changes. This revises the wording of D40 and D66. D40's order (the [workpiece] table, then the chuck function rule) stays the order of the built-in mechanisms. A plugin is written for one machine and listed by the user in ncx.toml, and it claims only what it recognizes. The fold belongs to the plugin, as the D66 answer says. So the 'or configuration' of the D66 row and of architecture 13 goes, and machine-config 5a says that a plugin's reader rule folds the sequence. Reasons: this is the only order in which the fold that the D66 answer gives the AddIn can work, and a plugin overrides a built-in reading only on the machine it was written for. Alternatives: (a) Tables first, as on main. The M5 M51 M3 example then leaves architecture 9, VM 7 and machine-config 5a, the ThroughCoolantSourceRule sample leaves P7-02, and D66 needs a second look, because a fold of codes the tables know has no place. (b) The reader itself folds, before the tables, a sequence that a requires/restore rule of the machine file generates (machine-config 5a read backwards). This is what D66's recommendation proposed and its answer handed to the AddIn.
Where: decisions.md rows D40 and D66; architecture 9 (ISourceRule row) and 13 (D66 line); VM 7 (reader-rule sentence); machine-config 5 ([func_meta] comment) and 5a ('Readers use the same rules backwards'); controller-mapping 4 (WORKPIECE row); 13-phase-3 P3-01 (ISourceRule bullet); 17-phase-7 P7-02 (ThroughCoolantSourceRule); D155, whose alternative leaves cases to a plugin's rule, which under tables first is never offered a code that a table names. Code: src/Ncx.Readers/ReaderBase.cs ReadSourceBlock (TODO(question) at line 275); the summary of src/Ncx.Readers/ISourceRule.cs ('The configuration tables of the machine are tried first'); tests/Ncx.Readers.Tests/ReaderRulesTests.cs FakeReaderWithThreeRules_ThreeLines_ReadsTheExpectedNcx and Tables_CodeTheTableNamesInAnotherSpelling_AreTriedBeforeTheRules.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. No manual in the library knows a plugin layer, so none can settle the order. What the manuals do show is the control's own layering, and it runs the other way round from the recommendation: Fanuc says the assignment of M codes to machine functions is the machine builder's, but the machine (the PMC, the builder's own program) processes all M codes except the ones the control itself claims — M98, M99, M198 and the codes configured through parameters 6071-6079 and 6080-6089 for subprogram and macro calls. Read as a model, with NCX's configuration tables in the place of the control's parameters and a plugin in the place of the builder's PMC program, that is alternative (a): the configured tables are consulted first and remove those codes from the builder's reach, and the builder-specific layer sees only what the tables did not claim. That is a structural analogy and not a rule about NCXchange — the D66 fold of M5, M51, M3 S1500 is a fold of codes the tables do name, and the control model has no case for it. It is worth the maintainer's eye only because recorded D40 already orders the built-in table first, and the recommendation is what revises it. Caveats: The parallel maps NCXchange's configuration tables onto the control's parameters and its plugin onto the builder's PMC program. That is my reading, not a manual's statement; a plugin reader rule has no counterpart on a control. I did not mark this as contradicting the recommendation on purpose: no page speaks about the order of a reader rule against a table, so the flag would claim manual evidence that does not exist, even though the analogy leans toward alternative (a). Searched: 'Hilfsfunktion', 'M-Code', 'Maschinenhersteller', 'Parameter 6071', 'Kundenmakro-Aufruf' in the FANUC 30i-B Betriebshandbuch B-64484GE/02 (chapter 11 Hilfsfunktion, chapter 16 Kundenmakro); 'Zuordnung', 'herstellerspezifisch', 'PLC', 'PMC' across 01_Steuerungen/Fanuc, Siemens and Heidenhain; the builder M-code lists under 02_Maschinenhersteller (Nakamura-Tome, Doosan, Mori Seiki, DMG, Hermle, Burkhardt+Weber) for a statement about precedence between a builder mapping and the control's own reading — none makes one. I added 'Plug-in'/'Plugin' across the whole cache: four hits, all unrelated (an Okuma Acrobat Reader plug-in, Siemens HMI graphic plug-ins, a Unisign USB note).
Evidence: FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 297, 11.1 Hilfsfunktion (M-Funktion) (The assignment of M codes to machine functions is determined by the machine builder, and the machine processes every M code except M98, M99, M198 and the M codes set by parameters 6071-6079 (subprogram call) and 6080-6089 (custom-macro call). A code the control's own configuration claims never reaches the builder's side.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)
Confidence: low.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Every source block goes first to the loaded plugins' reader rules, in load order (D317). A block no rule claims is read as today: tables, then the family's words. Without a plugin nothing changes. D40's order stays the order of the built-in mechanisms. The M5 M51 M3 S1500 fold is the plugin's job (ThroughCoolantSourceRule, P7-02). Do not strike 'or configuration' from D66's row: a configuration fold simply is not implemented in 1.0. That keeps D66 as recorded.
Basis: logical
Source: The D66 answer gives the fold of codes the tables name to a plugin, which only works when plugins come first. A plugin is per machine and claims only what it recognises. Fanuc B-64484EN p. 297 (the PMC sees only what the parameters leave) is an analogy for the opposite order and not a rule.
Differs from the recommendation: yes: keeps D66's 'or configuration' wording instead of removing it. Flag: this rewords the order sentence of settled D40; the maintainer should note the revision.
Confidence: medium
Code impact: ReaderBase.ReadSourceBlock offers rules first; ISourceRule summary; ReaderRulesTests order test inverted.

#### D232 How a reader rule claims a sequence of source blocks
Question: ISourceRule has one method, Read(SourceBlock, SourceState, NcxBuilder). It returns bool, is called once per offered block, and is not called after the last one. 13-phase-3 P3-01 says it returns 'whether the rule claimed the block or sequence', architecture 9 lets a rule decide what a 'sequence of source blocks' means, and D66 gives the fold of a sequence to a reader rule. No document says how a rule claims more than one block. A rule that holds blocks back finds the blocks decided without it written before the ones it held, and it loses a block held at the end of the file (D5). On main a claim covers the one block offered (P3-01 log, 2026-09-13), so the sequence claim of the P3-01 scope is open. Which blocks a rule is offered at all is D231.
Recommendation: A claim starts at the offered block and may take the blocks that follow it, by look-ahead. SourceBlock gives read-only access to the following source blocks of its section, up to the next structure block (O, M30, M99, a jump target), which stays with the structure pass. The rule writes the NCX blocks for the whole run before it returns. Read returns the number of source blocks it claimed instead of bool, 0 to decline. The reader applies each claimed block to SourceState and keeps their comments as comment-only lines after the rule's blocks, as today. Reasons: it keeps one method per interface (architecture 9; code-guidelines 11, 'four interfaces with one method each'); nothing is held back, so nothing is lost at the end of the file (D5); and the rule's NCX stands where the run stood. Under tables first (D231), a run can start only at a block the tables leave undecided. Alternatives: a second method or a call at the end of the input, which breaks one method per interface; or one-block claims, as on main, with 'or sequence' removed from P3-01 and architecture 9.
Where: 13-phase-3 P3-01 (ISourceRule bullet); architecture 9 (ISourceRule row); docs/plan/tasks/done/P3-01 (scope: 'may claim a sequence (D66)'); 17-phase-7 P7-01 (interface text); code-guidelines 11. Code: src/Ncx.Readers/ISourceRule.cs Read (TODO(question) at line 14); src/Ncx.Readers/ReaderBase.cs ClaimedByRule (TODO(question) at line 288); src/Ncx.Readers/SourceBlock.cs (the following blocks); tests/Ncx.Readers.Tests/ReaderRulesTests.cs and Fakes/CodeRule.cs.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27: the library does not answer this (searched confirmed the earlier search (Satzvorlauf, LookAhead, Satzzusammenfassung in the Siemens 840D sl manuals gives only the velocity look-ahead of the path control, Grundlagen 03/2013 p. 139, 230, 293, 308-313) and added three of my own. (1) The one control mechanism that does fold a run of consecutive blocks is the Siemens block compressor, COMPCAD/COMPSURF/COMPOF (Sinumerik ONE NC-Programmierung SW6.14, p. 605-606, 695-698): it is a modal G-group-30 mode switched on and off around the run, not a per-run claim, and it says nothing about who consumes which block. (2) I searched the whole cache for Postprozessor/postprocessor: besides Hermle there are the Mori Seiki ESPRIT post manual, six WFL Millturn post-processor notes, Grob's G750T post-processor description and Correa's requirements sheet; all of them prescribe output, none describes how the generator consumes its input. (3) Heidenhain's LOOK AHEAD entries are velocity pre-computation only. No manual describes a block-claiming interface, and how a reader rule claims one or several source blocks is an interface question inside NCXchange: the manuals describe the language a control reads, not how a translator consumes it). The recommendation above stands for the maintainer.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

ISourceRule.Read returns int, the number of source blocks claimed (0 declines). SourceBlock gives read-only look-ahead to the following blocks of its section, up to the next structure block. The rule writes the NCX for the whole run before it returns. The reader applies the claimed blocks to SourceState and keeps their comments as comment-only lines after the rule's blocks.
Basis: logical
Source: One method per interface (code-guidelines 11). Nothing is held back, so nothing is lost at the end of a file (D5). The manuals have no equivalent.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: ISourceRule.Read signature, ReaderBase.ClaimedByRule, SourceBlock look-ahead, fakes/tests.

#### D233 TOOL_END for the tool still in the spindle at PROGRAM_END
Question: VM 7 raises TOOL_END when a tool 'leaves the spindle', and VM 4 keeps the tool in the spindle at PROGRAM=END, so the last tool of a program never gets a TOOL_END. Its distance and block count (VM 7) therefore reach no listener. The tool list of VM 8 and architecture 9 is built from TOOL_BEGIN and TOOL_END. P4-02 (14-phase-4) asserts the distances of tool 1 of 2.5D_FRAESEN, its only tool, and has the tool list of INCREMENTAL_SUB name tools 2 and 3. In both examples the last tool has no TOOL_END. tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Expected/2.5D_FRAESEN.events.txt has TOOL_BEGIN(10) and nothing after it. Tool 3 of INCREMENTAL_SUB, from the bare TOOL of line 16, is never changed again. Should PROGRAM_END, or FILE_END, close every tool still in a spindle?
Recommendation: At the PROGRAM=END that ends the channel's program, raise TOOL_END for every tool that this channel brought into a spindle and that is still there, with its distance and block count, directly before PROGRAM_END. The state keeps the tool, so VM 4 is unchanged: the event closes the tool's use in this program, it does not empty the spindle. Only the channel's own tools close, because resources are per job (VM 2.8). In a two-channel job (nakamura-ntjx: T1 and T2), the channel that ends first must not close the tool the other channel still cuts with. PROGRAM=END is also reached by JUMP=END, so every walk of a program that ends pairs each TOOL_BEGIN with a TOOL_END. The PROGRAM=END of an external program that a CALL runs returns to the caller and closes nothing (D214). The walk of a subprogram that no program calls (D99) closes its tools the same way at its SUB=END. A run that an ERROR stops raises neither. With D134 as recommended, every program starts from the initial state, so a later program starts with empty spindles. If D134 is answered the other way, that program raises TOOL_BEGIN at its PROGRAM_BEGIN for each tool it inherits. Reason: every listener, a plugin's tool list included, then sees the end of each tool's use with its figures, and the state stays as VM 4 has it. P4-02's own tool list needs more than TOOL_END carries: cutting and rapid distance apart, rpm range, time. It reads MOTION for those in any case, but it still needs the end of the last tool's use. 2.5D_FRAESEN then gets TOOL_END(51) for tool 1 before PROGRAM_END(51). Alternative: raise them at FILE_END. In a file with several programs, the tools of earlier programs then close after later programs have run. Second alternative: no change. The tool list takes the end of the last tool from PROGRAM_END and sums MOTION lengths itself, and architecture 9 adds MOTION and PROGRAM_END to its events.
Where: VM 7 (TOOL_BEGIN, TOOL_END row: 'and at PROGRAM_END for every tool the channel brought in that is still in a spindle'); VM 3.5 (TOOL=n row) and architecture 5.2 (last sentence), one clause each; src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/Events/BlockEvents.cs AddToolChanges (TODO(question) at line 131) and Raise (closing step); tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/VirtualMachine/Events/ToolEventTests.cs ToolEnd_ProgramEnd_KeepsTheToolInTheSpindleAndRaisesNoToolEnd; tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Expected/2.5D_FRAESEN.events.txt.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals support the recommendation. Heidenhain's own per-program tool list, the Werkzeugeinsatzdatei, carries an entry with a usage figure for every tool the program uses: the iTNC manual says that with machining-time determination switched on a file can be generated holding the usage times of all tools used in a program, and the TNC 640 technical manual adds that it is generated for the selected NC program including its subprograms and holds each tool's number, index, name and radius, its usage time at 100 percent override and its program calls. Nothing is left open at the end of the program, so raising TOOL_END for every tool this channel still has in a spindle, with its figures, directly before PROGRAM_END gives NCX the same closed list that architecture 9 and P4-02 need. The manuals do not speak to the event mechanism, to the two-channel case (nakamura-ntjx T1 and T2) or to the FILE_END alternative; those stay a design choice. Caveats: The manuals say the file holds all tools used with their usage times; that the last tool's entry is therefore closed at program end is my inference, not a sentence. The control's per-tool figure is a time, not a distance and a block count (see D235). The nearest Siemens counterpart is not a per-tool record but a channel timer, $AC_CUTTING_TIME, which a machine datum can restrict to counting only while a tool is active.
Evidence: HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzerhandbuch Klartext-Dialog (NC-SW 340422, 2004), p. 561 (12.1 Grafiken, "Bearbeitungszeit ermitteln") (With machining-time determination switched on you can have a file generated in which the usage times of all tools used in a program are listed (pointing at the dependent files on page 593).); HEIDENHAIN Technisches Handbuch TNC 640 (NC-SW 34059x-10, 11/2019), p. 3027 (7.13.9 Werkzeugeinsatzprüfung) (The tool usage file (*.T.DEP, named after the NC program) holds all needed tools with number, index, name and radius, their usage times at 100 percent override and their program calls; in Program-Test mode it is generated for the selected NC program including its subprograms.).

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

At the PROGRAM=END that ends a channel's program (JUMP=END included), raise TOOL_END for every tool this channel brought into a spindle that is still there, with its distance and block count, directly before PROGRAM_END. The spindle state stays unchanged. Other cases close nothing: the PROGRAM=END of an external CALLed program, a run stopped by an ERROR. An uncalled SUB walk closes its tools at its SUB=END. 2.5D_FRAESEN gets TOOL_END(51).
Basis: manual (supporting) + logical
Source: TNC 640 Technisches Handbuch 34059x-10 p. 3027 and iTNC 530 p. 561 (the tool usage file lists every tool used, with figures) (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: BlockEvents.AddToolChanges/Raise closing step; ToolEventTests; 2.5D_FRAESEN.events.txt.

#### D234 CYCLE_CALL under ExpandCycles: with or instead of the MOTION events
Question: VM 7 raises CYCLE_CALL at 'every call'. VM 3.3 says that under ExpandCycles 'the call is raised as the individual MOTION events', and architecture 5.1 draws 'raise CYCLE_CALL or expanded MOTION events'. D37 ('raises the individual motions of a cycle call as MOTION events') does not say whether the CYCLE_CALL stays. Case: a DRILL call seen by ncx analyze, whose runtime estimate takes the cycle plunges from ExpandCycles (14-phase-4 P4-02), or by a listener plugin. Does it see one CYCLE_CALL followed by the rapid, feed and retract MOTIONs, or the MOTIONs alone? check and trace do not show the difference: check writes diagnostics only, and trace only STATE_CHANGE and VAR_CHANGE. Main raises CYCLE_CALL at every call and, under ExpandCycles, the MOTIONs of the sequence after it in the same block. Which motions the sequence holds is a separate question (D190).
Recommendation: Both, as main does: CYCLE_CALL at every call, and under ExpandCycles the MOTION events of its sequence follow it in the same block. Reasons: under ExpandCycles a `CYCLE:<controller>=n` call raises no MOTION (VM 3.3, D94), so without its CYCLE_CALL it would vanish from the events; the kinematics module subscribes to CYCLE_CALL and publishes a TOOL_POSE per CYCLE_CALL (VM 7, VM 10); and the option then only adds events, it never removes one. An expanded MOTION carries the CYCLE_CALL block as its Block (MotionEvents.AddCycleMotions), so a listener can tell it from a programmed motion. A listener that reads both, such as the runtime estimate (architecture 9), charges a call by its MOTIONs when they follow and by the CYCLE_CALL alone otherwise. VM 3.3 then reads 'under ExpandCycles the CYCLE_CALL event is followed by the individual MOTION events of the sequence', and architecture 5.1 reads 'raise CYCLE_CALL, and under ExpandCycles the MOTION events of the sequence'. Alternative: under ExpandCycles the MOTION events replace the CYCLE_CALL, except for calls whose sequence the VM does not know.
Where: VM 3.3 (ExpandCycles sentence); VM 7 (CYCLE_CALL row); architecture 5.1 flowchart (node H); D37 row (a Clarified line); src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/Events/BlockEvents.cs AddCycleCall (TODO(question) at line 250); MotionEvents.Of; CycleRules.Call.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27: the library does not answer this (searched 'Zyklusaufruf', 'CYCL CALL', 'Ereignis', 'Event', 'Schnittstelle' plus 'Zyklus' in the FANUC 30i-B Betriebshandbuch, SINUMERIK 840D Zyklen (2008) and 840D sl NC-Programmierung SW 4.92, HEIDENHAIN TNC 640 Zyklen 892905-18 and Klartext 892903-18; 'SBLOF', 'DISPLOF', 'Satzanzeige', 'Einzelsatz' with 'Zyklus'. My own additions: 'Einzelsatz' near 'Zyklus'/'Festzyklus' across the Heidenhain and Fanuc folders, which returns only cycle-by-cycle notes about where a cycle stops in single block, and nothing naming an event, a listener or a subscriber. Nothing in the library bears on whether an expanded cycle keeps its call event: the controls have no event stream for a program analyser to subscribe to, and a cycle call is a block that the control executes, so what a consumer sees of it is a display or single-block question, not a documented interface. This stays an NCX design choice, and the draft's reasoning (a CYCLE:<controller>=n call would vanish without its CYCLE_CALL, and the kinematics module publishes a TOOL_POSE per CYCLE_CALL) is the only evidence there is. The nearest thing on a control, which I did open this time, is the Sinumerik pair SBLOF/DISPLOF (840D sl SW 4.92, sections 3.2.2.5 and 3.2.2.6, PDF pages 512-518): DISPLOF says that in cycles and subprograms the display of the current block can be suppressed and the call of the cycle or subprogram is shown instead, and page 517 gives the single-block settings SB1 and SB2 (no stop inside cycles) against SB3 (stop inside cycles too) — the same 'two consumers, two levels of detail' the draft describes, but a display and stop mechanism, not an event stream. The earlier claim that the simulation still draws the motions while the blocks are hidden is not on those pages and is struck). The recommendation above stands for the maintainer.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Both, as main does. CYCLE_CALL is raised at every call. Under ExpandCycles the MOTION events of the sequence follow it in the same block, and they carry the CYCLE_CALL block as their Block. Reword VM 3.3 and architecture 5.1 to match.
Basis: logical
Source: Without the event, a CYCLE:<controller>=n call would vanish. The kinematics module publishes a TOOL_POSE per CYCLE_CALL, and the option only adds events.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none (docs only).

#### D235 Run statistics of PROGRAM_END and the figures of TOOL_END
Question: VM 7 gives PROGRAM_END 'run statistics', which VM 3.6 raises at PROGRAM=END, and gives TOOL_END 'distance and block count under the tool'. No document says what the run statistics are. None says what the distance counts either: feed and rapid moves together or apart, the motions of an expanded cycle, motions whose length is unknown. VM 2.7 has blocksExecuted, but it is counted in INTERPRETED mode only, for the block cap. Architecture 5.3 names Blocks and Distance on ProgramEvent, but P1-05 wrote that line itself (F18). What main does: (1) Both events carry blocks and distance, counted in both modes. The distance is the sum of the MOTION lengths that are known, rapid and feed together, the MOTIONs of an expanded CYCLE_CALL included. (2) A program counts from PROGRAM=BEGIN to PROGRAM=END inclusive, with the blocks of called subprograms once per walk. For 2.5D_FRAESEN, PROGRAM_END carries blocks 44 and distance 664.763, and four of its MOTIONs have no known length: the first two rapids and the two machine-frame moves. (3) In STATIC mode the figures follow the walk, so a REPEAT or a backward JUMP counts its blocks once (PATTERN_LOOP).
Recommendation: Keep what main does and write it into VM 7. The run statistics are the blocks executed and the distance, the same two figures TOOL_END carries for a tool. The distance is the sum of the known MOTION lengths, rapid and feed together, with the MOTIONs of an expanded CYCLE_CALL, and generated blocks count (VM 3.10). The figures are exact in INTERPRETED mode, the default of analyze. In STATIC mode they count what the walk executes. Reason: one definition for both events, taken from the MOTION lengths every listener already sees. Option: add a third figure, the number of MOTIONs whose length is unknown, so a report can say the distance is a lower bound. Alternative: split the distance into feed and rapid distance, since the P4-02 tool list asks for cutting and rapid distance apart (14-phase-4). The answer should also say whether the blocks of an external program that a CALL runs in INTERPRETED mode count under the calling program (D214 asks what its PROGRAM=BEGIN and PROGRAM=END do).
Where: VM 7 (TOOL_BEGIN, TOOL_END and PROGRAM_BEGIN, PROGRAM_END payloads); VM 3.6 (PROGRAM=END bullet); architecture 5.3 (ProgramEvent, ToolEvent); src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/Events/BlockEvents.cs ProgramEvent (TODO(question) at line 378); ProgramEvent.cs, ToolEvent.cs, RunStatistics.cs.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The controls do keep per-program run figures, and they are times and counts, never a distance or a block count. Sinumerik defines them as system variables: $AC_CYCLE_TIME is the run time of the selected NC program, reset automatically when a new program starts, and $AC_CUTTING_TIME is the machining time, measured as the run time of the path axes without active rapid traverse, with a machine datum (MD27860) deciding whether it counts only with an active tool. Heidenhain's figure is the same kind: in the run modes the time from program start to program end, halted at interruptions, and in Program-Test the approximate duration of the tool movements executed with feed, which the manual itself says is unfit for costing because machine-dependent times such as the tool change are left out; the per-tool figure of the usage file is a usage time at 100 percent override. Fanuc counts operating time and the parts count (#3901, #3902). That speaks against the clause "rapid and feed together": both families keep their machining figure free of rapid, so the draft's alternative (cutting and rapid distance apart, which P4-02 wants anyway) has the controls' own habit behind it, and the "unknown length" third figure has its counterpart in Heidenhain's disclaimer rather than in a number. What the manuals cannot settle is blocks-executed, the STATIC/INTERPRETED split and whether the blocks of a called external program count under the caller — no manual in the library counts executed blocks for a program run at all (every "Anzahl der Sätze" hit is look-ahead). Caveats: This proposal contradicts the recommendation. The control figures are times, the draft's figure is a distance, so the contradiction is about separating feed from rapid, not about the quantity; no manual states a path length for a program run. The Sinumerik variables are channel timers read from the part program, not a payload handed to a listener. $AC_CYCLE_TIME runs from NC start to program end and so covers whatever a called program takes, but that is a timer's nature, not a statement about counting a callee's blocks under its caller. The iTNC wording is from the 2004 NC-SW 340422 volume; I did not find the equivalent sentence in the TNC 640 user manual.
Evidence: SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D, Funktionshandbuch Grundfunktionen (07/2012, 6FC5397-0BP40-3AA0), p. 701 (8.16 Programmlaufzeit / Werkstückzähler) ($AC_OPERATING_TIME sums the run times of all programs in automatic mode; $AC_CYCLE_TIME is the run time of the selected NC program between NC start and program end or NC reset, reset to 0 when a new NC program starts; $AC_CUTTING_TIME is the machining time, measured as the run time of the path axes without active rapid traverse, with MD27860 deciding whether it is measured only with an active tool, and paused during a dwell. Times only - no distance and no block count.); SINUMERIK ONE, NC-Programmierung, Programmierhandbuch (CNC-SW 6.14, 10/2020), p. 990 (3.22 Programmlaufzeit / Werkstückzähler) (The same three channel timers in a programming manual of the current generation, with the same definition of $AC_CUTTING_TIME as the path-axis run time without active rapid traverse.); HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzerhandbuch Klartext-Dialog (NC-SW 340422, 2004), p. 561 (12.1 Grafiken, "Bearbeitungszeit ermitteln") (In the program-run modes the display is the time from program start to program end, stopped during interruptions. In Program-Test it is the approximate time the TNC computes for the duration of the tool movements executed with feed, and the manual states this time is unsuitable for calculating the production time because machine-dependent times such as the tool change are not taken into account.); HEIDENHAIN TNC 310, Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext (313 509-12, 2000), p. 163 (10.2 Programm-Test, "Bearbeitungszeit ermitteln") (The same two definitions on an older control: program start to program end in the run modes, and in Program-Test the approximate time for the duration of the tool movements executed with feed.); HEIDENHAIN Technisches Handbuch TNC 640 (NC-SW 34059x-10, 11/2019), p. 3027-3028 (7.13.9 Werkzeugeinsatzprüfung) (The per-tool figure the control keeps is a usage time at 100 percent override, with a machine parameter (MP_usageFactor, default 10 percent) that marks it up; the file also records each tool's program calls. No length figure appears.); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 485, custom-macro system variables (What Fanuc keeps for a program run is the operating time and the parts count, readable and writable through #3901 (total parts) and #3902 (required parts) and shown by the operating-time and parts-count display. Again a time and a count, no distance and no block count.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

PROGRAM_END and TOOL_END carry the same figures: blocks (executed), feedDistance, rapidDistance and unknownLengthMotions (the count of MOTIONs whose length is unknown, so a report can call the distances a lower bound). An optional derived total, distance, equals the sum. The distances are sums of the known MOTION lengths, the MOTIONs of an expanded CYCLE_CALL and generated blocks (VM 3.10) included. RAPID motions go to rapidDistance and all others to feedDistance. The figures are exact in INTERPRETED mode. In STATIC mode they count what the walk executes. The blocks of an external program run by CALL count under the caller's PROGRAM_END (settled D214). There is no time figure here, because that belongs to the runtime estimate (VM 8).
Basis: manual + logical
Source: Siemens Funktionshandbuch 07/2012 p. 701 ($AC_CUTTING_TIME excludes rapid) and Heidenhain iTNC 530 p. 561 (Program-Test time counts feed moves only): the controls keep machining figures free of rapid. P4-02 asks for cutting and rapid distances apart. D214 settles callee counting.
Differs from the recommendation: yes: the distance is split into feed and rapid, and the unknown-length count is added.
Confidence: medium
Code impact: RunStatistics, ProgramEvent and ToolEvent (new fields), the distance accumulator in the VM; VM 7 and architecture 5.3 text.

#### D236 Holder a block counts under when a channel has several holders
Question: VM 7 gives TOOL_END the 'distance and block count under the tool' but does not say under whose tool a block and its motion count when a machine has several holders. nakamura-ntjx and dmg-ctx-840d have T1 and T2, and mori-ntx1000-mapps has H1 and H2. Case: TOOL:TURRET1=1, TOOL:TURRET2=5, LINE Z=-10 F=100. Does the LINE count under tool 1, tool 5, or both? Main counts a block under the tool of lastHolder (VM 2.3), from the block that brought the tool in, so the LINE counts under tool 5. In ToolEventTests.ToolEnd_TwoHolders_CountsUnderTheHolderCalledLast, tool 1 ends with blocks 1 and distance 0, and tool 5 with blocks 2 and distance 10.
Recommendation: Keep what main does and write it into VM 7. A block counts under the tool of lastHolder. That is the holder VM 3.8 rule 2 sends OFFSET to, and the one VM 5 calls 'the current tool holder' for the spindle-OFF rule. So no motion counts under two tools. The block that changes the tool counts under the new tool. Reason: this is consistent with the holder rules already written, since the program names the working holder by its last TOOL. Alternative: count a block under every holder whose spindle holds a tool. That counts a two-turret block twice and gives a turret that waits the distance of the one that cuts.
Where: VM 7 (TOOL_BEGIN, TOOL_END row); VM 2.3 (lastHolder row); src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/Events/BlockEvents.cs Raise (TODO(question) at line 97); tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/VirtualMachine/Events/ToolEventTests.cs ToolEnd_TwoHolders_CountsUnderTheHolderCalledLast.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. No control documents a single program block under two tools: on every machine in the library each turret or tool carrier runs its own program with its own T word, and the multi-turret examples print the two programs side by side. What the manuals do support is the one-tool-at-a-time half of main's rule: under Fanuc tool life management the M06 block ends life management for the previously used tools and starts counting the life of the new tool selected with the T code, so usage accrues to the tool the program last called and the changing block starts the new tool's count. The only documented case in which one path's block moves the other path's slide is Fanuc's superimposed control, and even there the block belongs to one program with one T. Keeping lastHolder is therefore consistent with the controls; the choice itself stays NCX's. Two overreaches of an earlier draft were cut: the Fanuc sentence is in the singular only for the new tool — it ends management "für die vorher verwendeten Werkzeuge", plural — so it establishes that the last T owns the count, not that two tools can never be counted at once; and the Nakamura pages cited show two side-by-side programs with their own wait marks but carry no T words at all, so "each with its own T" is not borne out by those pages (it is borne out elsewhere, e.g. the WT150 example in Band 2). Nakamura's Kombinationssteuerung (M432/M442) lets one program command the other unit's C axis, but the tool still belongs to the program's own turret; I found no page that attributes a motion to two tools.
Evidence: FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 285 (Under tool life management, "M06" ends life management for the previously used tools and begins counting the life of the new tool selected with the T code.); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch Band 1 (4810004ECL-1), p. 303-304, 310-311 (Every back-milling example prints two separate programs side by side, headed "Programm für oberen Revolver" and "Programm für unteren Revolver", each with its own blocks and its own wait marks; no block belongs to both turrets.); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch Band 2 (4810004ECL-2), p. 69-71 (The WT150 example prints the upper-turret program "O1234 (UPPER MAIN)" and the lower-turret program "O1234 (LOWER MAIN)" as two separate programs, each with its own blocks and wait marks — the case where the tool words actually appear.); FANUC Series 16i/18i-TA Benutzerhandbuch (B-63004GE/02), p. 417-418 (Section 20.7 shows the two-path functions: synchronous control moves one path's axis with another's, composite control exchanges the two paths' axis commands, and superimposed control makes a move programmed in one system apply to an axis of the other — each figure labelled "Bearbeitung nach einem Programm für System 1", i.e. the block is still one program's block.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main. A block and its motion count under the tool of lastHolder, and a tool-changing block counts under the new tool. No motion counts under two tools. Write this into VM 7.
Basis: manual (supporting) + logical
Source: FANUC B-64484EN p. 285 (M06 starts counting the new tool); Nakamura 4810004ECL-1 p. 303-311 and ECL-2 p. 69-71 (one program per turret) (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none.

#### D237 Form of the trace table and the annotate comments
Question: VM 6 fixes the trace columns (channel, block, variable, old, new; old empty when unknown) and one annotate comment ('; X 33.22 -> 55.44', after an existing comment by one space). VM 8 says 'CSV or aligned columns', and architecture 10 and implementation 11 P1-07 give trace a --format of text or csv without naming a default. VM 3.10 says generated blocks appear in both 'with their origin'. No document says whether the table has a header row, which format is the default, how a CSV field is quoted, how the block column names a generated block, how several variables of one annotate block are joined, or how annotate writes an unknown value. Nor does one say in what form annotate shows a generated block. Its copy must parse (a pseudo-word in a user file is an ERROR, D95) and must format back to the original once the comments are stripped (P1-07), so only a comment line fits. Case: on the coolant clutch machine the spindle stop generated for line 5 needs a row in trace and a line in annotate.
Recommendation: Write the code's form into VM 6. (1) Trace starts with a header row of the five column names. (2) Aligned text is the default and --format csv the other form. (3) CSV follows RFC 4180: a field holding a comma, a quote or a line break stands in quotes with its quotes doubled, and every line ends in LF. (4) The block column of a generated block is the line it carries followed by its origin: '5 generated by [coolant] THROUGH (requires)', or 'rewritten by ...' for a block replaced in place. (5) Annotate joins several variables in trace order with ', '. (6) Annotate writes an unknown value as '?', as the printed events do ('UNITS ? -> MM'), and trace keeps the empty field of VM 6. (7) A generated block becomes a comment line where the VM executed it ('; generated by [coolant] THROUGH (requires): SPINDLE:TOOL=OFF ; SPINDLE:S1 CW -> OFF'). A block rewritten in place becomes such a line before the block of the file, which then carries no values. Reason: the five columns of VM 6 stay, and the copy stays a file the parser reads. The 2.5D_FRAESEN expected files already hold points 1, 2, 5 and 6, and the command tests hold points 3, 4 and 7. Points 1 to 3 then apply to every text table of VM 8 (TextTable of P4-02). Answer point 4 with D200: which line a generated block carries (D98 renders its diagnostics as 'file(line, from 12)'). Answer point 7 with D167. Alternative for point 4: a sixth column 'origin', empty for the blocks of the file, so the block column stays a number for spreadsheets.
Where: VM 6 (a paragraph on both forms), 3.10 (the origin text), 8 (the table rules); architecture 10 (trace row: text is the default); implementation 11 P1-07 and 14 P4-02 (TextTable); D167; D200. Code: src/Ncx.Cli/History/TraceTable.cs and AnnotatedText.cs (a TODO(question) above each class: TraceTable.cs line 11, AnnotatedText.cs line 13), GeneratedOrigin.cs. Tests: tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Expected/2.5D_FRAESEN.trace.txt and 2.5D_FRAESEN.annotate.txt; TraceCommandTests.TraceCsv_StringWithACommaAndQuotes_IsQuoted, TraceCsv_GeneratedBlocks_NameTheirOrigin; AnnotateCommandTests.Annotate_GeneratedBlocks_StandAsCommentLinesWithTheirOrigin, Annotate_BlockThatChangesSeveralVariables_WritesThemInTheOrderOfTrace.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27: the library does not answer this (searched 'CSV', 'RFC 4180', 'Protokolldatei', 'Log', 'Kopfzeile', 'Spaltenüberschrift', 'Trennzeichen', 'Anführungszeichen', 'Trace', 'Protokoll' across the whole library and specifically in the FANUC 30i-B Betriebshandbuch, SINUMERIK 840D sl NC-Programmierung SW 4.92 and HEIDENHAIN TNC 640 Klartext 892903-18. My own re-run of 'CSV' over the whole cache returns about two dozen hits, all of them builder data exports (Haas serial responses, Brother check results, Nakamura-Tome NT-Nurse and NT-IPS, Citizen M432 eco data) plus the Heidenhain tool overview; I opened Nakamura-Tome NT-Nurse pages 258-259 and Citizen M432 page 512 (printed 8-42), and none states a header, quoting or escaping rule. Nothing in the library bears on the form of the trace table or of the annotate comments: these are NCXchange's own CLI outputs, and no control manual defines a header row, a CSV quoting rule, how a generated block names its origin, or how several changed variables of one block are joined, so the question stays entirely a design choice and the draft's seven points plus the existing expected files are the only evidence. The library does hold builder-documented CSV layouts, which the earlier search missed: Nakamura-Tome NT-Nurse writes its offset history as comma-separated records of tag and value (H10, 0, H20, date, ...), and Citizen M432 documents the eco and machine-data files as one comma-separated record per line with a fixed field order — both machine logs with no header row and no quoting rule, so they settle none of the draft's seven points and are not entered as evidence. Heidenhain's tool overview *.T.CSV and the optional TOOLCHECK.LOG are named in the TNC 640 technical manual without a column form). The recommendation above stands for the maintainer.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Adopt points 1 to 7 as coded: 1. A header row comes first. 2. Aligned text is the default, and --format csv the other form. 3. CSV follows RFC 4180, with LF line ends. 4. A generated block's block column reads '<line> generated by …' or 'rewritten by …'. 5. Annotate joins several variables with ', '. 6. Annotate writes an unknown value as '?', and trace leaves the field empty. 7. A generated block becomes a comment line in annotate. Points 1 to 3 apply to every text table of VM 8. Answer point 4 with D200 and point 7 with D167.
Basis: logical
Source: These are internal CLI outputs, and the manuals are silent. RFC 4180 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4180) is the CSV norm.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none (docs: VM 6/8, architecture 10).

#### D238 Plugin assemblies and plugin settings in ncx.toml
Question: Machine-config 10 writes the plugin assemblies as plugins = ["MyShop.NcxPlugins.dll"]. D80 (answered) gives each plugin its own `[plugins.<name>]` section of the same file. Implementation 17 P7-01 uses both ('the [plugins] list of ncx.toml', '[plugins.MyShopRules]'), and in P7-02 'ncx plugin build' adds the line to ncx.toml. TOML cannot define plugins both as an array and as a table in one file. ProjectSettingsLoader on main reads an array as the assemblies and a table as the settings, so an ncx.toml can hold one or the other, never both.
Recommendation: Keep D80's sections and move the list into the table. [plugins] holds assemblies = ["MyShop.NcxPlugins.dll"], and each `[plugins.<name>]` below it holds one plugin's settings; no plugin may be named 'assemblies'. Machine-config 10, code-guidelines 11 and P7-01/P7-02 follow ('ncx plugin build' adds the DLL to assemblies). The loader reports a top-level array as the wrong type (CFG003). Reason: this is the smallest change that keeps the recorded form of D80 and the '[plugins] list' of P7-01. Alternative: ncx.toml names no assemblies and every DLL in plugins/ is loaded (P7-01 loads that folder already); plugins is then only the table of D80.
Where: Machine-config 10; architecture 10 (the ncx.toml sentence); code-guidelines 11; implementation 17 P7-01, P7-02. Code: src/Ncx.Config/ProjectSettingsLoader.cs ReadPluginSettings (TODO(question) at line 67); ProjectSettings (Plugins, PluginSettings).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27: the library does not answer this (searched 'TOML', 'Plugin', 'Plug-in', 'Konfigurationsdatei', 'Konfigurationsdatei' plus 'Abschnitt', 'DLL', 'Assembly', 'ini' across the whole library. I re-ran the two that matter over the whole text cache: 'TOML' returns zero hits in 1642 manuals, and 'Plug-in'/'Plugin' returns four, all unrelated (an Okuma Acrobat Reader plug-in note, Siemens HMI graphic plug-ins, a Unisign USB mouse note). No control or builder manual bears on it: this is a question about the shape of NCXchange's own ncx.toml, and the manuals describe controls and machines, not an application's configuration file, so the draft's own reasoning — that TOML cannot have plugins as both an array and a table, so the list moves into the table as assemblies — is the only evidence there is). The recommendation above stands for the maintainer.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

`[plugins]` holds `assemblies = ["MyShop.NcxPlugins.dll"]`, and each `[plugins.<name>]` holds that plugin's settings (D80). No plugin may be named 'assemblies'. A top-level array `plugins = [...]` is CFG003 (wrong type). 'ncx plugin build' adds to assemblies.
