#### D260 Siemens G75 fixed points against HOME POINT
Question: Controller-mapping 1 (HOME row) reads G74 as HOME, the reference point, and 'G75 X0 Z0 FP=2 = HOME X Z POINT=2 (fixed points 1..4)'. Language 4.3, VM 3 step 5 and machine-config 4 make HOME without POINT, and POINT=1, reference point 1 (home), and POINT=2 home2. So G75 FP=1 reads as the point of G74, and siemens 3 does not say what G75 without FP approaches. The [home] comment of millturn1.toml ('fixed points 1..4 for the second and further reference points') reads a third way. Case: G75 Z0 of the DMG TopSolid programs (controller-mapping 8, the paragraph on the Siemens machines of the corpus). SiemensFrames.ReadHome takes the missing FP as 1 and writes HOME Z POINT=1. The Siemens compiler writes POINT=1 as G74 Z1=0, which is another position wherever fixed point 1 is not the reference point.
Recommendation: Confirm from the 840D sl manual that G75 without FP approaches fixed point 1 (our reading, not in the documents). POINT keeps its meaning in machine-config 4. G75 FP=2 to FP=4 read as POINT=2 to 4, as the HOME row and both Siemens [home] point templates write. G75 FP=1, and G75 without FP, stay RAW:SIEMENS with a WARNING, because fixed point 1 is no reference point of machine-config 4 (D5). The HOME row and the millturn1.toml comments say so; the compiler does not change. Alternative: on a Siemens machine POINT=n is fixed point n and HOME without POINT is the reference point. This needs [[axis]] keys for the fixed points, and POINT=1 no longer equals HOME. Second alternative: keep the reader as coded, which is right only where fixed point 1 is the reference point.
Where: controller-mapping 1 (HOME row, Siemens cell), 8 (the G75 Z0 case); controllers/siemens.md 3 (G75 bullet); machine-config 4 (home, home2) only for the alternative; docs/spec/examples/machines/millturn1.toml:35 and machines/millturn1.toml:35 (point comment), machines/siemens-840dsl-mill.toml:44. Code: src/Ncx.Readers/Siemens/SiemensFrames.cs ReadHome (TODO at 293); src/Ncx.Compilers/Siemens/SiemensFrames.cs WriteHome. Test: tests/Ncx.Readers.Tests/Siemens/SiemensFrameTests.cs G74G75AndPreseton_AreHomeAndSetpos.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: G75 without FP approaches fixed point 1 — the manual says a missing FP, a missing fixed-point number or FP=0 is interpreted as FP=1 — so the reader's assumption is confirmed and G75 Z0 of the DMG programs is fixed point 1. But the recommendation's split does not survive the same pages: fixed points 1 to 4 are all machine-coordinate positions held in MD30600 $MA_FIX_POINT_POS, meant for tool-change, loading and pallet-change points, and G74 is a different function altogether, reference-point travel onto the reference mark after power-on. Fixed point 2 is therefore no more a reference point than fixed point 1, so reading FP=2..4 as HOME POINT=2..4 while keeping FP=1 RAW has no basis in the control. Either every G75 stays RAW:SIEMENS with a WARNING, or take the draft's first alternative and let POINT=n mean fixed point n on a Siemens machine with HOME without POINT meaning G74 — that is the split the control actually has.
Evidence: SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D Grundlagen, Programmierhandbuch 03/2013, p. 378 (Syntax G75 <Achsname><Achsposition> ... FP=<n>, fixed-point number 1 to 4. The position value "ist ohne Bedeutung" and is normally written as 0. A note states that if no FP=<n>, no fixed-point number, or FP=0 is programmed, this is interpreted as FP=1 and fixed point 1 is approached. FP may not exceed the number of fixed points configured for each programmed axis (MD30610).); SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D Grundlagen, Programmierhandbuch 03/2013, p. 377 (G75 moves axes individually and independently to fixed points in the machine room such as tool-change, loading and pallet-change points. The fixed points are positions in the machine coordinate system held in machine data MD30600 $MA_FIX_POINT_POS[n], at most four per axis, and they can be approached from any NC program independently of the current tool or workpiece position.); SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D Grundlagen, Programmierhandbuch 03/2013, p. 376-377 (Section 14.4, G74 Referenzpunktfahren, is a different function: after switching the machine on, with incremental measuring systems, every slide must be driven onto its reference mark before motion can be programmed, and G74 does that from the NC program, written in its own block as G74 X1=0 Y1=0 Z1=0 A1=0 with the machine-axis addresses.); SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D Grundlagen, Programmierhandbuch 03/2013, p. 379 (The worked example is a tool change: with MD30600 holding 151.6 for X (AX1) and 17.3 for Z (AX3) at fixed point 1, the block N120 G75 X0 Z0 FP=1 M0 drives X to 151.6 and Z to 17.3 in the machine coordinate system, each axis at its own maximum speed, and the next block returns to the position of N110 with the zero offset active again.).

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep the recommendation's split, but on a different basis. G74 maps to HOME (no POINT), the counterpart of Fanuc G28. G75 FP=2..4 maps to HOME POINT=2..4, the counterpart of Fanuc G30 P2..P4, whose 2nd to 4th reference points are parameter-set machine positions just like MD30600. G75 FP=1, and G75 without FP (which the manual defines as FP=1), stay RAW:SIEMENS with a WARNING: NCX has no POINT for it, because POINT=1/home is the reference point that G74 approaches. The compiler is unchanged. Fix the millturn1.toml comment to "fixed points 2..4 for POINT=2 and further; FP=1 is not written".
Basis: manual + logical
Source: SINUMERIK 840D sl/828D Grundlagen 03/2013 p.376-379 (connector): a missing FP means FP=1, fixed points live in MD30600, and G74 is reference-point travel. Siemens 802D sl manual on G75: https://manualslib.com/manual/1229863/Siemens-Sinumerik-802d-Sl.html?page=236. The manual answer's two options would either make every G75 non-portable or change what POINT means per family. The Fanuc G28/G30 analogy keeps one meaning across controls.
Differs from the recommendation: no. The reasoning changes: FP=2..4 are "further machine fixed points", not reference points.
Confidence: medium
Code impact: SiemensFrames.ReadHome: missing FP or FP=1 becomes RAW plus WARNING; comment fix in millturn1.toml (both copies).

### Eighth round: needed before release 1.0

#### D263 Defaults and limits of the [format] keys
Question: Machine-config 2 gives example values but no defaults for line_ending, block_numbers (with start and step), max_line_length and comment_charset. It does not say what a line longer than max_line_length does. For comment_charset it names only "ASCII" ('umlauts are transliterated'). It names no other value, and it does not say what becomes of a non-ASCII character that is no umlaut (Ø, °, é). The controller chapters fix some values. heidenhain 1 and 8 rule 1 number Klartext blocks consecutively from 0, as the machine-config 2 comment does. fanuc 10 rule 5 transliterates comments to ASCII. siemens 1 ends blocks with the line feed and allows at most 512 characters per block. doosan-puma-2600sy, mori-ntx1000-mapps, nakamura-ntjx, dmg-ctx-840d and millturn1 leave out max_line_length and comment_charset. siemens-840dsl-mill sets max_line_length = 0 (unlimited) where siemens 1 gives 512. Main writes LF and no block numbers, with start 10 and step 10 when block_numbers is enabled without them. It keeps a longer line with the WARNING CMP021. Without comment_charset, or with any value other than ASCII, it writes comments unchanged; under ASCII it writes ? with CMP022 for any other non-ASCII character. So a Fanuc machine without comment_charset writes umlauts (against fanuc 10 rule 5), and a Heidenhain machine without block_numbers writes Klartext without block numbers (against heidenhain 1).
Recommendation: A key left out takes the value that its controller chapter fixes, as program_layout (wave-3 question 3) and decimal_separator (wave-1 question 64) do. On Heidenhain that means block numbers from 0 in steps of 1 (heidenhain 1, 8 rule 1). On Siemens it means line_ending LF and max_line_length 512 (siemens 1). comment_charset defaults to "ASCII" on every family: fanuc 10 rule 5 requires it, and it is what the three shipped files that set the key write. Everything else keeps main: LF, no block numbers, start 10 and step 10 when enabled without them (the machine-config 2 example), and max_line_length 0. A longer line stays a WARNING. Our reading, not in the documents: a control that takes no longer block refuses the file rather than running it wrong. A non-ASCII character without a transliteration stays ? with CMP022. comment_charset takes "ASCII" or "UTF-8" (comments unchanged), and any other value is a CFG ERROR at load. Reason: every default is then either what the control requires or what main already writes. Alternative: the compiler requires these keys and reports a CMP ERROR when one is missing, which is the route D138's recommendation leaves to the compiler; for characters, the base letter by Unicode decomposition (é to e) before falling back to ?. If D229 is answered with its alternative ([format] encoding), comment_charset follows that key.
Where: machine-config 2 (the [format] block and one paragraph after it); heidenhain 1 and 8 rule 1; fanuc 10 rule 5; siemens 1; D138, D229. Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/OutputBuffer.cs (TODO line 8); src/Ncx.Compilers/CommentCharset.cs (TODO line 6); src/Ncx.Config/MachineConfigLoader.Identity.cs (comment_charset values, family defaults as in TemplateSet.DecimalSeparator); machines/siemens-840dsl-mill.toml (max_line_length); tests/Ncx.Compilers.Tests/OutputBufferTests.cs, CommentCharsetTests.cs.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals fix three of the values the recommendation wants as defaults but leave the fallback policy itself to NCX. Siemens: a block ends with LF and may hold at most 512 characters including the comment and the LF, so line_ending LF and max_line_length 512 are the control's own numbers, and an over-long or too complex block is alarm 12540 "Satz zu lang oder zu komplex" with a correction block - the control refuses it rather than running it wrong, which is what the recommendation assumed. Heidenhain: the control numbers the blocks itself in ascending order and generates them together with the BEGIN and END block; the manual's first example runs 0, 1, 2, 3, so start 0 and step 1 are right. For comment_charset = ASCII two families back it: on Fanuc a comment is read into memory but every code not in the manual's code table is skipped and not stored, and on Heidenhain the TNC 640's own automatic import of NC programs removes umlauts.
Evidence: SINUMERIK 840D sl NC-Programmierung, Programmierhandbuch 06/2019 (SW 4.92), 2.2.2.2 Satzregeln, p. 50 (A block ends with the LF character, which need not be typed because the line break produces it, and a block may contain at most 512 characters including the comment and the LF. Block numbers are optional but must be unique within a program for the block search; ascending numbers are recommended. The same text stands in the 2013 Grundlagen volume on page 37.); SINUMERIK 840D sl Parameter / Alarme (BS.000503-DE-000-00), p. 191 (Alarm 12540 "Satz zu lang oder zu komplex": the maximum internal block length after the translator must not exceed 256 characters, which resolving several macros in a block or deep nesting can exceed. The control reacts with a correction block and the alarm display, and the remedy given is to split the block into several.); TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung 10/2019 (NC-SW 34059x-10), 892903-18, p. 90 (Describes the structure of a Klartext program and states that the control numbers the NC blocks of a program in ascending order, the first block being BEGIN PGM with the name and the unit and the last END PGM with the same.); TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung 10/2019 (NC-SW 34059x-10), 892903-18, p. 94 (States that the control generates the block numbers and the BEGIN and END block automatically, and the worked example is numbered 0 BEGIN PGM, 1 BLK FORM 0.1, 2 BLK FORM 0.2, 3 END PGM - consecutive from zero in steps of one.); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), ch. 13 Programmkonfiguration, p. 322-323 (A comment is what stands between the control-out "(" and control-in ")" codes. When a program is read in for memory operation the comment is read in with it, but codes not listed in the appendix code table are skipped and not stored, and skipped codes are neither output nor displayed again. A separate note forbids EOB and % (ER in EIA) inside a comment.); Technisches Handbuch TNC 640, NC-Software 34059x-09, 11/2018, 892899-18, p. 55 and 678 (Heidenhain's own side of the same question. Page 55 describes the automatic import of NC programs and tables in the file manager and says that with NC programs "werden Umlaute entfernt und fehlende Programmende-Kennungen angefügt". Page 678 gives the import rule itself: IMPORT PGM imports NC programs (Klartext "H", DIN "I") "ohne Umlaute". So the control strips umlauts from a program it takes in, which is what an ASCII default writes out.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

A key left out takes its family value. Heidenhain numbers blocks from 0 in steps of 1. Siemens uses line_ending LF and max_line_length 512. comment_charset defaults to "ASCII" on every family and takes "ASCII" or "UTF-8"; any other value is a CFG ERROR. Otherwise main stays: LF, no block numbers, start 10/step 10 when enabled, max_line_length 0. An overlong line is a WARNING (CMP021). A non-ASCII character without a transliteration becomes '?' with CMP022. Fix siemens-840dsl-mill.toml to 512.
Basis: manual
Source: 840D sl SW 4.92 p. 50 (LF, 512 chars); alarms BS.000503 p. 191 (12540); TNC 640 892903-18 p. 90, 94; TNC 640 TH 892899-18 p. 55, 678 (umlauts removed); FANUC B-64484EN p. 322-323 (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: OutputBuffer, CommentCharset, MachineConfigLoader.Identity family defaults; siemens-840dsl-mill.toml.

#### D264 Where a subprogram that no program calls is compiled
Question: Language 4.13 places a SUB after the caller's M30 (Fanuc) or 'after the M30 of every program that calls it' (Heidenhain). VM 3.9 and D99 say the compiler 'emits each SUB section once', and once per calling program where the target needs it. D99 walks a SUB that no program calls once, from the default entry state. For such a SUB, these two rules give one copy and none. Main writes it after the last program under one_file. Under file_per_program it goes into no file, with the WARNING CMP003, and the job compiler does the same. Case: a Fanuc source O0001 ... M30 followed by an uncalled O9010 ... M99. Main reads it, as D210 recommends, as a PROGRAM and a SUB (StructurePass.DecideKinds). Compiled for heidenhain-itnc530, O9010 is lost. The same happens to a hand-written NCX file with an uncalled SUB. The Klartext reader is not affected: it makes an LBL a SUB only when a CALL LBL calls it.
Recommendation: Write every SUB at least once (VM 3.9 'each SUB section once'; language 2 rule 8, nothing disappears silently). Under one_file keep main: after the last program, before the end of the file. Under file_per_program, write it once into the file of the first program, the one that runs (language 4.13), after the subprograms that program calls, and drop CMP003. Reason: the conversion keeps the section, and its label stays local to one program. Alternative: keep main (no file, WARNING CMP003), and write into VM 3.9 and language 4.13 that under file_per_program a subprogram that nothing calls is not compiled. Answer together with D316, the same question for the channel files of a job.
Where: language 4.13 (the placing sentence); VM 3.9; D99 row; architecture 13 (D99 line); heidenhain 8 rule 6; D210 (which uncalled Fanuc O section is a SUB). Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/CompilerBase.Layout.cs OneFile (TODO line 26) and FilePerProgram (TODO line 67); src/Ncx.Compilers/DiagnosticCodes.cs CMP003; src/Ncx.Compilers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainProgramFrame.cs ProgramOf (comment at line 145); src/Ncx.Compilers/JobCompiler.Run.cs ReportUncalledSubs (TODO line 266, wave-3 question 172, D316, which follows the same answer); tests/Ncx.Compilers.Tests/SubprogramTests.cs.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. Write every SUB at least once, as recommended. The manuals do not say where NCX must put a SUB that nothing calls, but they fix the only placement that is safe: subprograms belong behind the block with M2 or M30, and a subprogram that stands before M2/M30 is executed at least once without a call. So an uncalled LBL section written after the M30 of the first program is never reached on the control, while the same section written anywhere before that M30 would be machined. One limit to record: an iTNC 530 main program takes at most 254 subprograms, the TNC 640 any number.
Evidence: iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 267 (Programming notes for subprograms: a main program may contain up to 254 subprograms; they may be called in any order as often as you like; a subprogram may not call itself; program subprograms at the end of the main program, behind the block with M2 or M30; and if subprograms stand in the machining program before the block with M2 or M30, they are executed at least once without being called. The same page gives the mode of operation (the control runs the called subprogram up to LBL 0 and then continues after the call)); TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung, 892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10 (2019), p. 247 (The same notes for the TNC 640, except that a main program may contain any number of subprograms ('beliebig viele'); the rule that a subprogram placed before the M2/M30 block runs once without a call is unchanged). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Write every SUB at least once. Under one_file it goes after the last program, as main does. Under file_per_program it goes once into the first program's file, after that program's subprograms and after its M30/M2. CMP003 goes. For a multi-channel job D316 applies instead: an uncalled SUB goes to a separate library file of the job, since one channel cannot reach another channel's file.
Basis: manual
Source: iTNC 530 340490-05 p. 267 and TNC 640 892903-18 p. 247: subprograms belong after M2/M30, and one placed before runs once without a call (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: CompilerBase.Layout FilePerProgram; JobCompiler.ReportUncalledSubs; CMP003 removed.

#### D266 File names under file_per_program
Question: Machine-config 2 gives file_per_program 'one output file per program' but does not name the files. heidenhain 1 says the program name 'is the file name without .h', and machine-config 10 compiles programs/part-123.ncx to out/dmu50/part-123.h. NAME is optional (language 4.1). Two sections with one NAME are already the ERROR PAR029 (VM 3.6: duplicates are ERRORs before execution), so a name is taken twice only in two ways: by programs without NAME, which all take the NCX file's name, or by a NAME equal to that file name. Main names each file after NAME, else after the NCX file. It gives a name that is already taken _2, _3 without a diagnostic, and it compares names with case. The Heidenhain compiler writes NAME, else the NCX file name, into BEGIN PGM. Case 1: part-123.ncx with two programs without NAME, compiled for heidenhain-itnc530, gives part-123.h and part-123_2.h, and the second file holds BEGIN PGM part-123 MM, against heidenhain 1. Case 2: NAME="SHAFT" and NAME="Shaft" pass the parser and give SHAFT.h and Shaft.h. On the default file systems of Windows and macOS those are one file, so the second replaces the first.
Recommendation: Keep main's names, with three additions. Names are compared without regard to case. A taken name gets _2, _3 in file order, with a WARNING. The name written inside the file (BEGIN PGM, END PGM) is the file's name (heidenhain 1). A program without NAME takes the name of the NCX file (machine-config 10). Reason: no output file replaces another, and the control shows the name the file has. The Siemens compiler already names its units this way (NAME, NUMBER, file stem, _2 with CMP503), and the answer can align the two, including NUMBER before the file stem. Alternative: under file_per_program, a second program without NAME is a CMP ERROR, so the user names it.
Where: machine-config 2 (the program_layout comment) and 10; heidenhain 1 and 8 rule 1; VM 3.6 (duplicates). Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/CompilerBase.Layout.cs FileNameOf (TODO line 185); src/Ncx.Compilers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainProgramFrame.cs NameOf; src/Ncx.Compilers/Siemens/SiemensFile.cs UnitNameOf; src/Ncx.Core/Parsing/StructurePass.cs CheckSectionNames (PAR029). The channel files of a job (wave-3 questions 162, 173 and 174, D310) follow the same rule.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. Keep main's names with the three additions, and constrain the generated name to what the control accepts. The name inside the file is the file's name: the control stores an NC program as a file of the same name and generates the BEGIN and END blocks itself. Limits to honour when _2, _3 is appended: on the iTNC 530 a file name should not exceed 25 characters, may not contain ; * \ / " ? < > or a dot, and no spaces or other special characters, with a maximum path length of 256; on the TNC 640 only A-Z a-z 0-9 _ - are allowed (POSIX, IEEE Std 1003.1-2004) with a path of at most 255 characters. The manuals say nothing about the case of file names on the control, so comparing names without regard to case is a precaution for the host file system (Windows, macOS), not a rule the manuals give either way.
Evidence: TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung, 892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10 (2019), p. 104 (You give an NC program a name when you enter it, and the control stores it in internal memory as a file 'mit dem gleichen Namen'; .H is the Heidenhain-format extension, .I the DIN/ISO one); TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung, 892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10 (2019), p. 105 (File, drive and directory names on the control follow the Posix standard (IEEE Std 1003.1, 2004 Edition). The permitted characters are listed as A-Z and a-z, the digits, underscore and hyphen; the last dot separates the extension, \ and / build the tree, : separates the drive; all other characters are to be avoided. Maximum path length 255 characters. Nothing on this page says whether the control distinguishes case); iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 112 ('Namen von Dateien': the control appends the type extension after a dot; a file name should not exceed 25 characters, otherwise the TNC no longer shows the program name in full; the characters ; * \ / " ? < > and the dot are not allowed, and other special characters, spaces above all, must not be used. The file name must stay short enough that the maximum path length of 256 characters is not exceeded); iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 99, 101 (The first block of a program carries BEGIN PGM, the program name and the unit, the last END PGM with the same; page 101 states that the TNC generates the block numbers and the BEGIN and END blocks automatically, so the name they show is the one entered when the file was opened). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main's names. A program without NAME takes the NCX file stem. Names are compared case-insensitively, and a taken name gets _2, _3 in file order with a WARNING. BEGIN/END PGM carry the file's final name. Align the Siemens unit naming (NAME, NUMBER, stem). The Heidenhain compiler raises a WARNING when a name breaks the control's limits: characters outside A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -, or more than 25 characters on the iTNC 530.
Basis: manual + logical
Source: TNC 640 892903-18 p. 104-105; iTNC 530 340490-05 p. 99, 101, 112 (cnc-manuals). Case-insensitive comparison protects the Windows/macOS file systems.
Differs from the recommendation: yes: adds the file-name-limit WARNING.
Confidence: high
Code impact: CompilerBase.Layout.FileNameOf; HeidenhainProgramFrame.NameOf; SiemensFile.UnitNameOf.

#### D267 auto_preload at the last change and in called subprograms
Question: VM 3.5 inserts 'a preload of the next tool after each change' when 'the program contains no PRELOAD words'. Under auto_preload, machine-config 3 fills the {next} of a change 'from the STATIC look-ahead'. (a) The last change of a program has no next tool. nakamura-ntjx (auto_preload = true, change = "G340 T{tool:02}{offset:02}. A{next:02}.") still needs a value. Main writes A00., that is {next} = 0 as in PRELOAD=0 (language 4.4); controller-mapping 3 reads the A word as PRELOAD. Outside auto_preload, for example in a program with its own PRELOAD words, a change with {next} and no preload pending gets no value, and main reports the ERROR CFG100. (b) VM 3.5 does not say whether the PRELOAD words of a SUB that the program calls count as the program's own. Main counts them, so such a program gets no inserted preload.
Recommendation: (a) Keep 0: after the last change no tool is prepared, which is what PRELOAD=0 means. Write 0 as well wherever a change with {next} has no preload pending, with or without auto_preload. The Nakamura manual 4810004E should confirm that A00. prepares nothing. (b) Keep main: every PRELOAD that the program's run executes counts, including those of the subprograms it calls, and a subprogram that nothing calls counts as a program of its own. Reason for (b): the SUB text is written once (D99), so its PRELOAD words are in the output anyway, and inserted preloads beside them would preselect two tools (the VM 3.5 WARNING, D42). Alternatives: (a) the first tool of the program, prepared for its next run (bar work), with 0 when that tool is already in the spindle; (b) only the program's own section counts.
Where: VM 3.5 (the auto_preload sentence); machine-config 3 (the {next} paragraph); controller-mapping 3 (ATC on turn-mills). Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/CompilerBase.Tools.cs NextOf (TODO line 212); src/Ncx.Compilers/LookAhead.cs MarkProgram (TODO line 359); tests/Ncx.Compilers.Tests/ToolChangeTests.cs.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: (a) Writing A00. at the last change is not the Nakamura convention and A00 has no documented meaning anywhere in the library. A of G340 is the number of the next tool to prepare; the cycle's own step list says the preparation command is issued "only when A value is specified", and the builder's own three-tool ATC example prepares the program's first tool at the last change (`G340 T0303. A01.` shortly before M30) — which is the draft's alternative, not 0. So the last change should write the program's first tool, or no A word at all where the machine file can express that, and the same holds wherever a change with {next} has no preload pending. (b) Nothing in the manuals bears on whether a called subprogram's PRELOAD words count as the program's own; that stays an NCX decision and main's reading is unopposed.
Evidence: Nakamura-Tome Precision Turning Center Programmierhandbuch 1, 4810004ECL-1, p. 326 (chapter 22-1-1, step list) (Step (9) of the [G340 Funktion] sequence is "Befehl für Vorbereitung des nächsten Werkzeugs (nur bei Programmierung des A-Werts)", beside step (12) "T-Befehl ... & M/S-Befehl (nur bei Programmierung des M/S-Werts)". So the preparation happens only when A is written); Nakamura-Tome Programming Manual (WY-250L), 4810004EEE, 2020, p. 372 (chapter 22-1-1) (The corpus machine's own manual, same step list in English: "(9) Next tool preparation command (only when A value is specified)"); Nakamura-Tome Programming Manual (WY-250L), 4810004EEE, 2020, p. 378 (chapter 22-1-2, Program example for ATC cycle) (The worked three-tool program runs `G340 T0101. A02.`, `G340 T0202. A03.`, then at the last change before M30 `G340 T0303. A01.; Tool exchange command for T0303 & Next tool preparation command for T01`. The last change prepares tool 1, the program's first tool; no A00 appears. The identical example stands in the 2013 German volume 4810004ECL-1 on page 331); Nakamura-Tome Programming Manual (WY-250L), 4810004EEE, 2020, p. 373 (chapter 22-1-1, address list) (`G340 T ;` basic command, `G340 T A M S E Z B K D X ;` detail command. "T : Tool exchange No. (Not omissible)", "A : Next tool No. to be prepared (Not omissible) ... Be sure to put an decimal point for A value (An example: 'A12.') ... (Specifying G341 performs the same operation as A value.)", while M and S are marked "(Omissible)". The German 4810004ECL-1 page 327 says the same with "Stets anzugeben" for T and A); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch (Walter Meier, 2019), p. 161, 165 and 166 (Page 161 gives `G340 T_ A_ M_ S_ B_ (W_)` and says "Im G340 ist die Angabe der Werkzeugnummer mit Offsetnummer zwingend erforderlich, alle anderen Angaben können weggelassen werden." Pages 165 and 166 write `G340 T006006 A07` beside two blocks `G340 T006006` with no A word at all); Nakamura-Tome Precision Turning Center Programmierhandbuch 1, 4810004ECL-1, p. 332 (chapter 22-3); the same text on page 380 of 4810004EEE (G341 T is a separate next-tool preparation command; preparation is "normalerweise" programmed with the A value of G340 and G341 is used for maintenance or when only the preparation is wanted).

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

(a) At the last change, {next} takes the program's first tool. This is the builder's own example (G340 T0303. A01.) and the common CAM post convention. Where the first tool is the tool being changed in (a one-tool program), still write that number and add a WARNING "no other tool to prepare". Never write 0/A00., which has no documented meaning. A change with {next} and no preload pending, outside auto_preload, fills {next} the same way, from the STATIC look-ahead: the next tool changed in, else the first tool. CFG100 remains only where the look-ahead knows no tool at all. (b) Keep main: the PRELOAD words of called subprograms count as the program's own.
Basis: manual + web
Source: Nakamura 4810004EEE p.372-373, 378 and 4810004ECL-1 p.326-327, 331 (connector): A is "not omissible" and the example prepares T01 at the last change. Mastercam last-tool preload pattern (next tool = 1 at the last tool): https://www.emastercam.com/forums/topic/90565-last-tool/
Differs from the recommendation: yes. The value is the first tool, not 0.
Confidence: high
Code impact: CompilerBase.Tools.NextOf (first-tool fallback plus WARNING); LookAhead unchanged.

#### D269 ROT of a tilt in the [transform] templates
Question: Language 4.2 (ROT row, D82) keeps ROT as written and lets only 'a target that has no such option' ignore it with a WARNING. Controller-mapping 1 (MOVE, ROT row) and heidenhain 3 give Heidenhain TABLE ROT and COORD ROT on PLANE, and phase 3 P3-04 writes PLANE 'with MOVE and ROT from [transform]'. Machine-config 5 gives [transform] a `move` map for {move}, but no key or placeholder for ROT. HeidenhainChain.WriteTilt therefore drops ROT=COORD with a WARNING (HeidenhainRotNotWritten) and writes nothing for ROT=TABLE. So PLANE SPATIAL SPA+0 SPB+45 SPC+0 TURN FMAX COORD ROT reads as TILT ... MOVE=TURN ROT=COORD (heidenhain 7 rule 6) and compiles back without COORD ROT. The documents also do not say which of the two the iTNC 530 takes when a PLANE names neither; the reader then writes no ROT, which NCX reads as TABLE.
Recommendation: Add `rot = { TABLE = "TABLE ROT", COORD = "COORD ROT" }` to [transform], next to `move`. Add the placeholder {rot} (the ROT of the block, TABLE when the block has none) to the list in the introduction (together with D152) and to the Heidenhain TILT_ON and TILT_AXIS_ON examples: 'PLANE SPATIAL SPA{a} SPB{b} SPC{c} {move} {rot}'. A machine without the map ignores ROT with the WARNING of language 4.2, as coded now, so Fanuc and Siemens files need nothing. Reason: it follows the `move` pattern, and the template stays the machine's business. Confirm on the iTNC 530 which option applies when a PLANE names neither. If it is COORD ROT, the reader writes ROT=COORD for such a PLANE (heidenhain 7 rule 6), and a machine can map COORD = "" to reproduce the source. Alternative: no key; heidenhain 8 gets a rule that the compiler itself appends TABLE ROT or COORD ROT after the template.
Where: machine-config introduction (placeholder list) and 5 ([transform] move, the Heidenhain TILT_ON and TILT_AXIS_ON comments); controllers/heidenhain.md 8 (and 7 rule 6 if the default is COORD ROT); src/Ncx.Core/Machine/TransformTable.cs; src/Ncx.Config/MachineConfigLoader.Functions.cs and Templates/Placeholder.cs; src/Ncx.Compilers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainChain.cs WriteTilt (TODO(question) at line 269).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. Add the rot map and the placeholder {rot} as recommended, but with two manual facts and without two of the previous claims. First, the confirmation the draft asks for is not in the library for the iTNC 530: only the TNC 640 manual names a default ('if no transformation type was chosen, the control uses COORD ROT for the PLANE functions'); no iTNC 530 edition in the library names one, so a Heidenhain reader that emits ROT=COORD for a PLANE naming neither rests on a TNC 640 sentence carried over and should be confirmed on the machine. Second, {rot} is pointless in the TILT_AXIS_ON template: with PLANE AXIAL the transformation types COORD ROT and TABLE ROT have no effect at all, as they also have none when the tilt leaves no free rotary axis, and this the iTNC 530 manuals state themselves. Leaving {rot} out of TILT_AXIS_ON therefore costs nothing on the control — but the ROT must then be reported, not dropped in silence.
Evidence: TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung, 892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10 (2019), p. 436 (The table of effects of COORD ROT and TABLE ROT closes with the sentence that if no transformation type was chosen, the control uses COORD ROT for the PLANE functions. COORD ROT positions the free rotary axis to 0 and orients the working-plane coordinate system to the programmed spatial angle; TABLE ROT orients the free rotary axis instead, in two cases distinguished by whether SPA or SPB is non-zero); TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung, 892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10 (2019), p. 435 (Entering COORD ROT or TABLE ROT is optional; the two act only through the axis position of a so-called free rotary axis, so their effect depends on the programmed spatial angles and the kinematics. Two programming notes: if the tilt produces no free rotary axis the two have no effect, and with the function PLANE AXIAL they have no effect); iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 452, 457 (Page 457, 'Auswahl der Transformationsart (Eingabe optional)': for machines with a C rotary table, COORD ROT rotates only the coordinate system and leaves the table where it is (the compensation is computed), TABLE ROT positions the table to the tilt angle and compensates by turning the workpiece. Both pages state that with PLANE AXIAL the functions SEQ, TABLE ROT and COORD ROT have no function. Neither page names a default); iTNC 530, Die PLANE-Funktion (2002), p. 19 (The short PLANE briefing gives the same two options as optional input and adds that the choice of transformation type acts only with rotary tables, and only where the plane definition is such that the transformation can be carried out in a single axis). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

NCX keeps its defined meaning for ROT: absent means TABLE (language 4.2 unchanged), so a program means the same on every control. The Heidenhain compiler always writes the transformation type explicitly, COORD ROT or TABLE ROT (as D191). The Heidenhain reader writes ROT=COORD for a PLANE that names neither, since COORD ROT is the Heidenhain default (TNC 640); for the iTNC 530, which names no default, the same reading is assumed by family continuity. Add `rot = { TABLE = "TABLE ROT", COORD = "COORD ROT" }` to [transform] with the placeholder {rot} for TILT_ON. A ROT on a TILT_AXIS block (PLANE AXIAL), or on a tilt that leaves no free rotary axis, gets an INFO "ROT has no effect" and is not written; never dropped silently. A machine without the map ignores ROT with the WARNING of language 4.2.
Basis: manual + logical
Source: TNC 640 Klartext 892903-18 p.435-436 (default COORD ROT); iTNC 530 Klartext 340490-05 p.452, 457 (optional entry, no default named) (connector). Reconciled on recording with D191: an NCX program must not depend on each control's own default, so the default is fixed in NCX and written out explicitly.
Differs from the recommendation: yes: the reader maps an absent Heidenhain ROT to COORD, and the compilers always write it.
Confidence: medium
Code impact: TransformTable plus loader `rot` key; placeholder {rot}; HeidenhainChain.WriteTilt; Heidenhain reader PLANE without ROT -> ROT=COORD.

#### D270 Name after CYCL DEF n in compiled Klartext
Question: Heidenhain.md 1, 2, 3 and 5 write every cycle with the name the control puts after the number: CYCL DEF 200 BOHREN, 247 INIT. REF.PKT, 7.0 NULLPUNKT, 9.0 VERWEILZEIT, 32.0 TOLERANZ. BOHREN.h adds 201 REIBEN, 203 UNIVERSALBOHREN and 207 GEW.-BOHREN GS NEU. Heidenhain 8 rule 7 says only 'CYCL DEF with the Q parameters in the control's order', and machine-config 6 has no key for the name. The phase 3 comparison rules drop only block numbers, comments and blank lines, so the P3-04 acceptance needs the names. HeidenhainCycles.s_names hard-codes the four names from BOHREN.h and writes the number alone for every other cycle, for example a CYCL DEF 251 or a native CYCLE:HEIDENHAIN=n. The documents do not say whether the control loads a CYCL DEF without its name, or with the name in another dialog language (the documented names are German).
Recommendation: Write the name. Add an optional catalog entry key `title` to machine-config 6: the text the compiler writes after CYCL DEF n, which the reader ignores. cycles/heidenhain.toml carries the four names from BOHREN.h. A native CYCLE:HEIDENHAIN=n takes the title of the catalog entry with that number, and an entry without a title is written with the number alone. The documented names of cycles 7, 8, 9, 10 and 247 (heidenhain 1, 3 and 5) stay in the compiler. TOLERANZ of cycle 32 (heidenhain 2) stays in the [tolerance] templates of the machine file. Reasons: cycle data belongs in the catalog, not in the compiler (D76). A shop with an English dialog overrides the title in its machine file (key by key, D140). Confirm on the iTNC 530 whether a CYCL DEF n loads without a name, or with another name. If it does, the alternative is to write the number alone and add to the comparison rules that the text after the cycle number of a CYCL DEF line counts as a comment.
Where: machine-config 6 (entry keys); controllers/heidenhain.md 8 rule 7; cycles/heidenhain.toml (200, 201, 203, 207); src/Ncx.Core/Machine/CycleEntry.cs; src/Ncx.Config/Cycles/CycleCatalogLoader.Entries.cs (s_entryKeys); src/Ncx.Compilers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainCycles.cs s_names and Head (TODO(question) at line 26); for the alternative, 13-phase-3 'Comparison rules' and code-guidelines 8.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: The control fact the draft asks to confirm is settled: the iTNC 530 cycles manual states outright, in its conventions for NC programs read in from older controls or created externally by a CAM system or an ASCII editor, that cycle names and comments need not be given, and that on reading the program in, the iTNC adds the cycle names and comments itself according to the set dialog language. So CYCL DEF 200 alone loads, and the catalog key `title` proposed in the recommendation is not needed to make the output run. Two conventions from the same page belong in heidenhain 8 rule 7: for cycles above 200 every continued line ends with the tilde and the last parameter of the cycle carries none (already the case), and for cycles below 200 a cycle text must not end with a dot.
Evidence: iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Zyklen-Programmierung, 670 388-12, NC-SW 340490-07 (2011), p. 50 ('Allgemeine Hinweise' for NC programs read in from old TNC controls or created externally, by a CAM system or an ASCII editor. For cycles above 200: mark each line end with the tilde, the last parameter of the cycle may carry none, and cycle names and comments 'müssen nicht zwingend angegeben sein' — on reading the program into the control, the iTNC adds the cycle names and comments according to the set dialog language. For cycles below 200: make sure no cycle text ends with a dot, because older dialog-language texts were not always converted correctly); TNC 640 Zyklenprogrammierung, 892905-28 (EN) and 892905-18 (DE), NC-SW 34059x-10 (2019), p. 163 (EN) (not in the connector); the German edition 892905-18 has the same example on page 168 (The same thread-milling programming example reads '14 CYCL DEF 200 DRILLING' with parameter comments ';SET-UP CLEARANCE' in the English edition and '14 CYCL DEF 200 BOHREN' with ';SICHERHEITS-ABST.' in the German one, which shows in the editions what page 50 of the iTNC 530 cycles manual states as a rule: the text after the number is the control's dialog-language name). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Add the optional catalog key `title`. The compiler writes `CYCL DEF n <title>` where the entry has one and `CYCL DEF n` alone otherwise, with no diagnostic: the control adds the name itself in its dialog language when it reads the program in. cycles/heidenhain.toml carries the four BOHREN.h names, and the names of 7, 8, 9, 10 and 247 stay in the compiler. Heidenhain 8 rule 7 gains the two page-50 conventions: for cycles above 200, a tilde at every continued line end and none on the last parameter; for cycles below 200, no cycle text ending with a dot. Drop the "confirm on the iTNC 530" step.
Basis: manual
Source: iTNC 530 Zyklen 670388-12 p.50 (connector): cycle names and comments need not be given, and the iTNC adds them per the dialog language. TNC 640 Zyklen 892905-18 p.168.
Differs from the recommendation: no. The confirmation it asked for is supplied, and the number-only fallback is now known to be valid.
Confidence: high
Code impact: CycleEntry/CycleCatalogLoader `title`; HeidenhainCycles.Head reads the title instead of s_names.

#### D271 LBL numbers the Klartext compiler writes
Question: Klartext labels are program-local, and the LBL sections of the subprograms stand inside every calling program (heidenhain 1; language 4.13). Language 4.9, however, keeps a LABEL unique only per program or subprogram, lets a LABEL or SUB name be an identifier, and allows LABEL=0. In Klartext, LBL 0 ends a subprogram. HeidenhainLabels.Check reports CMP116 for an LBL written twice in one program or written as LBL 0, and renumbers nothing. HeidenhainFlow.Label writes an identifier as LBL "NAME", which heidenhain 1 gives only 'on newer controls' without naming the iTNC 530. These are refused today: a Fanuc reading with LABEL=100 (N100, a GOTO target) next to SUB=BEGIN NAME=100 (O0100); LABEL=1 in two subprograms of one program; and LABEL=0. If the iTNC 530 takes no names, every WHILE_12 or IF_7 label that the readers lower (controller-mapping 6) is refused as well.
Recommendation: The compiler numbers the LBLs of each Klartext program itself. A LABEL or SUB name that is a number other than 0 and unique in that program keeps its number. Every other one (a number taken twice, 0, an identifier or a string) gets the next free number above the highest in the program, in block order. The compiler already numbers the LBL of JUMP=END this way (HeidenhainFlow.EndLabel). The Fanuc compiler numbers identifier labels the same way (FanucLabels.Number), but that code is itself an open marker (wave-3 question 69, D277), so answer both together and make them agree. CMP116 goes, LBL "NAME" is never written, and heidenhain 8 gets one rule. Reason: an LBL is only a jump or call target, so the output is valid whatever the iTNC 530 accepts. A program read from Klartext keeps its numbers, because its labels are already unique. Alternative: renumber only duplicates and 0, and write names as LBL "NAME" once the maintainer confirms that the iTNC 530 accepts them (CMP116 for names otherwise).
Where: heidenhain.md 1 (LBL "NAME") and 8 (a new rule, or rule 6); controller-mapping 6 (LABEL row, optional). Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainLabels.cs Check (TODO(question) at line 22); HeidenhainFlow.cs Label (TODO(question) at line 19), EndLabel, WriteLabel, WriteJump, WriteRepeat; HeidenhainSubprograms.cs WriteBegin and CallLine; CMP116 in DiagnosticCodes.Heidenhain.cs. Related: wave-3 questions 49 and 69 (D277; src/Ncx.Compilers/Fanuc/FanucLabels.cs Number, TODO(question) at line 80).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: Number as recommended, but bound the numbers to the target control's range and drop the premise that the iTNC 530 takes no names. Label numbers run 1 to 999 on the iTNC 530 from NC-SW 340 49x-01 on (1 to 254 on the older 340422 software, 1 to 65535 on the TNC 640); each number or name may be set only once per program, and LBL 0 is reserved for the subprogram end, may stand any number of times, and cannot be called (CALL LBL 0 is not allowed). So the renumbering rule reads 'the next free number in the target control's label range', not 'above the highest in the program'. LBL "NAME" need not be forbidden: from that software level the iTNC 530 accepts label names in LBL SET and LBL CALL (softkey LBL-NAME) and as the jump target of FN 9 to FN 12, the manual's own examples being GOTO LBL "UPCAN25" and GOTO LBL "ANYNAME"; heidenhain 1's 'on newer controls' is imprecise and should name the software level instead.
Evidence: iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 266 (Labels get a number between 1 and 999 or a name you define; each label number or name may be set only once per program with LABEL SET, and setting one twice gives an error message when the LBL SET block is closed (MP7229 can limit the check in very long programs). LABEL 0 marks a subprogram end and may therefore be used as often as you like. The number of label names is limited only by internal memory); iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 11 (The list of new functions of software 340 49x-01 against the predecessors 340 422-xx / 340 423-xx records that the number of available label numbers was raised to 1000 and that label names can now be given as well, and that FN 9 to FN 12 can use label names as jump targets); iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 267, 292 (Page 267: CALL LBL 0 is not allowed, since it would call a subprogram end; the softkey LBL-NAME switches both LBL SET and LBL CALL to text entry. Page 292: if a jump condition is met the control continues at the LBL programmed behind the condition, and the softkey table's examples are FN 9: IF +Q1 EQU +Q3 GOTO LBL "UPCAN25" and FN 12: IF+Q5 LT+0 GOTO LBL "ANYNAME" beside numeric targets); iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340422 (2004), p. 492 (The older iTNC 530 software level: labels get a number between 1 and 254, no names are mentioned at all, each number may be set only once per program, and LABEL 0 marks a subprogram end and may be used as often as you like); TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung, 892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10 (2019), p. 246, 248 (On the TNC 640 labels get a number between 1 and 65535 or a name; the same once-per-program rule and the same reservation of LBL 0 apply, CALL LBL 0 is not allowed, and a call target may also be given as the label name held in a QS string parameter (softkey QS)). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

The compiler numbers the labels of each Klartext program. A numeric LABEL or SUB name that is unique, not 0 and within the target's range keeps its number. Every other one (a duplicate, 0, an identifier, a string, or a number out of range) gets the next free number in the target's label range, in block order. The range is a new optional machine key `[format] label_max`, default 999 (iTNC 530 from 340 49x; 254 for 340422, 65535 for the TNC 640). If no free number is left, the result is a CMP ERROR. LBL 0 is written only as the subprogram end, and CALL LBL 0 is never written. LBL "NAME" is never written, because numbers run on every software level. CMP116 goes. Heidenhain 1 replaces "on newer controls" with "from NC-SW 340 49x-01". Answer D277 so that the Fanuc numbering agrees.
Basis: manual + logical
Source: iTNC 530 Klartext 340490-05 p.11, 266-267, 292; 340422 p.492; TNC 640 Klartext 892903-18 p.246, 248 (connector). Names are accepted only from 340 49x, so numbers are the form every target loads.
Differs from the recommendation: yes. Numbers are bounded by the target range (a new key) instead of "above the highest".
Confidence: high
Code impact: HeidenhainLabels (renumber in range, CMP116 removed); HeidenhainFlow.Label/EndLabel; machine-config `label_max`.

#### D272 A RETURN before the end of a Klartext subprogram, and a RETURN under IF
Question: Machine-config 2 writes sub_end 'for SUB=END and RETURN', so the compiler writes LBL 0 where a RETURN stands inside a subprogram (HeidenhainFlow.ReturnLabel). In Klartext, however, LBL 0 also closes the section. Heidenhain 7 rule 3 reads 'LBL n closed by LBL 0' as a subprogram; the reader closes the section at the first LBL 0 (HeidenhainLabels.DecideSubs) and keeps a later LBL 0 RAW. Case: SUB=BEGIN NAME=5, JUMP=7 IF={$Q1 > 0}, RETURN, LABEL=7, LINE X=10, SUB=END compiles to LBL 5, FN 11 ... GOTO LBL 7, LBL 0, LBL 7, L X+10, LBL 0. Read back, the SUB ends at the first LBL 0, and the jump inside it names a label outside its section (the pre-pass ERROR of VM 3.6). The same form leaves no conditional return. Language 4.9 lets RETURN return early 'for example under a condition', but IF needs a JUMP or CALL in its block (language 5 rule 5, PAR016). So a RETURN can have a condition only as RETURN plus JUMP under IF, which is D221's construct and whose JUMP the VM never reaches. LBL 0 takes no condition, so the compiler reports that block (CMP101). A RETURN under IF in a program, by contrast, is already written as the conditional FN jump to the LBL before the M30.
Recommendation: The Klartext compiler writes a RETURN before the end of a subprogram as a jump to an LBL m that stands directly before the section's closing LBL 0. Without IF this is FN 9: IF +0 EQU +0 GOTO LBL m. Under IF it is FN 9 to FN 12 with the block's condition. The compiler already writes JUMP=END, and a RETURN in a program, as a jump to an LBL before the M30 (controller-mapping 1, JUMP=END). A RETURN directly before SUB=END writes nothing. Every section then has exactly one LBL 0, and the reader stays as it is. The jump reads back as a JUMP to a LABEL before SUB=END, which returns at the same point, and the CMP101 for a RETURN under IF goes. The JUMP of a RETURN plus JUMP block is still written after the return, where nothing reaches it. If D221 takes its alternative (that JUMP names a label of the caller), such a block becomes the CMP ERROR that D221 names. The machine-config 2 comment then reads: sub_end is written for SUB=END, and for RETURN where the control returns from inside a subprogram (M99, RET). Heidenhain 8 rule 6 gives the Klartext form. The number of LBL m follows D271. Alternative: keep LBL 0 for RETURN, as machine-config 2 reads. Heidenhain 7 rule 3 then adds that an LBL 0 is a RETURN inside the section when it is followed, before the next LBL 0, by an LBL that a jump inside the section names. A RETURN under IF then stays CMP101.
Where: machine-config 2 (sub_end comment); heidenhain.md 7 rule 3 and 8 rule 6; language 4.9 (RETURN row, 'under a condition'). Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainFlow.cs ReturnLabel (TODO(question) markers at lines 250 and 253) and WriteJump, HeidenhainProgramFrame.WriteSubEnd; for the alternative, src/Ncx.Readers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainLabels.cs DecideSubs. Related: D221.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals do not force the change, but they do not stand in its way either, so take the jump form for the round trip as recommended. On the control both forms run: LBL 0 marks a subprogram end and may be used as often as you like, and from the CALL LBL the control works the called subprogram up to the subprogram end LBL 0 and then continues after the call, so an LBL 0 written at an early RETURN returns there and the section's own closing LBL 0 returns on the other path. And the form the recommendation writes is the manual's own idiom: FN 9: IF +0 EQU +0 GOTO LBL 99 is given as the forced jump over a part of a program, and FN 9 to FN 12 are the conditional jumps, with unconditional jumps described as jumps whose condition is always met. What decides is therefore only the NCX side (the reader closes a section at the first LBL 0, and CMP101 for a RETURN under IF), not the control.
Evidence: iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 266-267 (LABEL 0 marks a subprogram end and may therefore be used as often as you like — the one label exempt from the once-per-program rule of page 266; page 267 gives the mode of operation: from the CALL LBL the control works the called subprogram up to the subprogram end LBL 0 and then continues with the block that follows the call); iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 269 (In the CALL PGM programming notes the manual itself uses FN 9: IF +0 EQU +0 GOTO LBL 99 as the way to force a jump over the part of a program that holds the label subprograms — the always-true FN 9 the recommendation writes for a RETURN); iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 292 (If the condition of a jump is met, the control continues the program at the LABEL programmed behind the condition, otherwise it executes the next block; unconditional jumps are described as jumps whose condition is always met, with the example FN 9: IF+10 EQU+10 GOTO LBL1, and FN 9 to FN 12 are the four comparisons). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

A RETURN before the end of a SUB compiles to a jump to an LBL m placed directly before the section's closing LBL 0. Without IF this is `FN 9: IF +0 EQU +0 GOTO LBL m`; under IF it is FN 9..12 with the condition. A RETURN directly before SUB=END writes nothing. Each section keeps exactly one LBL 0, and CMP101 for a RETURN under IF goes. The sub_end comment of machine-config 2 is reworded; LBL m numbering per D271.
Basis: manual
Source: iTNC 530 340490-05 p. 266-267, 269 (FN 9 forced jump idiom), 292 (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: HeidenhainFlow.ReturnLabel/WriteJump.

#### D274 Subprograms as separate .h files
Question: Heidenhain 8 rule 6 writes subprograms as LBL sections after the M30 of every caller, 'or as separate .h files with CALL PGM when the machine setting says so'. Machine-config 2 has no such setting: program_layout has one_file and file_per_program, and file_per_program says 'subprograms copied after the M30 of every caller (Heidenhain)'. The compiler writes every SUB as an LBL section. A separate file would be a program that CALL PGM runs. How such a file ends (D214; a TNC CALL PGM file holds no M30) and how it is named (D215) are both still open.
Recommendation: Strike the option from heidenhain 8 rule 6 for 1.0. Every SUB section is an LBL section after the M30 of each program that calls it, as program_layout = "file_per_program" already says and the code does. Separate subprogram files wait until D214 and D215 settle how a called file ends and how it is named. They then get a program_layout value of their own. Alternative: add a third value now, program_layout = "file_per_section": one file per program and per SUB section, CALL PGM name for CALL=name, and each subprogram file without M30 before END PGM.
Where: heidenhain.md 8 rule 6; machine-config 2 (program_layout, alternative only). Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainSubprograms.cs (TODO(question) at line 14); src/Ncx.Compilers/CompilerBase.Layout.cs. Related: D214, D215.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. Keep the strike for 1.0 as recommended; the manuals settle nothing about a machine or builder setting, but they do settle what D214 and D215 were waiting for, so the option can be specified whenever it is taken up. A program called with CALL PGM needs no LABELs, must not contain M2 or M30 (the manual's own workaround, where the called file holds LBL subprograms, is FN 9: IF +0 EQU +0 GOTO LBL 99 to skip past them), and may not call back into its caller. The called file still ends with END PGM: the TNC 640 checks called programs before running them and aborts with an error if the END PGM block is missing, and it puts out a warning, not an error, when the called program does contain M2 or M30. Given as a bare name the file must lie in the caller's directory, otherwise the full path is required (TNC:\ZW35\SCHRUPP\PGM1.H; the TNC 640 also accepts relative paths such as ..\PGM1.H and DOWN\PGM2.H); a DIN/ISO file is called with the .I extension; Q parameters act globally across the call, so changes in the called file reach the caller; cycle 12 PGM CALL is the equivalent call, and SEL PGM the variable one.
Evidence: iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 269 ('Beliebiges Programm als Unterprogramm': the control runs the calling program until CALL PGM, runs the called program to its end, then continues with the block after the call. Programming notes: the TNC needs no LABELs to use any program as a subprogram; the called program must contain no M2 or M30, and where it defines subprograms with labels you use the jump function FN 9: IF +0 EQU +0 GOTO LBL 99 to force a jump over that part; the called program must contain no CALL PGM back into the caller (endless loop)); iTNC 530 Benutzer-Handbuch Klartext-Dialog-Programmierung, NC-SW 340490-05 (2008), p. 269-270 (Calling: enter the complete path name of the program to be called. The called program must be stored on the TNC's hard disk; if only the program name is entered it must be in the same directory as the calling program, otherwise give the full path, example TNC:\ZW35\SCHRUPP\PGM1.H. For a DIN/ISO program add the file type .I after the name. Any program can also be called through cycle 12 PGM CALL. Q parameters act globally with a PGM CALL, so changes in the called program can affect the caller); TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung, 892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10 (2019), p. 252 (The TNC 640 repeats all three rules for CALL PGM: no labels needed, no CALL PGM back into the caller, and the called NC program must contain no M2 or M30, with the same FN 9: IF +0 EQU +0 GOTO LBL 99 as a replacement; SEL PGM is named for variable calls through string parameters, SEL CYCLE as a further way to call a program, and editing of every called program is locked while the caller runs); TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung, 892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10 (2019), p. 253 ('Prüfung der gerufenen NC-Programme': if the called NC program contains M2 or M30 the control puts out a warning, which it clears by itself as soon as another program is selected; and it checks called programs for completeness before running them — if the NC block END PGM is missing it aborts with an error message. The same page gives the path rules, including the relative forms ..\PGM1.H and DOWN\PGM2.H. This is the D214 fact: a CALL PGM file ends with END PGM and no M30). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Strike the option from heidenhain 8 rule 6 for 1.0. Every SUB is an LBL section after the M30 of each caller. Record the facts for later: a CALL PGM file ends with END PGM, contains no M2/M30, is named by path relative to the caller, and Q parameters are global across the call.
Basis: manual
Source: iTNC 530 340490-05 p. 269-270; TNC 640 892903-18 p. 252-253 (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none.

#### D276 The Fanuc output-habit keys of [format]
Question: 13-phase-3 (Risks) asks for a [format] option rather than a special case for the habits of the Fanuc sources. 12-phase-2 (Risks) and the machine-config status line expect the compilers to add keys. Machine-config 2 names none of them. P3-06 added four keys; only machines/fanuc-mill-30i.toml sets them and only the Fanuc compiler reads them. (1) header: the lines after O, "G0 G40\nG80 G90 G94 G98". Its G codes become the control's active state. Without it the compiler writes G90, and in system A nothing. (2) plane_with_first_motion: N70 G0 G17 X50.4. (3) motion_code_after_tool_change: N3080 G0 G90 X10. after T2 M6 in BOHREN. (4) length_offset_with_tool_axis: G43 H goes into the first block after the OFFSET:LEN word that moves the tool axis in the workpiece frame, N80 G43 Z2. H1. Such a block is a RAPID, LINE or ARC with a word of the tool axis, or a cycle block (the definition that calls at its position, or a CYCLE_CALL), where H stands before F. HOME and G53 end at machine positions and leave it waiting. Main writes it on a line of its own before: a LABEL, JUMP, CALL or RAW block; a skipped block that moves the tool axis or sets the length offset; the line of a SETPOS of the tool axis; the end of a program or subprogram. Are these the right keys, names and values, and is header a template like program_end?
Recommendation: Adopt the four keys as coded. Add them to machine-config 2 with one comment line each, saying that only the Fanuc compiler reads them today, and add one sentence to fanuc 10. header is a template like program_end: normalized per D105, split into lines at \n as machine-config 3 allows, rendered without placeholders, and its G codes are the control's state after it. Each flag is false when left out. The waiting G43 H keeps the places it has in the code. Reasons: with these keys the three round trips reproduce the sources, and no example changes. The places follow language 2 rule 8 (nothing is dropped) and language 4.2 (SETPOS declares the position with the offset active). channel_files (wave-3 questions 173 and 174, D310) is a key of the same kind and can be answered with this one, and so can the motion-code key of D299. Alternative: make the three flags fixed rules of fanuc 10 and keep only header as a key, since G17 with the first motion and G43 with the first tool-axis move are the common Fanuc habit.
Where: machine-config 2 ([format] block); fanuc 10 (new rule); 13-phase-3 Risks; machines/fanuc-mill-30i.toml:31-35; src/Ncx.Core/Machine/OutputFormat.cs:73; src/Ncx.Config/MachineConfigLoader.Identity.cs:124; FanucProgramFrame.WriteHeader; FanucMotion (WORKPLANE); FanucToolWords AfterChange, AddOffsets, WriteWaitingLength; FanucCompiler.TakesWaitingLengthBefore.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. No manual names these keys — the shape of [format] is an NCX decision — but the manuals do justify making all four machine settings rather than fixed rules of fanuc 10. The modal state after power-on or reset is parameter-dependent on every Fanuc (G00 or G01 by 3402 bit 0, G90 or G91 by 3402 bit 3, G17/G18/G19 by 3401 bits 1 and 2), so a header that writes G0 G40 G80 G90 G94 G98 is the machine's own safety block and belongs in the machine file, as the Nakamura habit (`G54 G18 M87` and `G50 S4000`, then `G0 G40 G99 T0505 M8`) shows. For the G43 key, Fanuc's documented format is `G43 Z_H_` and its own drilling example writes `N003 G43 Z0 H11` immediately after the change — but the manual also states that G43 with no motion word simply does not move the axis, so putting H into the first tool-axis block is a habit and main's waiting behaviour is safe either way.
Evidence: FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 62-63, Erläuterung note 1, sub-items (1) to (6) (At power-on or reset the modal G codes go to the states marked in the tables; G20/G21 keep their state, G22/G23 come from 3402 bit 7; the user chooses G00 or G01 with bit 0 (G01) of parameter 3402, G90 or G91 with bit 3 (G91) of 3402, and on a machining centre G17, G18 or G19 with bits 1 (G18) and 2 (G19) of parameter 3401. So the state a program starts from is set per machine, not by the control family. (The earlier run cited this as "notes 1 to 6"; it is note 1 with six sub-items, and notes 5 to 8 on page 62-63 are about something else.)); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual Milling (B-64484EN-2), p. 85-86, section 5.1.15 (Fanuc's own canned-cycle example writes `N002 G90 G00 Z250.0 T11 M6;` for the change and then `N003 G43 Z0 H11;` — the length offset is taken with the first block that moves the tool axis — and repeats the pattern at N012/N013 and N020/N021, with G49 written on the retract block before the next change (`N012 G49 Z250.0 T15 M6;`)); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual Milling (B-64484EN-2), p. 176 to 178, chapter 6.1 (The documented formats are `G43 Z_H_` (compensation A), `G17 G43 Z_H_` (compensation B, with the plane selection in the block) and `G43 α_H_` (compensation C). "Wurde zusammen mit dem Befehl G43, G44 oder G49 kein Verfahrbefehl spezifiziert fährt das Werkzeug nicht entlang der Achse"; with a motion command the coordinate system is shifted first and the tool then moves); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch (Walter Meier, 2019), p. 36 (The builder's model program opens each section with `G10 P10005 R0.4 Q3`, `G54 G18 M87 (SPINDELBREMSE AUS)`, `G50 S4000 (DREHZAHL BEGRENZUNG)`, `G53 X#528 (WZW. *X*)` and then `G0 G40 G99 T0505 M8` — a builder-specific header and a motion code written into the tool block, i.e. exactly the kind of habit that varies per machine rather than per control). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Adopt the four keys as coded (header, plane_with_first_motion, motion_code_after_tool_change, length_offset_with_tool_axis). Each gets one comment line in machine-config 2, which says only the Fanuc compiler reads them. header is a template like program_end (D105 normalisation, split at \n), and its G codes are the control state after it. Each flag defaults to false. The waiting G43 H keeps its coded places.
Basis: manual
Source: FANUC B-64484EN p. 62-63 (power-on modal state is per machine, 3401/3402); B-64484EN-2 p. 85-86, 176-178 (G43 Z_ H_ habit); Nakamura 2019 p. 36 (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none (docs: machine-config 2, fanuc 10).

#### D277 Block numbers of Fanuc labels
Question: Controller-mapping 6 (LABEL row) writes a label as 'Nn targeted by a GOTO', fanuc 1 says N numbers 'need not be in order; they matter as jump targets', and machine-config 2 and fanuc 10 rule 6 number the lines per block_numbers. None says how a label's N shares that numbering. Language 4.9 also allows identifier labels (the Fanuc reader's own WHILE_n, DO_n and IF_n, and the Siemens structure labels) and a conditional JUMP=END ('IF [#503 EQ 0] GOTO 9090 with N9090 M30'), and nothing gives the Fanuc N for either. On main a numeric label keeps its number on a line of its own ('N300'), and block_numbers passes over every number that a label line carries. Identifier labels and the end of a conditional JUMP=END take the numbers after the greatest numeric label of their O program, in file order, with the end last. A source GOTO 9090 therefore compiles back as, for example, GOTO 301.
Recommendation: Keep main and write it into fanuc 10 rule 6 and the Fanuc cell of the controller-mapping 6 LABEL row. A numeric label keeps its number. Identifier labels and the end of a conditional JUMP=END are numbered after the greatest numeric label of the program, in file order, with the end last. block_numbers skips every number a label line carries, so each N names one block. Because the reader keeps no number for JUMP=END, code-guidelines 8 then compares a GOTO target and its N line up to a consistent renumbering of the numbers the compiler chose. Reason: the source numbers survive the round trip, the targets are unique, and no key is needed. Alternative: a [format] key for the first generated label number (for example 9000). Or renumber every label into the block_numbers sequence, which loses the source numbers. Answer together with D271, the numbering of Klartext labels.
Where: controllers fanuc.md 1 (N bullet), 10 rule 6; controller-mapping 6 (LABEL row); machine-config 2 (block_numbers); code-guidelines 8 (comparison rules); src/Ncx.Compilers/Fanuc/FanucCompiler.cs OwnBlockNumber (TODO(question) at line 67); src/Ncx.Compilers/Fanuc/FanucLabels.cs Number (TODO(question) at line 80); src/Ncx.Compilers/OutputBuffer.cs ToText and OwnNumbers; tests/Ncx.Acceptance/NcComparer.cs.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals do not number labels for us, but they fix the constraints and main's rule meets them: N runs from 1 to 99999999, need not be in order and may be omitted block by block; GOTOn branches to that N; the N of a branch target must stand at the start of its block; and a program must not contain two blocks with the same N, because the branch target is then ambiguous and actually changes with parameter 6000 bits MGO and HGO. So keeping a numeric label's own number and numbering the generated labels above the greatest numeric label of the program is compatible with the control — but write the uniqueness as a hard rule in fanuc 10 rule 6, not as a convenience: the compiler must make sure no N it emits, label or block number, repeats another N of the same O program.
Evidence: FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 324, "Satznummer und Satz" (A block may begin with the address N and a number of at most eight digits (1 to 99999999); sequence numbers may stand in any order, individual numbers may be left out, and all or only some blocks of a program may be numbered. N0 must not be used); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 518, section 16.8.1 (`GOTOn ;` branches to sequence number n, 1 to 99999999; a number outside that range raises alarm PS1128 and n may be an expression. The WARNUNG says several blocks of one program must not have the same sequence number, because the GOTO target is then not unique; note 2 says that at the target the sequence number must stand at the beginning of the block, otherwise the branch is impossible); FANUC 30i-B Operator's Manual (B-64484EN), p. 519, section 16.8.2 (With the stored-sequence-number search (parameter 6000 bit 1 MGO or bit 4 HGO set to 1) a duplicated target number before the GOTO is reached, and with both bits cleared the one after it — so a duplicate silently changes which block runs. The VORSICHT adds that branching into a DO-END loop is not possible). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main. A numeric label keeps its number. Identifier labels and the end of a conditional JUMP=END are numbered above the program's greatest numeric label, in file order, with the end last. block_numbers skips every label number. fanuc 10 rule 6 adds a hard rule: no N may repeat within one O program, and the compiler checks this (ERROR on a clash).
Basis: manual
Source: FANUC B-64484EN p. 324, 518-519 (a duplicate N makes the GOTO target depend on 6000 MGO/HGO) (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no (adds the uniqueness check)
Confidence: high
Code impact: FanucLabels/OutputBuffer: assert unique N per O program.
