#### D311 A channel-bound word in a subprogram
Question: D56 and VM 3.8 rule 2a move a word bound to channel n into channel n's program "at the same mark", and duplicate a channels = "all" word behind a generated SYNC. VM 3.9 and D99 write each SUB once, from an unknown state, and run its blocks at every CALL, possibly behind a different mark each time. No document says what the job compiler does with a bound word in a SUB that another channel's program calls, or with a word whose mark in the owning channel stands in a SUB. Case: SUB 100, called twice from channel 1 between different marks, holds SPINDLE_SYNC with [spindle_sync] channel = 2. Main reports the ERROR CMP703 in both cases.
Recommendation: Keep the ERROR CMP703 and write it into VM 3.8 rule 2a. A bound word that must be moved or duplicated may not stand in a subprogram, and neither may the mark it would follow. The author writes such a word in the program, or in a subprogram that only the owning channel calls. Reason: D99 writes each SUB once and requires its text to be right for every caller, while a word taken out of the SUB would need one place per CALL in the other program. Alternative: the job compiler takes the word out of the SUB and places it once per CALL in the owning program, after the mark the calling channel last passed before the word on that call (the STATIC run knows this per call).
Where: VM 3.8 rule 2a, 3.9; implementation 16 P6-02. Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/JobCompiler.Binding.cs:25 (BindWords) and Destination (mark in a subprogram); src/Ncx.Compilers/DiagnosticCodes.Jobs.cs (CMP703).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27: the library does not answer this (searched For the rule itself: Unterprogramm together with M-Code für Warten / WAITM / Synchronisierung, subprogram together with waiting M code, M98 together with waiting M code, across the Fanuc 30i-B Betriebshandbuch, the Nakamura Band 1 and the Siemens 840D sl manuals — no hit. For the worked case: the whole of Nakamura chapter 15 (15-1 M-Codes, 15-2 Hinweise, 15-3 Programmierung per series, 15-3-7 Bemerkungen, 15-4 Einstellen der Spindelphasen-Synchronposition) and chapter 2-4 Steuerung von Mehrbahn-Maschinen. The per-series programming examples in 15-3 (cache pages 256 to 271) are scanned figures with no text layer and could not be read). The recommendation above stands for the maintainer. Nothing in the library says what a control does with a channel-bound code inside a subprogram, so CMP703 stays an NCX choice; the Fanuc 30i-B, the Nakamura Band 1 and the Siemens manuals carry no restriction on waiting or synchronisation codes in a subprogram. The draft's worked case also survives: contrary to a reading of the Nakamura note on page 255 alone, the same manual requires on page 274 that on multi-path NC machines the synchronisation M codes M92, M93, M96 and M97 be programmed with the turret-base selection of the lower unit for the WT/WY, STS, NTJ, NTJ-100, NTJX, NTMX and MX5 machines — which is exactly what examples/machines/nakamura-ntjx.toml line 206 (channel = 2, "the lower unit on NTJX and WY") and VM 3.8 rule 2a say. The manual is inconsistent on the point (pages 255 and 272 say the command may come from either side, and the page-255 note even lists the TW series in both halves of its own sentence), so neither the example machine nor the VM sentence should be changed on this evidence. The pages behind that half of the finding are Nakamura-Tome_Fanuc_Programmierung_Programmierhandbuch-1_4810004ECL-1_DE_2013.pdf: 15-4 on p. 274 (printed 15-21), which lists the turret-base selection per series and names the lower unit for WT/WY, STS, NTJ, NTJ-100, NTJX, NTMX and MX5; 15-1 on pp. 254-255, whose note contradicts itself by putting the TW series in both halves; 15-3-7 on p. 272 (printed 15-19), "Der Befehl kann vom oberen oder unteren Revolver aus gehen"; and 2-4 on pp. 20-22, where each unit has its own program memory and M100 to M199 synchronise the two programs, with no statement anywhere about such a code inside a subprogram.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep ERROR CMP703. A bound word that must be moved or duplicated may not stand in a SUB, and neither may the mark it would follow. Write this into VM 3.8 rule 2a.
Basis: logical
Source: D99 writes each SUB once, valid for every caller, while a moved word would need one place per CALL. The manuals carry no rule.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none.

#### D313 Where a moved word stands in the owning channel's program
Question: D56 and implementation 16 P6-02 move a word bound to channel n "to the owning channel's program at the same mark". They do not say where between that mark and the next it stands. They also do not say what happens when channel n takes no part in the mark before the word (a SYNC whose WITH names other channels, language 4.8). Case: a three-channel job where channel 1 writes FUNC:DOOR=OPEN ([func] DOOR channel = 2) after SYNC=110 WITH=1,3. Main puts the word, as a block of its own, directly after the SYNC of the same release in channel n's program, after any blocks the job compiler inserted there. When no mark precedes the word, it goes after PROGRAM=BEGIN and the start mark. A channel without the same mark is CMP704.
Recommendation: Keep main and write it into VM 3.8 rule 2a: the word stands directly after the SYNC of the same release, and a channel without that mark is the ERROR CMP704. Reason: the release is the only point the two programs share; any later place depends on the timing of the owning channel. Alternatives: when the owning channel takes no part in the mark, use the last mark before the word that both channels pass together; or generate a SYNC between the two channels at the word's place, as for channels = "all", so that the word runs where the author wrote it.
Where: VM 3.8 rule 2a; implementation 16 P6-02. Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/JobCompiler.Binding.cs:196 (Destination); src/Ncx.Compilers/DiagnosticCodes.Jobs.cs (CMP704).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. Keep main, with one qualification the manual forces. Mori Seiki states the rule for the duplicated case: the synchronised-operation code M34/M35 must stand in both the tool-spindle and the turret-2 program, with the program-execution-synchronisation M code "in the block immediately preceding" it, and M480 likewise must stand in both programs with a synchronisation M code "in the block preceding" it. The machine therefore requires the duplicated code to follow a shared wait, which backs CMP704 (a channel that does not take part in the mark cannot take the word); but it does not require the word to be the very next block, and the worked NTX1000 example proves it — M100 (wait), then the per-channel preparation M69/M269, then M480 in both, then M101. "Directly after the SYNC of the same release" is a defensible NCX rule, not one the manual states. Caveats: The manual states the rule for the duplicated (channels = "all") case; the moved (channel = n) case carries over by analogy and is not stated anywhere. "Unmittelbar" (immediately preceding) appears only in note 4 for M34/M35; note 3 for M480 says only "in the block preceding", and the example inserts two blocks between the wait and the code. One detail worth taking into machine-config 5: Mori Seiki requires M480 (and M34/M35) in both programs but says M481 need be written in only one of them, and note 5 on page 540 says the same of M36, so on a real machine "all channels" is a property of the state, not of the whole table, while machine-config puts channels = "all" on the table.
Evidence: Mori-Seiki_NT-NTX-Serie_Programmierung_Programmieranleitung-NTX1000SZM_PX-NT_4-K0DEEN_2011.pdf, 2-1 M34, M35, M36 Synchronbetrieb EIN/AUS, p. 539 (Note 4 requires the same synchronised-operation calling M code (M34 or M35) in both the tool-spindle and the turret-2 program, and requires the program-execution-synchronisation M code in the block immediately preceding the one that carries it, so that the two programs run in step (NT-SZ, NT-SZM). M34 synchronises speed and phase, M35 speed only, M36 cancels either); Mori-Seiki_NT-NTX-Serie_Programmierung_Programmieranleitung-NTX1000SZM_PX-NT_4-K0DEEN_2011.pdf, 2-1, notes 5 to 11, p. 540 (Note 5: the cancel M36 is specified in either the tool-spindle or the turret-2 program; "It is not necessary to specify this M code in both of the programs." The duplication requirement therefore attaches to the state that is switched on, not to the whole M34/M35/M36 table); Mori-Seiki_NT-NTX-Serie_Programmierung_Programmieranleitung-NTX1000SZM_PX-NT_4-K0DEEN_2011.pdf, 1-32 M480/M481 C-Achsen-Synchronisierungsmodus, p. 292-293 (Note 3: specify M480 in both the tool-spindle and the turret-2 program, and in the block preceding the one containing M480 a program-execution-synchronisation M code. Note 5: M481, the cancel, need be specified in only one of the two programs. The example on the facing page runs M45/M245 (a), G28 H0 (b) in both, G43 H3./M211 and G28 U0 per side, M100 (d) in both, M69/M269 (e), M480 (f) in both, M101 (g), machining, M481 in the tool-spindle program only, M102 (j) in both). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main. The word stands directly after the SYNC of the same release in the owning channel's program, as an NCX rule. A channel without that mark is ERROR CMP704. Write this into VM 3.8 rule 2a.
Basis: manual (supporting)
Source: Mori Seiki NTX1000 SZM PX-NT_4 p. 292-293, 539-540 (a duplicated code follows a shared wait in both programs) (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none.

#### D314 start_mark when the channel programs synchronize at it later
Question: Machine-config 5 writes start_mark "as the first block of every channel program", the comment in nakamura-ntjx.toml says "first block of both programs", and language 4.8 calls a SYNC that is the first block after the header the program start synchronization (Nakamura M199). The WY-250L sources wait at M199 after their set-up blocks (path 1 line 22, path 2 line 31), and the reader writes SYNC=199 there. Read literally, the job compiler adds a second M199 after the header, both paths wait twice, and the M9 acceptance (wait codes in the order of the sources) fails. Main writes start_mark only when some channel program does not already pass it as its first mark together with every channel of the job.
Recommendation: Keep main. Reword machine-config 5 and the comment in nakamura-ntjx.toml: the job compiler writes start_mark after the header of every channel program, unless every channel program already passes that mark as its first mark with all channels of the job, wherever that SYNC stands. Reason: the sources are written back as they were, and no program waits at the mark twice. Alternative: always write start_mark after the header, as the text says; the WY pair then waits twice at M199, and M9 compares against a leading extra M199. Where a written start_mark stands beside START_CHANNEL or WAIT_CHANNEL is the separate marker of RunWrittenJob (CMP712), which RF-P6-02 added after this round was drafted.
Where: machine-config 5 ([sync] start_mark); language 4.8 (SYNC row); the start_mark comment in nakamura-ntjx.toml (docs/spec/examples/machines and machines/). Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/JobCompiler.Marks.cs:59 (InsertStartMark, StartsAtMark); tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Jobs/NakamuraJobCompileTests.cs; the marker of RunWrittenJob at src/Ncx.Compilers/JobCompiler.Run.cs:130 (related).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: Keep main and reword machine-config 5 and the comment in nakamura-ntjx.toml. Nakamura's own program-header template puts the program-start synchronization mark at the end of the header — after the macro presets, the G10 machine and work datums, the C-axis release and off codes, the bar-end query and the skipped M99 P9999 bar-change jump — not as the first block, and each program carries exactly one; M199 is otherwise an ordinary wait code of the M100–M199 range, which the builder's own examples also place just before M401 and M30. A start_mark written blindly after the header therefore adds a rendezvous the sources do not have, and the written-back program no longer matches the source. A second correction falls out: on the Super NTJX the same author's header template ends with M198 (SYNCHRONISATION MIT *U* / *O*), not M199, so nakamura-ntjx.toml's start_mark = 199 with the comment "M199 program start synchronization" appears to be taken from the WY-series template; the start mark is a machine fact and should be checked per machine file.
Evidence: Nakamura-Tome_Fanuc-31i-Model-A_Programmierung_Programmieranleitung-NC-Wort-Adresse_DE_2008.pdf, p. 21 (Muster-Programmkopf, Revolver oben and Revolver unten) (The builder's header template for both turrets ends with the same sequence: macro variable presets, G10 machine and external datums, the six G10 L2 program datums, C-axis release and off, M198 "** STANGEN-END ABFRAGE **", the skipped /M99 P9999 bar-change jump, then M199 "(PRG.-START SYNCHRONISATION)", then M01. The mark is the last block of the header, not the first of the program, and each program carries exactly one); Nakamura-Tome_Fanuc_Programmierung_Programmierhandbuch-2_4810004ECL-2_DE_2013.pdf, p. 72 (§30-7 Vorsichtsmaßnahmen (5)) (An ejection-cycle caution whose remedy is to program the wait code before M401: the example shows M199 immediately before M401 and M30 in both the upper and the lower turret program. M199 is a wait mark like any other, not a reserved first block); Nakamura-Tome_Super-NTJX_Programmierung_Liste-M-G-Codes_DE_2016.pdf, p. 2 (The NTJX code list gives M100 bis M199 simply as "WARTEFUNKTIONEN" — one range, with no separate meaning for 199); Nakamura-Tome_Fanuc-18i-TB_Programmierung_Programmieranleitung-NC-Wort-Adresse_DE_2009.pdf, p. 19–20 (Muster-Programmkopf, Revolver oben and Revolver unten) (On the NTJX the same author's header template closes with M198 — "(SYNCHRONISATION MIT *U*)" in the upper turret program and "(SYNCHRONISATION MIT *O*)" in the lower — followed by M01. The start-synchronization mark of this machine is M198, not M199); Nakamura-Tome_Fanuc-16-21i_Bedienung_NT-Nurse-Bedienungsanleitung_4800001EBG_DE_2013.pdf, p. 118 (Kap. 11 Transferzyklus G196, HINWEIS 6) (The waiting M code M199 is already defined at the start of the transfer cycle, so M199 must not be commanded directly before that cycle; otherwise the control issues the alarm "Wrong waiting M code input". The statement is scoped to that cycle); Mori-Seiki_NT-NTX-Serie_Programmierung_Programmieranleitung-NTX1000SZM_PX-NT_4-K0DEEN_2011.pdf, p. 254-255 (§1-4, HINWS. 1 and 3) (M02 and M30 have the same function as the program-execution synchronization M codes, so they must be specified in the HEAD 1 and HEAD 2 programs in pairs, and each in a block without other commands. (Cited only as a second case of a mark that is paired across the channel programs; it says nothing about doubling a mark.)). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main. The job compiler writes start_mark after the header only when some channel program does not already pass that mark as its first mark with all channels, wherever that SYNC stands. Reword machine-config 5 and the comment in nakamura-ntjx.toml. Also check start_mark per machine: the NTJX template uses M198, the WY template M199.
Basis: manual
Source: Nakamura 31i-A guide 2008 p. 21; 18i-TB guide 2009 p. 19-20; ECL-2 p. 72; NTJX code list p. 2 (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none (machine-file comment and value check).

#### D315 Mark of the SYNC the job compiler generates
Question: D56 has the job compiler "insert the SYNC it needs" for a channels = "all" word, and VM 3.8 rule 2a has it "add the SYNC it needs", but no document says which mark that SYNC takes. VM 3.7 and language 4.8 allow marks to be reused, paired in execution order. Machine-config 5 gives only the range: [101, 197] on the Mori Seiki, whose ESPRIT post counts up from 101; [0, 99] on the DMG, where 95 is used by BARLOAD_SYNC. Main takes the first mark in the range of all the job's channels that no channel program of the job uses and that is not start_mark, otherwise the first mark of the range. It reports CMP711 when [sync] has no wait template or no range.
Recommendation: Keep main and write it into VM 3.8 rule 2a or machine-config 5 ([sync]). Reason: an unused mark cannot be mistaken for one of the program's own waits in trace or on the control, and reuse stays allowed when the range is exhausted. Alternatives: an optional [sync] key that names the mark of generated waits, for builders that reserve marks inside the range (DMG 95); or the mark after the last one before the word, counting up as the ESPRIT post does.
Where: VM 3.8 rule 2a; machine-config 5 ([sync]). Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/JobCompiler.Marks.cs:100 (GeneratedMark).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, corrected 2026-10-26 after the manual audit, not confirmed by the maintainer: Keep main as the default, but the manuals turn the optional [sync] key (or a reserved-marks list) into part of the answer. Four rules are documented to write beside the number: the mark must lie in the machine's wait range (Fanuc, parameter 8110 <= wait M code <= 8111, valid values 0 or 100 to 99999999; Mori M100-M197; Nakamura M100-M199, with M800-M849 a second group on the WTW; Siemens at most 100 marks, 0 to 99, in a multi-channel system and only mark 0 in a single-channel one); inside that range no other function may sit (a Fanuc wait code is not output to the PMC, and parameter 11100 must lie outside the range); the same mark must stand in every participating channel, each in a block of its own, because a channel that meets a different number alarms (Mori PS0160, Nakamura 160); and reuse is normal (the Nakamura three-path example writes M100 twice in the left unit's program, P12 then P13; Siemens deletes the mark after the synchronization). So mark_range = [0, 99] on the DMG is exactly the documented Siemens range, and the maximum number of marks is 100. What the pages bear against main is its first pick on the DMG: the builder's templates use marks inside [0, 99] that no NCX file of the job shows. The GMX/CTX training examples write WAITM(10), WAITM(15) and WAITM(20) in both channels and WAITM(0) before M30, and the ShopTurn 3G documents give 0, 1, 10, 15, 20, 25, 80, 90 and BARLOAD_SYNC's 95. "The first mark no channel program of the job uses" then picks 0, the builder's end-of-program mark, so "unused by the job" is not "unused on the machine". On the Nakamura side the code list gives M100-M199 to the wait function as a block, but Nakamura's own cycles use marks of it too (the G196 transfer cycle of the TW and WT series writes M199 at its start), so not every mark of the range is free for a compiler either. Which number a generator should pick is in no manual. That reuse on Fanuc pairs in execution order is still an inference: the Nakamura example shows one code used twice with different P, and the Mori/Nakamura wording is "until the identical M code is executed", but no sentence states pairing by order. The proposal agrees with keeping main as the default and adds the key.
Evidence: FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-MODEL B Operator's Manual B-64484EN, p. 1033-1037 (23.2 waiting function for paths: wait M codes set by 8110 and 8111; P names the paths by binary sum or path numbers, selected by 8103 bit 1 (MWP); without P, paths 1 and 2 wait; a wait M code stands in a block of its own and is not output to the PMC.); FANUC Parameter Manual B-64490EN-05, p. 455 (8110/8111 range of wait M codes, valid range 0, 100 to 99999999) and p. 578 (11100 to be set outside the range of the wait M codes); Mori Seiki NT/NTX Programmieranleitung NTX1000SZM (PX-NT/4-K0DEEN), p. 284 (M100 to M197 synchronize HEAD1 and HEAD2; block of its own; a different number in the other head raises PS0160.); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch Band 1 (4810004ECL-1), p. 125-129, the reuse on p. 126-127 (M100-M199 wait codes; alarms 160 and 161; three-path example with M100P12 and then M100P13 in the left unit; M800-M849 on the WTW.); SINUMERIK 840D sl NC-Programmierung, Programmierhandbuch 06/2019 (SW 4.92), p. 490-492 (WAITM sets the mark in the own channel, the mark is deleted after synchronization, at most 10 marks per channel at once; MarkNr: a multi-channel system has at most 100 wait marks (0 to 99), a single-channel system only mark 0; CLEARM(0) deletes only mark 0.); SINUMERIK 840D sl Parameter Alarme BS.000503, p. 285-286 (alarm 15000 for a mark number below 1 or not below the maximum number of markers, CLEARM(0) deleting all markers; older wording that the 2019 programming manual supersedes.); SINUMERIK 840D sl/828D Programmierhandbuch Arbeitsvorbereitung (03/2013), p. 116-121 (WAITM, mark deleted after synchronization, each command in a block of its own.); DMG MORI GMX-CTX TC Trainingshandbuch Sinumerik 840D (2010), p. 135-141 (two-channel examples with WAITM(10,WAIT_K1,WAIT_K2), WAITM(15,...), WAITM(20,...) in the builder's template.); DMG MORI CTX/NTX Schulung Strukturprogrammierung Teil 1 (2016), p. 118-119 (WAITM(0, WAIT_K1, WAIT_K2) before M30 in both channels.); DMG MORI CTX/GMX Technik Programmierung ShopTurn 3G V2.1, p. 42-45, and ShopTurn 3G BARLOAD V1.0 p. 104-105, V2.1 p. 134 and 146 (cited by the earlier answer for the marks 0, 1, 10, 15, 20, 25, 80, 90 and 95; listed in the connector, but their text cannot be read there.); Mori Seiki ESPRIT-Postprozessor (IX-ESPRITPOSTNL12-D0DEEN), p. 93 (wait codes from M101 up to M197, never above.); Liste M- und G-Codes Nakamura NTJX (Walter Meier/KOST), p. 2 of 6 ("M100 bis M199 = WARTEFUNKTIONEN"); Nakamura-Tome NT-Nurse Operation Manual (Fanuc 31i-A, 4800001EBK, 2015), p. 120 (G196 transfer cycle of the TW and WT series: the waiting M code M199 is specified at the beginning of the cycle and must not be specified just before it.).
Corrected: Dropped "[0, 99] is documented as wrong at its lower bound" and the unresolved mark-0 contradiction, because NC-Programmierung 06/2019 p. 491-492 allows marks 0 to 99 in a multi-channel system and only mark 0 in a single-channel one, and the alarm 15000 text is older wording. Softened "every mark of the range is free" on the Nakamura, since Nakamura's own G196 cycle uses M199.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main's rule (first mark of the range of all the job's channels that no channel program uses and that is not start_mark), plus an optional [sync] key `reserved_marks` (list of integers, default empty) that the pick also skips. When every mark is used, reuse the first mark of the range that is not reserved; when every mark is reserved, CMP711. Each generated wait stands in a block of its own. Machine files: dmg-ctx-840d sets reserved_marks = [0, 1, 10, 15, 20, 25, 80, 90, 95] (builder template marks, BARLOAD_SYNC 95); Nakamura files set [199] (G196 transfer cycle).
Basis: manual
Source: SINUMERIK 840D sl NC-Programmierung 06/2019 p. 490-492 (marks 0-99); DMG-MORI_CTX-NTX_Schulung-Strukturprogrammierung-Teil1_DE_2016.pdf p. 114-119 (WAITM(0,...) before M30, marks 10/15/20...); Nakamura-Tome NT-Nurse Operation Manual p. 120 (M199 in G196); Fanuc B-64484EN p. 1033-1037 (wait code alone in its block).
Differs from the recommendation: yes: adds the reserved_marks key (the recommendation's first alternative in list form).
Confidence: medium
Code impact: JobCompiler.Marks GeneratedMark (skip reserved); machine-config [sync] schema; DMG and Nakamura machine files.

#### D316 A subprogram that no channel program of a job calls
Question: Language 4.13 places a SUB where the target wants it (Fanuc: after the caller's M30). VM 3.9 (D99) has the compiler emit each SUB section once, not once per CALL, or once per calling program where the target needs the section per program (Heidenhain). A job compile writes one file per channel, which holds its program and the SUBs that program calls. No document says where a SUB of a job file goes that no channel program calls. One example is a Fanuc O section that D210 reads as a SUB and that a program outside the file calls on the control. Main writes it into no file and reports the WARNING CMP720, as the file_per_program compile does with CMP003 (wave-3 question 5, D264). The one_file compile writes it after the last program (wave-3 question 4, D264).
Recommendation: Write the SUB once, into the file of the first channel in the manifest that runs a program of its NCX file, after that program's subprograms, just as one_file writes an uncalled SUB after its programs. Reason: D99 emits each SUB once where the target does not need it per program (Fanuc, Siemens). And on the control another program may still call the O number: D210 notes that every O number is a program until something calls it. Dropping the SUB loses code of the file. Alternative: keep main (no file, CMP720) and treat the channel files like file_per_program, where D99's "once per calling program" writes it nowhere. Answer together with D264 (wave-3 questions 4 and 5).
Where: language 4.13; VM 3.9 (D99 sentence); architecture 10 (compile --job row); implementation 16 P6-02. Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/JobCompiler.Run.cs:266 (ReportUncalledSubs; line 183 before RF-P6-02, baca158), JobChannel.Build; src/Ncx.Compilers/CompilerBase.Layout.cs:26 and :67 (D264).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The control has a place for a subprogram that no channel program of the job calls, and it is not simply the first channel's program folder. Fanuc program memory holds one folder per channel (//CNC_MEM/USER/PATHn/) with that channel's main programs, subprograms and macros, plus a common folder LIBRARY for the subprograms and macros the channels share; an M98, G65/G66, M96 or G72.1/G72.2 call searches the folder of the running main program first and LIBRARY after it (MTB2, MTB1 and SYSTEM only when parameter 3457 adds them), while a call by M code, address or T code searches only the folders that parameter 3457 names. One file may legitimately hold several O programs. On a Nakamura the units have wholly separate program memories and the external convention is one file per program named after its O number, so a SUB carried in the first unit's file is reachable only from that unit. None of this says what a converter should write, so the manuals narrow the choice — a file of its own, the shared-library form, or main's CMP720 — without deciding it.
Evidence: Fanuc_30i-B_Bedienung-Drehen-Fraesen_B-64484EN_EN.pdf, p. 310–311 (The start folders of program memory are the root, SYSTEM, MTB1, MTB2 and USER; inside USER there is one channel folder PATHn per channel holding that channel's main programs, subprograms and macro programs, and a common program folder LIBRARY holding the subprograms and macro programs used jointly. The figure shows //CNC_MEM with USER/PATH1, PATH2 and LIBRARY. Start folders can be neither deleted nor renamed); Fanuc_30i-B_Bedienung-Drehen-Fraesen_B-64484EN_EN.pdf, p. 315–316 (For a call by M98, G65/G66/G66.1, M96 or G72.1/G72.2 the folders are searched in order: <1> the folder holding the main program, <2> LIBRARY; with bit 7 (SCF) of parameter No. 3457 also MTB2, MTB1 and SYSTEM. The first program found is called. A subprogram or macro called by M code, address, second auxiliary function, G code or T code searches instead only the folders set in bits 0 to 3 of 3457 (LIBRARY, MTB2, MTB1, SYSTEM)); Nakamura-Tome_Fanuc_Programmierung_Programmierhandbuch-1_4810004ECL-1_DE_2013.pdf, p. 20–24 (§2-4) (On every Nakamura multi-path series the programs are stored in a separate program memory per unit; no common memory is described for them); Nakamura-Tome_Fanuc_Programmierung_Programmierhandbuch-1_4810004ECL-1_DE_2013.pdf, p. 152–153 (§8-5) (A subprogram kept outside the control lives in its own file on the memory card whose name is its program number, with the turret's .P-n suffix; one program, one file. A memory-card program may not itself call another memory-card subprogram); Fanuc_30i-B_Bedienung-Drehen-Fraesen_B-64484EN_EN.pdf, p. 322 (ch. 13) (Note to the program-start code: if a file contains several programs, no label-skip end-of-block may appear before the second and further program numbers. Several O programs in one file are therefore normal). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Do not drop it and do not put it in the first channel's file. The job compile writes every SUB that no channel program calls once into a separate library file of the job (Fanuc: one O program per SUB, as in a file_per_program layout, ready for //CNC_MEM/USER/LIBRARY; Siemens: an SPF per SUB), and keeps the WARNING CMP720, reworded to name that file. Answer D264 consistently (an uncalled SUB is written once, never lost).
Basis: logical
Source: Fanuc_30i-B_Bedienung-Drehen-Fraesen_B-64484EN_EN.pdf p. 310-311, 315-316 (per-path folders plus a common LIBRARY searched after the main program's folder): a SUB in path 1's file is not reachable from path 2, so the first-channel file is the wrong place; a library file mirrors the control's own shared location and loses no code, while CMP720 alone silently loses code. Nakamura (separate memories, one program per file, 4810004ECL-1 p. 152-153) is served by the same separate file.
Differs from the recommendation: yes: separate library file instead of the first channel's file.
Confidence: medium
Code impact: JobCompiler.Run ReportUncalledSubs (write library file instead of nothing); CMP720 message.

#### D317 Load order of the plugins and where a listed DLL is found
Question: Implementation 17 P7-01 gives each DLL 'from plugins/ and the [plugins] list of ncx.toml' its own context and keeps PluginSet 'in load order'. Machine-config 10 names the list (plugins = ["MyShop.NcxPlugins.dll"]) but not where a listed file lies, and its layout has no plugins/ folder. No document gives the order. The order decides how the rewriters of several plugins nest on one block (D199), and which reader rule is offered a block first (D231). Main (PluginLoader.Files) takes the listed DLLs first, in list order. Then come the DLLs of plugins/ that the list does not name, in ordinal order of their names, and each file loads once. A listed name is a path from the working directory, or else the file of that name in plugins/. The classes of one DLL come in ordinal order of their full names.
Recommendation: Keep main. Add plugins/ and the sentence to machine-config 10, with one line in architecture 9. Reasons: the list is where a user fixes the order when it matters, and the rest comes in an order that does not depend on the file system. A bare name finds the DLL that ncx plugin build puts into plugins/, and a path reaches a DLL elsewhere. Answer together with D238 and D199. Under D238's alternative there is no list, and the order is that of plugins/ alone. Alternative: a DLL of plugins/ loads only when the list names it, in list order, so that deleting a line switches a plugin off without deleting its file.
Where: Machine-config 10 (layout and plugin sentence); architecture 9 (plugin paragraph), 10 (ncx.toml sentence); implementation 17 P7-01; docs/plugins.md ('Where ncx finds plugins'); D199, D238. Code: src/Ncx.Plugins/PluginLoader.cs Files and FindListed (TODO(question) at line 38); PluginClasses.Load (class order); src/Ncx.Cli/Commands/NcxTomlPlugins.cs (the bare name that build writes).

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The plugin half of the question has no counterpart in the library, but the name-resolution half does, and it supports main. Siemens documents a fixed search order for a subprogram or cycle called by a bare name: the current directory first, then the subprogram directories of the NC and the global program memory, then a CALLPATH extension, then the user-cycle directory _N_CUS_DIR, then the manufacturer cycles _N_CMA_DIR, then the standard cycles _N_CST_DIR; the first match along the path wins, and no nested directory is searched. That is the machine analogue of main's rule — a listed name is a path from the working directory, or else the file of that name in plugins/ — and of a user extension taking precedence over what the maker shipped. Nothing in the library bears on the order in which several user extensions are offered one block (D199, D231); that stays an NCX choice. Caveats: Searched: full-text grep over the whole cache for "Plugin" (no hit anywhere in the library) and "Ladereihenfolge" (no hit), confirmed. "Erweiterungsmodul" hits only Heidenhain and Bumotec hardware expansion boards; ".dll" hits only the Siemens 840D sl Software-Tools and the Heidenhain TNC 620/640 technical manuals, listing files of the control software with no ordering rule. My own searches: "Suchreihenfolge" (hits in nine Siemens manuals plus Stama and Index, all the subprogram search path), "Suchpfad", "_N_CUS_DIR", "Anwenderzyklen" (39 files) — these are the analogue reported above.
Evidence: Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl_Programmierhandbuch-NC-Programmierung_SW492_DE_2019.pdf, 3.4.1.4 Suchpfad bei Unterprogrammaufruf, p. 572-573 (For a subprogram call without a path the absolute path is found by walking a fixed search path, and the table gives the order: 1-3 the current directory (the directory the program was selected in) with name, name_SPF, name_MPF; 4 the subprogram directory _N_SPF_DIR of the NC and of the global program memory; 5 a CALLPATH extension if one was programmed; 6 _N_CUS_DIR (user cycles); 7 _N_CMA_DIR (manufacturer cycles); 8 _N_CST_DIR (standard cycles). Page 573 adds the rules: the path is walked for every single call, different file types count in different directories, and nested subdirectories are never searched); Siemens_Sinumerik-840Dsl_Programmierhandbuch-NC-Programmierung_SW492_DE_2019.pdf, 3.2.1.2 / 3.2.1.4, p. 502-503 (If a main program and a subprogram of the same name exist, the extension must be given, "Ansonsten wird das Programm verwendet, das entlang des Suchpfades als erstes mit dem angegebenen Programmnamen gefunden wird" — the first match along the search path wins. Page 503: for a call without a path the control searches the available program memories in a predefined search order. CALLPATH (page 545) inserts its extension ahead of the user-cycle directory). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main. Listed DLLs load first, in list order. A listed name is a path from the working directory, else the file of that name in plugins/. Unlisted DLLs of plugins/ follow in ordinal name order, and each file loads once. The classes of one DLL load in ordinal full-name order. Add plugins/ to the machine-config 10 layout.
Basis: logical (manual analogy)
Source: 840D sl SW 4.92 p. 502-503, 572-573 (fixed search order, first match wins) (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none.

#### D318 Block count of the plugin INFO line
Question: Code-guidelines 11 (step 6) prints 'plugin MyShopRules: inserted 2 blocks at line 12' for the template's CoolantClutchRule. Implementation 17 P7-01 (PluginDiagnostics) gives the same count as 'plugin <name>'. P7-02 (tests first, and the done-when of its task file) prints 'plugin CoolantClutch: inserted 2 blocks at line 12' for the clutch sample. The rule's Surround inserts three blocks (code-guidelines 11): @SAVE=SPINDLE:MAIN and SPINDLE:MAIN=OFF before the block, and @RESTORE=SPINDLE:MAIN after it. The recorded D98 row names the INFO ('a plugin's inserted blocks') but gives no count. Main (PluginRewriter.Rewrite) counts every block of a Surround answer and prints 'inserted 3 blocks'. The template README, docs/plugins.md, samples/plugins/CoolantClutch/README.md and the tests print 3. P7-02 stays in inbox/ until this is answered.
Recommendation: Count every block the answer inserts, before and after the block: 3 for the clutch rule. A Replace inserts none and prints no INFO. Code-guidelines 11 step 6, implementation 17 P7-01 and P7-02 and the P7-02 task file then read 'inserted 3 blocks at line 12'; the generic example of D98 and code-guidelines 6 may stay. Reason: the count is taken in the expander, for check as for compile. It does not depend on what a compiler writes, and it equals the generated comment lines that annotate shows with the plugin's name, @SAVE among them (VM 3.10, D237 point 7). Trace has only two rows for it, since @SAVE changes no variable. Alternative: count only the inserted blocks that change a state variable, which are the rows trace shows (docs/plugins.md). That leaves out @SAVE and gives 2 for the clutch rule, the spindle stop and the restored spindle (M5 and M3 S1500, VM 3.10), and the documents stay as written.
Where: Code-guidelines 11 (step 6), 6 (INFO example); implementation 17 P7-01, P7-02; docs/plan/tasks/inbox/P7-02 (done when); D98; D167 (pseudo-words in blocks of their own, related). ### Eighth round: later

#### D319 Setpos shift after a RESET of a turning entry before it
Question: Language 4.2 declares SETPOS 'in the active workpiece frame', and a RESET removes its entry and everything after it (D31). SETPOS is not a chain entry: VM 2.1 keeps its shift per axis until ORIGIN, and VM 3.4 reads the workpiece coordinates through it. Nothing says where that shift acts once a ROTATE, MIRROR, TILT or TILT_AXIS that stood before the SETPOS, and turns its axis, is removed. Case: ROTATE=90, then SETPOS X=0 Y=0 while at X=10 Y=0, then ROTATE=RESET. Does the shift keep its displacement in space, turned into the unrotated axes? Or does the vector (10, 0) now act along the unrotated X? The VM keeps the numbers and marks the positions unknown. The Fanuc and Siemens compilers write G92 or PRESETON and leave the answer to the control. The Heidenhain compiler must place a cycle 7 (D55, machine-config 3), and reports such a RESET as CMP114 (HeidenhainSetpos.CheckRemoved).
Recommendation: The setpos shift keeps its displacement in space. After such a RESET it acts directly after the entries that remain. A removed ROTATE or MIRROR turns its vector into the remaining frame (R·s); a removed SHIFT only folds back, as VM 3.4 already says. VM 3.4 states this rule. The VM turns the setpos shifts for a removed ROTATE or MIRROR whose value is known, and marks them unknown after a removed TILT, TILT_AXIS, or an angle given by an expression (no kinematics module). Reason, from our reading of the manuals (not in the documents): Siemens PRESETON writes the system frame, which stands before the programmable frames, so it behaves this way; Fanuc allows no G92 in G68 mode (D244's reading). The maintainer confirms. The Heidenhain compiler then writes a cycle 7 with the turned shift after the cancels. Where turning entries remain before it, it keeps CMP114 until D253 says where a replacing cycle 7 acts. Alternatives: the numbers stay and act along the axes of the remaining frame, as the VM stores them today; or such a RESET is an ERROR of the VM, and only ORIGIN may end a SETPOS declared under a turning entry.
Where: language 4.2 (SETPOS row, chain paragraph); VM 2.1 (setpos shift row), 3.4; src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/FrameRules.cs (the RESET fold); src/Ncx.Compilers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainSetpos.cs CheckRemoved (TODO(question) at line 101); D253 for the Klartext place of the cycle.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals do not settle the VM rule, but they back both the chain reading and CMP114. Heidenhain fixes the order: a datum shift programmed before cycle 19 shifts the machine-fixed system, one programmed after it the tilted system, and "the result of transformations that build on each other depends on the programming order", for setting as for resetting. Both cycle manuals then require resetting the transformations in the reverse order of defining them (define 1 shift, 2 tilt, 3 rotation; reset 1 rotation, 2 tilt, 3 shift), so a program that cancels a rotation while a shift defined after it is still active is outside the control's own guidance - which is manual backing for keeping CMP114, given that NCX maps SETPOS onto a cycle 7 (D55). What is left to the maintainer: Klartext has no operation that removes an entry from the middle of the chain, so the R*s rule and the "unknown" marking after a removed TILT remain an NCX design choice.
Evidence: Heidenhain_iTNC530_Zyklen_670_388-12_NC-SW-340490-07_DE_2011.pdf, p. 301 (Combining coordinate-transformation cycles: tilting always happens about the active datum; a datum shift before cycle 19 shifts the "machine-fixed" system, one after it the "tilted" system. Marked "Wichtig", it then requires resetting the cycles in the reverse order of defining them, listing activate shift / tilt / rotation and reset rotation / tilt / shift); Heidenhain_TNC640_Zyklen_892905-18_NC-SW-34059x-10_DE_2019.pdf, p. 245 (The same passage on the TNC 640, with the same numbered activate and reverse-order reset lists); Heidenhain_TNC640_Programmierung-Klartext_892903-18_NC-SW-34059x-10_DE_2019.pdf, p. 81 (In the reference-system chapter: the result of transformations that build on each other depends on the programming order, and only the listed transformations should be programmed in each coordinate system, "sowohl fuer das Setzen als auch fuer das Zuruecksetzen"; other use can give unexpected constellations); Heidenhain_TNC640_Programmierung-Klartext_892903-18_NC-SW-34059x-10_DE_2019.pdf, p. 80 (The workpiece coordinate system W-CS has the active Bezugspunkt as its origin. Its transformation list contains cycle 7 and cycle 8 only "vor dem Schwenken der Bearbeitungsebene"; page 82 lists cycles 7, 8, 10, 11, 26 and PLANE RELATIVE again in the machining-plane system WPL-CS. The same cycle therefore sits in a different system depending on where it stands - the order dependence itself); Heidenhain_iTNC530_Programmierung-Klartext_NC-SW-606420-01_DE_2010.pdf, p. 322 (FN 25: PRESET sets a new Bezugspunkt in a selectable axis during the program run, from a coordinate in the active system and the coordinate that value should have afterwards. The page says nothing about where this stands in a chain of transformations; that it acts below cycles 7, 8 and 10 is our inference from the Bezugspunkt being the origin of W-CS (TNC 640 page 80)); Heidenhain_iTNC530_Zyklen_670_388-12_NC-SW-340490-07_DE_2011.pdf, p. 289 (Cycle 10 rotates the coordinate system in the working plane about the active datum and is reset only by re-defining it with ROT+0; nothing in that reset touches a datum shift (it does cancel an active radius compensation). Cycle 247 by contrast states expressly (page 286) that activating a preset resets an active datum shift). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

The setpos shift keeps its displacement in space. When a ROTATE or MIRROR with a known value before it is removed, the VM turns the shift into the remaining frame (R·s). A removed SHIFT only folds back. After a removed TILT, TILT_AXIS or expression angle, the shift becomes unknown. The Heidenhain compiler keeps CMP114 for such a RESET until D253 settles where the cycle 7 goes.
Basis: manual (partly) + logical
Source: iTNC 530 Zyklen 670388-12 p. 289, 301; TNC 640 Zyklen 892905-18 p. 245; Klartext 892903-18 p. 80-81 (reset in reverse order) (cnc-manuals). Keeping the displacement in space matches Siemens PRESETON, which writes the system frame.
Differs from the recommendation: no (CMP114 kept in all cases until D253)
Confidence: medium
Code impact: FrameRules RESET fold turns setpos shifts.

#### D320 Heidenhain SETPOS of an axis known only in the MACHINE frame
Question: D55 and machine-config 3 ([setpos] comment) fold SETPOS into a cycle 7 on Heidenhain: a shift against the active preset of oldPos minus the declared value, where oldPos is in the workpiece frame (VM 3.4). After HOME or a FRAME=MACHINE move, the axis is known only in the MACHINE frame, and D101 records the shift against the machine position. Without a datum table (D35) the preset's machine position is unknown, so the compiler has no number for the cycle 7. Case: HOME Z, SETPOS Z=100, which is how an older Fanuc program's G28 Z0 followed by G92 Z100 reads, compiled for the iTNC 530. HeidenhainSetpos.NamedAxes reports CMP113 and writes nothing, and heidenhain 8 has no rule for this case.
Recommendation: Make it an ERROR of the Heidenhain compiler, as coded (CMP113), stated in heidenhain 8 next to rule 5. This matches D100, which makes HOME without reference coordinates an ERROR of this compiler and not of check. Reason: the compiler has nothing to compute the shift from, and CAM output does not use the idiom. Alternative: read the position at run time with FN 18: SYSREAD into a spare Q parameter (heidenhain 6), subtract the declared value in a formula block, and write CYCL DEF 7 with the result. That needs the FN 18 ids of D182.
Where: controllers/heidenhain.md 8 (rule 5 or a new rule); machine-config 3 ([setpos] comment); src/Ncx.Compilers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainSetpos.cs NamedAxes and KnownInWorkpieceFrame (TODO(question) at line 184); D182 for the alternative.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. Keep the ERROR (CMP113), and let heidenhain 8 give the manual reasons next to the compile-time one. Page 278 of the cycles manual lists every coordinate-transformation cycle and none of them takes a machine-frame position: cycle 7 - and its Klartext equivalent TRANS DATUM AXIS - shifts against the datum set by Bezugspunkt-Setzen or by a preset, and cycle 247 only activates a preset row. The one Klartext function that sets a datum from a current coordinate, FN 25: PRESET = Z/+50/-20, can be programmed on the iTNC 530 only after key number 555343 and does not exist on the TNC 640, and the run-time route the draft names as its alternative is documented (FN 18: SYSREAD ID270 NR1 IDX n for the position in the active system, ID240 NR1 for the REF setpoint, ID220 for the active datum shift, with FN 20: WAIT FOR SYNC to stop the look-ahead before the read) - which fills D182, at the cost of a look-ahead stop per read.
Evidence: Heidenhain_iTNC530_Programmierung-Klartext_NC-SW-340490-05_DE_2008.pdf, p. 314-315 (FN 25: PRESET sets a new Bezugspunkt in a selectable axis during the program run. Dialog: axis, the value to be converted (a coordinate in the active system), and the coordinate that value should have in the new system. Examples FN 25: PRESET = X/+100/+0 and Z/+50/-20. A note says the function can only be programmed after entering key number 555343); Heidenhain_iTNC530_Programmierung-Klartext_NC-SW-606420-01_DE_2010.pdf, p. 322 (The same FN 25: PRESET description, the same two examples and the same key-number restriction on the newest iTNC 530 software level); Heidenhain_TNC640_Programmierung-Klartext_892903-18_NC-SW-34059x-10_DE_2019.pdf, p. 614 (In the TNC 640 versus iTNC 530 differences table, the Q-parameter row "FN 25: PRESET" is marked absent on the TNC 640 and present on the iTNC 530 (as are FN 15, FN 31 and FN 32)); Heidenhain_iTNC530_Programmierung-Klartext_NC-SW-340490-05_DE_2008.pdf, p. 310-312 (FN 18 system-data table: ID 220 index 1-9 the active datum shift per axis, ID 240 NR1 index 1-9 the setpoint position in the REF system, ID 270 NR1 index 1-9 the current position in the active coordinate system. Page 628 adds ID 360 (last probe point), ID 500/501 (datum table) and ID 502/503 (preset table). The extracted text of this table is garbled in the columns; the ids and meanings are confirmed by the clean TNC 640 table on page 580); Heidenhain_TNC640_Programmierung-Klartext_892903-18_NC-SW-34059x-10_DE_2019.pdf, p. 297 (FN 20: WAIT FOR SYNC stops the control's internal look-ahead; the manual says to use SYNC whenever FN 18: SYSREAD reads system data that require synchronization to real time, and its worked example is "FN 20: WAIT FOR SYNC" followed by "FN 18: SYSREAD Q1 = ID270 NR1 IDX1". Page 580 lists ID 220 NR2 (active datum shift), ID 240 NR1 and ID 270 NR1; it calls ID 270 the current setpoint position in the input system and notes it returns uncorrected values for X, Y, Z under active radius compensation and an error for a rotary axis); Heidenhain_iTNC530_Zyklen_670_388-12_NC-SW-340490-07_DE_2011.pdf, p. 278 (The complete list of coordinate-transformation cycles: 7 (datum shift), 247 (set preset), 8, 10, 11, 26, 19. Of these only cycle 7 - absolute values referred to the datum from Bezugspunkt-Setzen (page 279) - and cycle 247, which activates a row of the preset table (page 286), touch the datum, and neither takes a machine-frame position); Heidenhain_iTNC530_Programmierung-Klartext_NC-SW-340490-05_DE_2008.pdf, p. 416-417 (Besides the cycles there is the Klartext function TRANS DATUM: "Alternativ zum Koordinaten-Transformationszyklus 7", with TRANS DATUM AXIS X+10 Y+25 Z+42, TRANS DATUM TABLE and TRANS DATUM RESET. Absolute values refer to the workpiece datum from Bezugspunkt-Setzen or a preset, so this form does not take a machine-frame position either). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

ERROR CMP113 in the Heidenhain compiler, as coded. heidenhain 8 states it next to rule 5. The reason: no cycle 7 or TRANS DATUM takes a machine-frame position, and FN 25 is locked on the iTNC 530 and absent on the TNC 640. The FN 18 ID270/ID240 route waits for D182.
Basis: manual

#### D323 What a spindle start, stop or reversal adds to the runtime (accel_time)
Question: Machine-config 5 defines accel_time as "seconds from stop to rpm_max", and VM 8 says "a spindle start or stop adds accel_time of that spindle". Neither says whether a start to less than rpm_max adds all of it, whether CW to CCW counts as a start, a stop or both, or whether an RPM change while the spindle turns adds anything. Main adds the whole accel_time per start and per stop, adds it twice for a reversal, and adds nothing for a speed change. Case: SPINDLE=CW RPM=1500 on a spindle with rpm_max 6000 and accel_time 2.5 adds 2.5 s, where a linear ramp takes 0.6 s.
Recommendation: Keep the code and write it into VM 8. Each start (OFF to CW or CCW) and each stop adds the whole accel_time, a reversal adds it twice, and a speed change while turning adds nothing. Reason: this is VM 8 read literally, and it needs neither rpm_max, which is optional in machine-config 5, nor the rpm under CSS, which is known only per motion. Alternative: add accel_time times the change of rpm over rpm_max, for starts, stops, reversals (twice the rpm) and speed changes alike. That is closer to a real ramp, but it applies only where rpm_max and both speeds are known.
Where: VM 8 (runtime estimate); machine-config 5 (accel_time comment); src/Ncx.Analytics/Runtime/RuntimeEstimator.cs AddSpindleChange and StartsAndStops (marker at line 256); tests RuntimeAnalyticTests.SpindleAccelTime_StartAndStop_AddTheAccelTimeOfTheSpindle, SpindleAccelTime_Reversal_CountsAsAStopAndAStart.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, corrected 2026-10-26 after the manual audit, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. The manuals give no ramp model; they contradict two of the code's simplifications and support the third. Siemens says the axis motion waits for the spindle to run up to the commanded speed (Solldrehzahl), not to rpm_max, and that whether it waits at all is a machine datum, so charging the full stop-to-rpm_max time for a start to 1500 of 6000 rests on nothing the manuals say. Nakamura implies that changing the programmed spindle speed costs acceleration and deceleration time even in normal operation, so a speed change while the spindle turns is not free either. A reversal, on the other hand, contains a stop: in Heidenhain's tapping cycle 207 the spindle can be stopped a set time before the thread bottom (thrdPreSwitch) and the control waits at the bottom after the spindle stop (thrdWaitingTime) before it turns the other way, which supports main's reversal as a stop plus a start. So the proposal agrees with the recommendation on reversals and goes against it on a start below rpm_max and on a speed change while turning; which formula replaces those stays an NCX choice, because no page gives a ramp, a time or a proportionality. Caveats: The draft's Alternative (accel_time scaled by the rpm change over rpm_max) is consistent with these pages but is not what they say; a linear ramp is an assumption. No manual gives a spindle acceleration time in seconds. Fanuc parameter 4914 is the time from a change of the programmed spindle speed to the start of speed-deviation monitoring, a monitoring allowance, not the ramp. Searched: Hochlaufzeit, Beschleunigungszeit, Spindelhochlauf, Solldrehzahl erreicht, Anlaufzeit.
Evidence: SINUMERIK 840D sl/828D Grundlagen, Programmierhandbuch (03/2013), 6.1 Spindeldrehzahl (S), Spindeldrehrichtung (M3, M4, M5), p. 83-84 (In a block with axis commands M3/M4/M5 are switched before the axis motions start; the example's spindle runs up to 270 rpm before X and Y move. A machine datum decides whether the axis motions wait until the spindle has reached the setpoint speed or has stopped, or start immediately after the programmed switching.); Nakamura-Tome Programmierhandbuch (Fanuc), Band 1, 4810004ECL-1 (2013), 15-2, p. 255 (If the programmed spindle speed is changed appreciably during synchronisation control, the actual speed follows more slowly than in normal operation because of the additional acceleration and deceleration time.); HEIDENHAIN TNC 640 Benutzerhandbuch Zyklenprogrammierung (892905-18, NC-SW 34059x-10, 2019), 5.3 Zyklus 207, p. 136-137 (Steps: the spindle direction is reversed at the drilling depth and the tool retracts; at the safety distance the control stops the spindle. CfgThreadSpindle: thrdPreSwitch (113602) stops the spindle this time before the thread bottom, thrdWaitingTime (113601) is waited at the thread bottom after the spindle stop; Q200 should leave room for the acceleration distance.).
Corrected: Withdrew "the reversal is one step, with no separate stop": TNC 640 Zyklen p. 137 (thrdPreSwitch, thrdWaitingTime) has the spindle stop before it turns the other way, which supports main's stop plus start. The proposal now agrees with the recommendation on reversals.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Where rpm_max and both speeds are known, add accel_time x |rpm_new - rpm_old| / rpm_max for a start, a stop and a speed change while turning; a reversal is a stop plus a start, accel_time x (rpm_old + rpm_new) / rpm_max. Where rpm_max is missing or a speed is unknown (CSS, no S yet), fall back to the whole accel_time per start and per stop (reversal twice) and nothing for a speed change, as main does. CSS speed changes during a motion add nothing. VM 8 states the linear ramp is an NCX estimate.
Basis: logical
Source: Siemens 840D sl/828D Grundlagen 03/2013 p. 83-84 (spindle runs up to the commanded speed, not rpm_max), Nakamura 4810004ECL-1 p. 255 (speed changes cost ramp time), TNC 640 Zyklen p. 136-137 (reversal contains a stop). No manual gives a ramp; a linear scale is the simplest model consistent with all three and degrades to main's rule when data is missing.
Differs from the recommendation: yes: proportional time (the recommendation's alternative) with main's rule as fallback.
Confidence: medium
Code impact: RuntimeEstimator.AddSpindleChange/StartsAndStops; RuntimeAnalyticTests.

#### D324 Where a user gives the histogram bins of segments and tool vectors
Question: Implementation 14 P4-03 asks for a segment-length histogram "with configurable bins" and gives the tool-vector change only a "histogram". Main treats both alike. Architecture 10, the one list of ncx options (F28), has no option for them, and neither ncx.toml (machine-config 10) nor the machine file has a key. Main gives both analytics the bounds as a constructor parameter, for a front end or a plugin. ncx analyze writes the defaults, 0.01 to 100 mm and 0.01 to 90 degrees, which the report prints. Case: a CAM programmer who wants segments below 0.05 mm counted separately cannot do so from the command line.
Recommendation: Add two options to ncx analyze, --segment-bins (mm) and --vector-bins (degrees). Each takes a comma-separated list of bounds that rises from above 0. Without the option, the default bounds apply. A list that does not rise from above 0 is CLI001. Architecture 10 lists the options, and implementation 14 names them for both analytics. Reason: "configurable" in the plan reads as configurable by the user. D67's answer put the analysis range (--from/--to) on the command line. The analytics already take the bounds, so only the CLI changes. Alternative: keep the code, with bins configurable through the API only, and implementation 14 says so.
Where: architecture 10 (analyze row); implementation 14 P4-03; src/Ncx.Analytics/Segments/SegmentAnalytic.cs DefaultBins (marker at line 47); src/Ncx.Analytics/ToolVectors/ToolVectorAnalytic.cs DefaultBins (marker at line 53); AnalyticOptions and AnalyticsRegistry (passing the bounds); src/Ncx.Cli/Commands/AnalyzeCommand.cs and AnalyzeSettings.cs; AnalyzeCommandTests.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27: the library does not answer this (searched cache-wide, case-insensitive: histogram/Histogramm (only the four TNC 640 files: the 2018, 2019 and 2021 technical manuals and Aktuelle Information Nr. 9, all the same component-monitoring feature), Klassenbreite, Klasseneinteilung, Klassengrenze, "Anzahl der Klassen", Häufigkeitsverteilung (0 files each), Balkendiagramm (11 files, all screen bar displays: spindle load, Mori Seiki, WFL, Siemens HMI), Segmentlänge/Segmentlaenge (0), Satzlänge (62 files, all block transfer and block processing time on Brother, Bumotec, Nakamura NT-IPS), Punktabstand (48 files, probe point spacing and CAM point density), Sehnenfehler (41 files, the CAM chord tolerance against cycle 32 / G5.1 — checked Hermle_Allgemein_Schulung_CAM-Anwender-Seminar-iTNC-530_DE.pdf p. 72 and the Grob G350 postprocessor description p. 17 (not in the connector): a tolerance recommendation, no statistics), Werkzeugvektor, Vektoränderung; also re-checked the Mori Seiki ESPRIT postprocessor manual. No manual in the library documents a CAM or analysis tool's histogram bin option, and none reports a distribution of NC segment lengths or tool-vector changes at all. The only histogram any manual parametrises is the TNC 640 component monitoring, a different feature: since NC software 34059x-10 the bounds live in a named template under System\Monitoring\CfgMonHistory (path, histogramMinValue, histogramMaxValue, timeValuePairs) that several monitoring tasks reference by key (Heidenhain_TNC640_Technisches-Handbuch_NC-SW-34059x-10_DE_2019.pdf, p. 2218, machine-parameter list 762-763, old/new comparison 46-47), and the earlier per-component form under CfgComponentMon had minValue, maxValue, an interval and an explicit numberOfBins, both of which HEIDENHAIN dropped in the rework. If the maintainer wants a precedent from the shop's own controls, it is bounds in a reusable named configuration object, never a list passed per run — and the one control that did offer a bin count made that a configuration value too; but it is a control-side monitoring feature for machine components and should not be read as support for either side of D324). The recommendation above stands for the maintainer.

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Add the ncx analyze options --segment-bins (mm) and --vector-bins (degrees). Each takes comma-separated rising bounds greater than 0, and a list that is not rising or not positive is CLI001. Without the option the defaults apply (0.01..100 mm, 0.01..90°). List both in architecture 10 and implementation 14.
Basis: logical
Source: 'Configurable' in P4-03 means by the user, and D67 put the analysis range on the command line. The analytics already take bounds.
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high

#### D325 Head or table: rotary axes of the tool-vector convention
Question: Implementation 14 P4-03 turns the tool vector by "a rotary axis named A, B or C". The axis is a head axis when its "owner is the tool spindle" and a table axis when its "owner is a work spindle or table". The paragraph does not place a rotary axis without an owner, such as B1, the tool-spindle swivel of mori-ntx1000-mapps.toml and dmg-ctx-840d.toml, or A and B of the D103 default machine. Nor does it place an axis owned by a tool holder, or a name with digits (C2 of a sub spindle, C3 on the DMG). Machine-config 4 describes owner only as "rotary axis of a work spindle". Main takes every rotary axis whose owner does not hold the workpiece as a head axis. It turns C2 about Z like C. It applies a table axis only while its owner is the workpiece holder (language 4.10), so C2 turns nothing while MAIN holds the part. Case: on the Mori Seiki, B1 with C1 while MAIN holds the part, then B1 with C2 after WORKPIECE=SUB.
Recommendation: Keep the code and write it into implementation 14 P4-03 and the report header. A table axis is a rotary axis whose owner holds the workpiece (a work spindle or a table), and every other rotary axis is a head axis. The letter of the NCX name without its digits gives the machine axis it turns about. A table axis counts only while its owner is the workpiece holder. Reason: B1 is the tool swivel on both files, and a spindle's C carries the part as a table does. This is also the definition of table kinematics that D191 recommends, so answer the two the same way. Alternative: every rotary axis must name an owner, a tool spindle for a head axis, so that the convention never guesses. Machine-config 4 then documents owner for head axes, and B1 of the Mori Seiki and DMG files gains owner = its tool spindle.
Where: implementation 14 P4-03 (the convention paragraph); machine-config 4 (owner key, one sentence); src/Ncx.Analytics/ToolVectors/ToolVectorConvention.cs constructor (marker at line 26); ConventionAxis.AppliesWhile and Turns; ToolVectorAnalytic report header; related D191, D147.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: This contradicts the recommendation in part. The owner-based rule is confirmed for every rotary axis of both machine files, and the manuals supply the owners the files leave out: on the NTX1000 address B is the tool-spindle index angle and address C the work-spindle index angle (address A there is the headstock-2/tailstock slide, a linear direction, so the letter alone decides nothing), and on the CTX L707 and L705 switch the main and the counter spindle into C-axis mode (C4, C3) while B is the tool carrier's swivel — "Interpolation mit B-Achse" moves the tool computation from the static ToolCarrier system to the dynamic ORIWKS with X and Z compensating the offset. Where the manuals bite is the fallback "every other rotary axis is a head axis" together with "the letter gives the machine axis it turns about". Two documented cases break it: on the same CTX, L701 and L703 switch tool spindles 1 and 2 into C-axis mode and the builder's own training manual lists C1, C2, C3 and C4 as the machine's axes, so a C axis of a tool spindle — which spins the tool about its own axis and tilts nothing — would turn the WORKPLANE normal about machine Z as soon as B is not zero; and the shop's Hermle C 22 U is a swivelling rotary table with kinematics A/C, where both rotary axes carry the workpiece and neither has a work spindle to name as owner. So write the owner rule as recommended but take the alternative with it: every rotary axis names an owner (B1 = the tool spindle on the Mori, tool carrier 1 on the DMG, per the manuals), and the convention turns the vector only for an axis that swivels the tool or carries the workpiece. The letter mapping is safe as a default: Fanuc's 5-axis primer says rotary-axis names follow DIN 66217, from the orientation of the rotary axis to X, Y and Z, and that a two-axis table's rotary axes are installed coaxial with the machine's linear axes. The contradiction is narrow: the manuals confirm the owner-based definition and confirm B1 as a head axis on both files; what they bear against is the blanket fallback. Both counter-cases are latent, not present defects. dmg-ctx-840d.toml declares only B1, C4, C3 and Z3, so no C1 or C2 axis exists there today, and that the coded convention would invent a vector change for a tool-spindle C is my reading of ToolVectorConvention, not a manual sentence — the manual only says L701/L703 put a tool spindle into C-axis mode. No Hermle machine file exists in machines/ yet, and heidenhain-itnc530.toml has no rotary axes; the Hermle document is Hermle's information for a HEIDENHAIN postprocessor while the corpus C22 U program runs on 840D (the kinematics table is the machine's, not the control's), and "SRT" is read as the Schwenkrundtisch of section 5 rather than expanded in the table. I found no page that states the swivel plane of B on either turn-mill; that B swivels about Y rests on the DIN 66217 sentence in the Fanuc primer, whose coaxial statement is about a Robodrill's add-on two-axis table.
Evidence: Mori-Seiki_NT-NTX-Serie_Programmierung_Programmieranleitung-NTX1000SZM_PX-NT_4-K0DEEN_2011.pdf, ch. Achsensteuerung und Bewegungsrichtung, p. 73 (axis table), 74 (C axis) and 75 (B and BW) (The axis table on 73 names the component behind each address: C = Spindel 1 / Spindel 2, Y and B = Werkzeugspindel, A = Spindelstock 2/Reitstock with a linear + direction ("nach rechts"). Page 74 gives address C as the spindle index angle for milling, C0 at the C-axis zero; page 75 gives address B as the tool-spindle index angle, B0 at the position reached after zero return, and BW on the NTX1000 as the workpiece-discharge and spindle-2 index angle. So B belongs to the tool spindle and the C axes to the work spindles, and A — a rotary letter — is a linear slide here, which the machine file already records as kind = "linear".); DMG-MORI_CTX-GMX_Technik-Programmierung-Sinumerik840Dsl_V2.1_DE_2015.pdf, p. 29, 31, 33, 35, 112 and 114 (not in the connector: listed without readable text apart from its index; the L701 to L708 table is readable in DMG-MORI_CTX-NTX_Trainingshandbuch-Sinumerik-Operate_A-D213DE-1_DE_2018.pdf, p. 76, and the B-axis interpolation, TRANS_5A and TRANS_OFF passages in DMG-MORI_Technologycycle_5-Achs-Simultanbearbeitung_B-A0329_V1.1_DE_2015.pdf, p. 18-19 and 21) (L701 switches tool spindle 1 into C-axis mode and positions it to an angle (L702 off), L703/L704 do the same for tool spindle 2, L705 switches the counter spindle (C3) and L707 the main spindle (C4) — C-named axes exist on both the tool side and the workpiece side of one machine. On 112, "Interpolation mit B-Achse": the tool computation is switched from the static ToolCarrier system to the dynamic ORIWKS so that the B angle may be changed during machining, with X and Z compensating the offset; TRANS_5A's first parameter selects the workpiece spindle (S3 = 3, S4 = 4). The TRANS_OFF page adds that on deselection "die aktuellen Bi- und Ci-Koordinaten als Winkel des ToolCarriers eingetragen" werden.); DMG-MORI_CTX-NTX_Schulung-Strukturprogrammierung-Teil1_DE_2016.pdf, p. 19 and 20 (not in the connector: no readable text on these pages; the spindle precondition of page 20 is readable in DMG-MORI_CTX-NTX_Trainingshandbuch-Sinumerik-Operate_A-D213DE-1_DE_2018.pdf, p. 20) (Page 19 lists the machine's axes for manual traverse: "Achse C1, C2, C3, C4", X, Y, Z and "Achse B1" — four C axes and one B on one machine. Page 20 states the precondition for running the spindles: spindle 1 or 2 must have a tool clamped, spindle 3 or 4 a workpiece. The builder states the head/table split of this family by spindle number, which matches dmg-ctx-840d.toml (S3, S4 work spindles carrying C3 and C4; S1, S2 tool spindles).); Hermle_Allgemein_Technische-Information_Postprozessor-Heidenhain_DE-EN_V2_2016.pdf, p. 3 and 6 (The machine table lists the C 22 U with table variant SRT Ø 320 mm (and SRT Ø 450 x 360), kinematics "A / C", A from -135° to +135°, C 0–360°; the C 22 V with a rigid table has no rotary axis. Section 5 Anordnung then gives three arrangements: rigid = 3 axes X, Y, Z; rotating clamping device = 4 axes X, Y, Z, A; "Schwenkrundtisch / swivelling rotary table" = 5 axes X, Y, Z, A, C. Reading SRT as that Schwenkrundtisch, both rotary axes of the C 22 U carry the workpiece.); Fanuc_5-Achshandbuch_DE.pdf, 2.2.1 Maschinenkinematik / 3.1 Achsanordnung, p. 8–11 (Apart from special kinematics, two types have established themselves in milling-machine building, decided by how rotary motion is realised in the machine space: Kopftyp- and Tischtyp-Maschinen; the illustrations add a Drehfräszentrum as "gemischte Kinematik". The rotary-axis names follow DIN 66217: "Die Achsbezeichnungen der Rotationsachsen richtet sich nach deren Ausrichtung bezüglich der Linearachsen im Maschinenkoordinatensystem", with X Y Z against A B C and a figure. The section is about the add-on two-axis table of a Robodrill, whose rotary axes "werden bei der Installation koaxial zu den Linearachsen der Maschine ausgerichtet"; a machine that deviates from the standard causes trouble when programs move between machines.). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Every rotary axis should name an owner. owner = a work spindle or table that holds the workpiece: table axis, counted only while its owner is the workpiece holder (as coded). owner = a tool holder (turret, tool carrier, swivel head): head axis. owner = a tool spindle: the spindle's own rotation (C-axis mode of a tool spindle), which turns no tool vector. A rotary axis without an owner (D103 default machine) stays a head axis as today, but the report header carries a WARNING naming the axis and the assumption. The letter without digits gives the machine axis it turns about (DIN 66217). Machine files: B1 of mori-ntx1000-mapps.toml and dmg-ctx-840d.toml gains owner = its tool holder (DMG: tool carrier 1); machine-config 4 documents owner for head axes.
Basis: manual
Source: Mori NTX1000SZM PX-NT/4-K0DEEN p. 73-75 (B = tool-spindle index, C = work spindles); DMG-MORI_CTX-NTX_Trainingshandbuch-Sinumerik-Operate_A-D213DE-1_DE_2018.pdf p. 76 (L701/L703 tool spindles in C-axis mode); Hermle_Allgemein_Technische-Information_Postprozessor-Heidenhain_DE-EN_V2_2016.pdf p. 3, 6 (A/C both on the table); Fanuc_5-Achshandbuch_DE.pdf p. 8-11 (DIN 66217 naming).
Differs from the recommendation: yes: owner documented and set for head axes; tool-spindle C axes turn nothing; ownerless axes get a WARNING instead of a silent head-axis default.
Confidence: medium
Code impact: ToolVectorConvention constructor and ConventionAxis.Turns; report header WARNING; machine-config 4 text and two machine files.

#### D328 Expansion-rule blocks of a word the job compiler moves or duplicates
Question: Machine-config 5a puts a rule's generated blocks (pre, post, requires with @SAVE/@RESTORE) around the triggering block, and architecture 5.5 expands each program once. VM 3.8 rule 2a and D56 have the job compiler move a word bound to channel n into that channel's program, and duplicate a channels = "all" word. No document says whether the rule's blocks go with the word. Case: [func] DOOR = { OPEN = "M62", channel = 1, pre = ["HOME Z"] } with FUNC:DOOR=OPEN in the program of channel 2. Main expands first, so HOME Z stays in channel 2 before the block, and only M62 moves behind the mark in channel 1. Before the P6-02 review fix, the rule fired in channel 1 instead. No example machine has a rule on a bound table.
Recommendation: Keep main. The rule's blocks stay where the expander put them, in the program that writes the word. Only the bound word moves or is duplicated, and it is not expanded again. Bound words among the rule's blocks move by the same rule. Reason: the expander runs once per file (architecture 5.5), and the rule's blocks address the axes and resources of the channel that runs them; HOME Z moved to channel 1 would home the other turret. Alternative: the blocks that the bound table's rule generated for the word move or are duplicated with it, in their order and behind the same mark, since the table and the machine function its rule prepares belong to channel n.
Where: VM 3.8 rule 2a; machine-config 5 (channel, channels) and 5a; architecture 5.5. Code: src/Ncx.Compilers/JobCompiler.Binding.cs:20 (BindWords); tests/Ncx.Compilers.Tests/Jobs/JobBindingTests.cs.

ANSWER:
Proposed from the manual library 2026-09-27, not confirmed by the maintainer: the manuals do not settle this. Keep main; the machine manuals support the reason the draft gives, though none addresses expansion rules as such. In the Mori Seiki C-axis-synchronisation sequence the preparation for a code that both channels must carry is written per side with that channel's own codes — M45 in the tool-spindle program against M245 in the turret-2 program, M69 against M269 — while the shared M480 and the waits M100/M101 stand identically in both; G28 H0 also stands identically in both and returns each side's own spindle C axis to zero, which makes the point directly: the same text in the other program addresses the other channel's axis. Nakamura says the same of whole programs: each unit's program drives its own axes, so far that a unit's program may be written as though it sat on the other unit. A HOME Z moved into the other channel's program would therefore home the other turret, exactly as the draft argues. Caveats: No manual discusses generated blocks or an expander, so this is the machine reasoning behind the rule rather than the rule itself; the Mori sequence is written by hand by the programmer, not produced by a rule. Searched: Nakamura 2-4 Mehrbahn-Maschinen, Mori Seiki M480/M481 and M34/M35/M36 notes and the transfer examples, DMG CTX/NTX Strukturprogrammierung parts 1 and 2, the Siemens Grundlagen chapter on channel and geometry axes.
Evidence: Mori-Seiki_NT-NTX-Serie_Programmierung_Programmieranleitung-NTX1000SZM_PX-NT_4-K0DEEN_2011.pdf, 1-32 M480/M481, programming example, p. 292-293 (The two programs of the example run side by side: M45 connects spindle 1 as the C axis in the tool-spindle program while M245 does the same for spindle 2 in the turret-2 program; M69 and M269 release the two spindle brakes; G28 H0 stands in both and returns that side's C axis to zero, and the turret-2 program adds G28 U0; G43 H3. and M211 stand only in the tool-spindle program. The shared items are M480, the waits M100/M101/M102 and G28 H0. Note 2 requires both M45 and M245 before M480, note 10 both M69 and M269); Nakamura-Tome_Fanuc_Programmierung_Programmierhandbuch-1_4810004ECL-1_DE_2013.pdf, 2-4-1 to 2-4-3 Steuerung von Mehrbahn-Maschinen, p. 20-22 (printed 2-5 to 2-7) (Each unit has its own program memory and drives its own axes: ZL/XL/CL against ZR/XR/CR on the TW series (page 20), Z1/X1/C1 against Z2/X2/C2 on the WT/WY/Super NTJ/NTJ-100 (page 21). On the TW series the right-unit program may be written on the assumption that it sits on the left unit (page 20), and on the WTW the lower-unit program as though it sat on the upper one (page 22), so the same address in another path's program means a different physical axis). (Citations re-paged to the cnc-manuals connector 2026-10-26.)

Decided 2026-10-27 by Claude on the maintainer's delegation (Peter, 2026-10-27: most of these cases never appear in a program, he knows no more than the manuals and has no machine to test on; so a short web research first, and failing that the most logical approach, as if we were the control manufacturer).

Keep main. A rule's generated blocks stay in the program that writes the word. Only the bound word moves or is duplicated, and it is not expanded again. Bound words among the generated blocks move by the same rule.
Basis: manual (supporting)
Source: Mori Seiki NTX1000 p. 292-293 (per-side preparation codes); Nakamura ECL-1 p. 20-22 (the same address in another path's program is another axis) (cnc-manuals).
Differs from the recommendation: no
Confidence: high
Code impact: none.
