#### D189 A drilling-axis word in a CYCLE_CALL block
Question: VM 3.3 says 'the other axis words of the call block position the hole', and its sequence starts with a 'rapid in the plane to the axis words at the current drilling-axis position'. Language 4.7 calls 'at the position given by the axis words'. Neither says what CYCLE_CALL X=10 Y=10 Z=20 does under WORKPLANE=XY. On Fanuc the Z of a cycle block is the depth, and on Heidenhain L X Y Z FMAX M99 pre-positions Z. heidenhain 5 also names CYCL CALL POS X Y Z, a call that carries a tool-axis coordinate. The documents do not say what that Z does, and the Heidenhain reader keeps the block RAW (HeidenhainCycles.ReadCall). Neither reader writes a drilling-axis word into a CYCLE_CALL. The Fanuc reader reads it as DEPTH (FanucCycles.Positions), and the Heidenhain reader writes a tool-axis positioning as a RAPID of its own before a bare CYCLE_CALL (HeidenhainCycles.ReadM99). Main moves the axis with the rapid to the hole, before the sequence (CycleRules.Drill).
Recommendation: For the built-in family, a word on the drilling axis in a CYCLE_CALL block is an ERROR, with a new VM code in VM 5. The cycle's planes move that axis, and a pre-positioning is a RAPID of its own, as both readers already write it. Reason: design rule 1 (one meaning). The word means the depth on Fanuc and a pre-positioning after Heidenhain M99, and VM 3.3's sequence moves in the plane at the current drilling-axis position. CYCL CALL POS stays RAW, as on main, until the meaning of its tool-axis coordinate is confirmed from the iTNC 530 manual. Under this rule the reader can never write that coordinate on the CYCLE_CALL itself. For a cycle outside the family, the call moves the axes it names (D187). Alternative: keep main, where the word moves its axis with the rapid to the hole (Heidenhain's M99 meaning), and the Fanuc compiler writes it as a G0 block of its own before the call.
Where: VM 3.3, 5; language 4.7 (CYCLE_CALL row); heidenhain.md 5 (CYCL CALL POS); src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/CycleRules.cs Drill (TODO(question) at lines 114-116) and PositionTheHole; src/Ncx.Readers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainCycles.cs ReadCall; DiagnosticCodes and docs/spec/generated/diagnostics.md (new code).

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: The manuals give a drilling-axis word in a call block three incompatible meanings, so the ERROR for the built-in family is right and CYCL CALL POS must stay RAW. On Fanuc the Z of a G8x block is the distance from point R to the hole bottom, that is the depth. On Heidenhain the Z of a positioning block with M99 is a real move the TNC makes before it calls the cycle. And in a CYCL CALL POS block the tool-axis coordinate is neither: the manual says three coordinate axes must always be programmed and that the tool-axis coordinate changes the start position, acting "wie eine zusätzliche Nullpunkt-Verschiebung" on the whole cycle — so the reader can never write it as a CYCLE_CALL axis word.
Evidence: HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Zyklenprogrammierung (670 388-12, NC-SW 340490-07), p. 55 (Section 2.1 on CYCL CALL POS: the block's position is the cycle's start point; three coordinate axes must always be programmed; the tool-axis coordinate is a simple way to shift the start position and acts as an additional datum shift; the block's feed applies only to the approach; the position is always approached with the radius compensation inactive (R0). It also gives the positioning logic: above the surface coordinate Q203 the control positions first in the working plane and then in the tool axis, below it first in the tool axis to the safe height and then in the plane); HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Zyklenprogrammierung (670 388-12, NC-SW 340490-07), p. 54, 55 (CYCL CALL calls at the position programmed last before the block; M99 at the end of a positioning block makes the TNC travel to that position and then call the cycle. The words of an M99 block are therefore an ordinary move, not cycle data); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-MODEL B, Bedienungshandbuch Fräsen (B-64484GE-2), p. 75, 84 (PDF; printed 59, 68) (The formats of G83 and G85 define Z as the distance between point R and the hole bottom and R as the distance between the initial level and the R level; X and Y are the hole position. The drilling-axis word of a Fanuc cycle block is thus the depth); HEIDENHAIN iTNC 530, Benutzer-Handbuch Zyklenprogrammierung (670 388-12, NC-SW 340490-07), p. 79, 80 (Cycle 200's programming notes require the positioning block to go to the hole centre in the working plane with R0, and step 1 of the cycle positions the tool in the spindle axis at FMAX onto the safety clearance. The tool-axis motion belongs to the cycle, not to the call block).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D193 Modulo rotary axis or travel-limited rotary axis
Question: Machine-config 4 says the limits of a modulo rotary axis are 'the display range, not a travel limit (D100)'. VM 5 compares every target with the axis limits, and the travel-limit analytic of VM 8 checks 'min and max per axis'. No key tells a modulo axis from a rotary axis with real travel limits. The example files tell them apart only in comments. B1 of mori-ntx1000-mapps.toml and of dmg-ctx-840d.toml has [-120, 120], 'the swivel range, a travel limit', and every spindle C axis has [0, 360], 'modulo axis'. The code on main neither compares (VM442, MotionValidation.CheckLimits) nor clamps (LimitClamp.ClampTarget) any rotary axis, so `RAPID B=130 FRAME=MACHINE` on the Mori gets no WARNING.
Recommendation: Add an optional key `modulo = true` to a rotary [[axis]]. The limits of such an axis are its display range: they are never compared, clamped or used by the travel-limit analytic. Without the key (default false) the limits of a rotary axis are travel limits, like those of a linear axis. They are compared in the MACHINE frame (VM442), reported by VM 8, and clamped under "clamp" for the same targets as a linear axis (the FRAME=MACHINE targets of D203). The C1 example of machine-config 4 and every spindle C axis of the five example files (C1 and C2; C3 and C4 on the DMG) get `modulo = true`. The key decides only the limits; how a modulo position wraps is not part of this decision. Reason: the controls set this per axis (fanuc.md 2: 'rotary axes usually modulo 360 with a roll-over setting'; the Siemens modulo axis, siemens.md 3). It also cannot be derived from the owner. On a mill, a rotary table axis turns endlessly as a C table but has travel limits as a trunnion A, whichever resource owns it (D146 would let a table resource own it). Alternative with no new key: a rotary axis owned by a work_spindle is modulo, and every other rotary axis has travel limits. It fits the five example files but not a rotary C table.
Where: machine-config 4 (the [[axis]] keys, the C1 example and the paragraph after it); VM 5 (the limits item); VM 8 (travel limits); docs/spec/examples/machines/*.toml and their copies in machines/. Code: src/Ncx.Core/Machine/AxisDef.cs; src/Ncx.Config/MachineConfigLoader.Resources.cs (key list, ReadAxes); src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/Validation/MotionValidation.cs CheckLimits (TODO(question) at line 114) and HasLinearLimits, which gates the check in the RunValidation constructor (_comparesLimits); src/Ncx.Core/Expander/LimitClamp.cs ClampTarget (TODO(question) at line 155); test LimitClampTests.D64_WorkpieceTargetAndRotaryTarget_AreNotRewritten.

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: Add the key: all three controls carry exactly such a per-axis flag, and they treat a modulo axis's range as a display range, not a travel limit. Fanuc enables roll-over per axis with bit ROAx of parameter 1008 (one revolution in parameter 1260, with ROTx/ROSx in 1006 deciding linear or rotary first), Heidenhain has the per-axis machine parameter `isModulo` ("Moduloanzeige") under CfgAxis, and Siemens the per-axis modulo range MD30330/MD30340, default 0 to 360°. Siemens's travel-range calculation states that rotary axes are monitored "nur … wenn es keine Modulo-Rundachsen sind", Heidenhain that its extended limit-switch monitoring does not act on modulo axes, and the Siemens swivel data record asks for the real angular range on a swivel axis (for example −90/+90) but "Bei Moduloachsen ist der Verfahrbereich zwischen 0 und 360 grd einzutragen". The alternative without a key is contradicted by a real machine: on the WFL Millturn the work-spindle axes C1 and C2 are deliberately not defined as modulo rotary axes but like linear axes.
Evidence: Fanuc 0i-D Connection Manual (Function) Vol.1 (B-64303EN-1-02), p. 137-138 (printed 111-112) (Section 1.5.4 Rotary Axis Roll Over: the roll-over function prevents the rotation axis coordinates from overflowing and is enabled by setting parameter ROAx (No. 1008#0) to 1 for that axis; for an incremental command the tool moves the angle specified, for an absolute command the coordinates after the move are rounded by the angle of one revolution set in parameter 1260. Parameter 1006#0/#1 (ROTx/ROSx) first decides whether the axis is linear or rotary at all, and the rotary A type has machine coordinates rounded in 0 to 360°. Both parameters are bit-axis type — the property is per axis, not per resource.); Heidenhain TNC 640 Technisches Handbuch (892899-18, NC-SW 34059x-09), p. 801 (Machine-parameter overview: under CfgAxis (300100, "Allgemeine Beschreibung einer Achse") stand isAng "Rundachse" (300101), isModulo "Moduloanzeige" (300102) and restoreModuloCntr "Modulo-Zähler der Achse im SRAM sichern" (300111). A separate per-axis set CfgRollOver (300400) holds shortestDistance "Verfahrweg bei Rundachsen mit Modulo-Zählweise" and startPosToModulo. Heidenhain marks the modulo property on the individual axis and calls it a display property.); Heidenhain TNC 640, Aktuelle Information Nr. 6, p. 11 (On the new optional extended limit-switch monitoring MP_extendedLimitCtrl (400504, path CfgPositionLimits/extendedLimitCtrl), whose limits lie 0.2 mm or degrees outside CfgPositionLimits/MP_swLimitSwitchNeg and MP_swLimitSwitchPos in a system without functional safety, the manual notes: "Diese Überwachung wirkt nicht für Modulo-Achsen."); Siemens SINUMERIK 840D sl, Programmierhandbuch NC-Programmierung (SW 4.92, 2019), p. 603 (In the "Weitere Informationen" to CALCPOSI(), which computes the permissible travel path against software limit switches, working-area limitation and protection zones, under the heading "Rundachsen": "Rundachsen werden nur überwacht, wenn es keine Modulo-Rundachsen sind." Modulo rotary axes are excluded from that check.); Siemens SINUMERIK 840D sl/840D/840Di sl Programmierhandbuch Zyklen (01/2008), p. 253 (CYCLE800 swivel data record, "Winkelbereich" $TC_CARR30[n]..$TC_CARR33[n]: every rotary axis must be given a valid angular range (for example −90 +90 degrees), and this need not be the software limit range of that axis; "Bei Moduloachsen ist der Verfahrbereich zwischen 0 und 360 grd einzutragen." The 0–360 of a modulo axis is a definition range, a real swivel axis gets its real travel.); Siemens SINUMERIK 840D sl, Programmierhandbuch Arbeitsvorbereitung (08/2018, BS.000504), p. 644 (MODAXVAL determines the modulo position of a modulo rotary axis, the modulo remainder with respect to the parameterised modulo range, which in the standard setting runs from 0 to 360 degrees and whose start and size are changed with MD30340 MODULO_RANGE_START and MD30330 $MA_MODULO_RANGE.); WFL Millturn, Programmierung Sinumerik 840D, Kapitel 15, p. 9 (Section 5 "C-Achse nullen (MCC1ZERO, MCC2ZERO)": on the MILLTURN the axes C1 and C2 are "nicht als Modulo - Rundachsen, sondern wie lineare Achsen definiert", so that absolute degree values can be programmed in both directions and over several revolutions; the drawback is that the C axis winds up, which is what MCC1ZERO/MCC2ZERO undo by shifting the datum by whole revolutions. A work-spindle C axis is not automatically a modulo axis.).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D194 Verbs of 'spindle OFF before a LINE'
Question: VM 5 warns for 'spindle OFF before a LINE (the spindle of the current tool holder, the default spindle when the holder has none)'. VM 3.9 and VM 5 suppress the rule in a subprogram nothing calls (D99). F30 fixed which spindle is checked, not which verbs. ARC cuts as a LINE does, and CYCLE_CALL of the built-in drilling family feeds to DEPTH at CYCLE_F (VM 3.3). Controller-mapping 5 maps TAP to rigid tapping: Fanuc G84 with M29, Heidenhain cycle 207, and Siemens CYCLE84, whose POSS is a spindle position before tapping (siemens 7). In rigid tapping the cycle drives the spindle itself. Case: an ARC, or a CYCLE_CALL of CYCLE=DRILL, while the checked spindle is OFF. On main only LINE is checked (SpindleValidation.CheckSpindleBeforeLine, VM500), so neither gets a diagnostic. Widening the rule also widens the false alarms of D129. On millturn1.toml (H1 carries S3) and nakamura-ntjx.toml (T1 carries S3), every turning ARC, and every face-drilling CYCLE_CALL with a stationary tool while MAIN turns, would warn, as lines 13 and 14 of MILLTURN_TRANSFER do for LINE.
Recommendation: Cover LINE, ARC and CYCLE_CALL of the built-in drilling family except TAP. TAP is rigid tapping in controller-mapping 5: the cycle positions and runs the spindle itself, so the spindle state before the call does not decide the cut. Catalog cycles and `CYCLE:<controller>=n` cycles are not checked: the VM does not know their sequence (D94), and a measuring cycle runs with the spindle stopped. The checked spindle stays the one of F30, with the same D99 suppression. Answer this together with the option of D129 (the rule passes while the workpiece holder's spindle runs as well), which removes the turning false alarms for all three verbs at once. Code: widen the verb test in CheckSpindleBeforeLine, and for CYCLE_CALL require that the active cycle is a built-in drilling name other than TAP. The VM500 text and the VM 5 WARNING and suppression lists then read 'before a LINE, ARC or drilling CYCLE_CALL'. None of the five examples changes: their ARCs and CYCLE_CALLs all run with the checked spindle on. Alternative: LINE only, as coded.
Where: VM 5 (WARNING list, suppression list) and VM 3.9 (suppression list); implementation 11 P1-04; src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/Validation/SpindleValidation.cs CheckSpindleBeforeLine (TODO(question) at line 51); docs/spec/generated/diagnostics.md (VM500 row); D129 (its option).

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: The manuals back widening the rule to the drilling family and back the TAP exception, but only because NCX writes TAP as rigid tapping. Each of the twelve Fanuc canned-cycle sections from G73 to G89 repeats the same "Spindeldrehung" sentence — before the cycle is specified the spindle must be set turning with an auxiliary function (M code) — so a CYCLE_CALL of a built-in drilling cycle with the checked spindle off is as wrong as a LINE and deserves the same WARNING. Rigid tapping is the documented exception: with M29 S… before or in the G84 block the control drives the spindle motor like a servo and interpolates it with the tapping axis, and the cycle diagram starts and ends at spindle standstill, so the spindle state before the call does not decide the cut. Siemens behaves the same way: CYCLE84 begins with an oriented spindle stop (SPOS at POSS), switches the spindle into axis mode, taps with G331, retracts with G332 and only then rewrites the speed and direction that were active before the call. Note, though, that the plain G84 without M29 carries the same "spindle must be turning first" sentence and is driven by M03/M04/M05 — the exemption is only safe as long as controller-mapping 5 keeps TAP pinned to the rigid form. Nothing in the manuals bears on ARC; that part of the widening rests on machining sense, not on a page.
Evidence: FANUC 30i/31i/32i-B Bedienerhandbuch Fräsen (B-64484GE-2/02), p. 72 and 82 (printed 56 and 66) (Each cycle section has a paragraph "Spindeldrehung" reading that before the cycle is specified the spindle must be set turning with an auxiliary function (M code). The paragraph appears for G73, G74, G76, G81, G82, G83, G84, G85, G86, G87, G88 and G89 on cache pages 66, 68, 70, 72, 74, 75, 82, 84, 86, 87, 89 and 91; for G74 it names counter-clockwise rotation, otherwise the wording is identical); FANUC 30i/31i/32i-B Bedienerhandbuch Fräsen (B-64484GE-2/02), p. 108 (printed 92) (Section 5.3: in the standard mode the spindle is turned and stopped with M03, M04 and M05 alongside the motion of the tapping axis; in the rigid-tapping mode the spindle motor is controlled as if it were a servo motor and interpolated with the tapping axis, one spindle revolution per pitch of feed, including during acceleration and deceleration. The G84 figure on the same page marks spindle standstill at the start, the reversal at the hole bottom and standstill again after the retract); FANUC 30i/31i/32i-B Bedienerhandbuch Fräsen (B-64484GE-2/02), p. 109 (printed 93) (Rigid tapping is entered by writing M29 S… before the tapping command, by writing M29 S… in the same block, or by bit 0 (G84) of parameter 5200 making G84 rigid; the sequence text says the spindle stops and dwells at the bottom, then turns the other way for the retract and stops again); Programmierhandbuch Zyklen SINUMERIK 840D sl/840D/840Di sl, p. 61 (The CYCLE84 sequence: approach the reference plane with G0, oriented spindle stop with SPOS (value in POSS) and transfer of the spindle into axis mode, tap to depth with G331 at speed SST, dwell DTB, retract with G332 at SST1 with reversed direction, then retract with G0 and re-establish spindle operation by rewriting the speed programmed before the cycle call and the direction in SDAC).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D198 Which states of a function table trigger its expansion rule
Question: Machine-config 5a gives pre, post, requires and restore to 'every function state', and D63 records them 'on function states'. But the 5a example writes them once per table (THROUGH = { ON = "M51", OFF = "M9", requires = ..., restore = ... }), and architecture 6 keeps one ExpansionRule per FunctionTable. The 5a prose, its reader sentence and the architecture 5.5 walk-through name COOLANT:THROUGH=ON only. So does the CoolantClutchRule of code-guidelines 11 ('Only the block that switches the through-spindle coolant on'). P7-01 requires that plugin to produce the same generated blocks as the configuration rule of P1-06. On main (ExpansionRules.RuleOf) a table's rule fires on every word that sets one of its states. COOLANT:THROUGH=OFF therefore also stops and restarts the spindle, and a [spindle.MAIN] rule fires on RPM, ORIENT, CSS, VC and RPM_MAX as well as on CW.
Recommendation: Keep one rule per table, as the example and the model have it, and add an optional key `states`: the list of states that trigger the rule. Without the key every state does, as main does now. The 5a example gains states = ["ON"], so the clutch sequence runs only when the coolant is switched on. That is what the 5a prose, its reader sentence and code-guidelines 11 say, and P7-01's comparison then holds. The 5a sentence becomes 'every function table, the tool change and every catalog cycle may carry four optional keys; a function table also `states`'. A word triggers the state it sets, under the state names machine-config 5 gives its table. SPINDLE=CW, CCW or OFF triggers the state of that name. RPM, ORIENT and RPM_MAX trigger their own state, CSS=ON and VC the state VC, CSS=OFF the state CSS_OFF. SPINDLE_MODE, COOLANT and FUNC trigger their value. SPINDLE_SYNC with two roles triggers ON, SPINDLE_SYNC=OFF triggers OFF, and PHASE triggers PHASE. This is the mapping that the open entry D154 recommends, read backwards; D154 must keep it. Alternative: a rule per state, written in the state's value as an inline table (ON = { code = "M51", requires = ..., restore = [...] }). Two states of one table could then carry different rules (DOOR OPEN and CLOSE), but the value form of machine-config 5, the loader and the model all change.
Where: machine-config 5 (table keys) and 5a (the 'every function state' sentence, the THROUGH example); architecture 6 (ExpansionRule gains States); D154 (open; must keep the word-to-state mapping). Code: src/Ncx.Core/Machine/ExpansionRule.cs; src/Ncx.Config/MachineConfigLoader.Functions.cs; src/Ncx.Core/Expander/ExpansionRules.cs RuleOf (TODO(question) at line 42); tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/Expander/ExpanderMachines.cs (CoolantClutch), CoolantClutchRuleTests.cs.

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: Keep one rule per table and add the `states` key: a rule must fire only on the states it names, because on real machines the states of one table carry different conditions. DMG-MORI's chuck has M436 'Spanner öffnen' which opens it only with the spindle stopped — and a second code M433 to open it with the spindle running — while M437 'Spanner schließen' has no spindle condition at all but a clamping-pressure one; Biglia's door M68 may be opened only with the spindle stopped and only after spindles and coolant have been switched off, while M69 close carries no condition and even runs automatically at cycle start. Builder M-code tables hang their attributes on the individual code, i.e. on the state, not on the pair. Applied to NCX, that is an argument against main's present behaviour: COOLANT:THROUGH=OFF should not stop and restart the spindle, and a [spindle.MAIN] rule should not fire on RPM, ORIENT, CSS, VC and RPM_MAX. Caveats: The manuals settle the behaviour (the condition belongs to the state) but not the TOML shape; `states = ["ON"]` and the Alternative's inline per-state rule both express it. Note that DMG needs two different codes for one state under two different conditions, which the `states` form can only reach through two function entries — worth a thought before the shape is fixed. The step from a builder's M-code table to main being wrong is mine, not a manual's.
Evidence: DMG MORI CTX/GMX Technik und Programmierung ShopTurn 3G, V2.1 (2015), p. 210 (Hauptspanneinrichtung; the same table for spindle 3 on 212 with M336/M333/M337) (M436 opens the chuck with the spindle standing still, M433 opens it with the spindle running (for bar feed), and M437 closes it with the set clamping pressure and no spindle condition - open and close of one chuck carry different preconditions.); Biglia Smart-Turn Programmierhandbuch, T140-00379-IM1 (2010), p. 48 (section 5.14, M68/M69) (M68 opens the front door and is possible only with the spindle stopped, and the note says to program the opening after the spindles and the coolant have been stopped; M69 closes it and need not even be programmed, because the door closes automatically at cycle start.); BURKHARDT+WEBER MCX 800 HVP Betriebsanleitung Band 1 (2019), p. 370-371 (section 6.9.2, Tabelle 6-8) (Each M code is a row of its own with its own attributes - modal or block-wise, Löschstellung (default state), cleared by which codes; M7 internal coolant is cleared by M9/M77/M107 and M8 external coolant by M9/M77/M108, and of the pair M10/M11 only M10 carries the default-state mark.); Hermle M-Funktionen C 400 / C 12 / C 22 / C 32 / C 42 / C 52 / C 60 (2015), p. 2-5 (M-Funktionstabelle) (Every state is its own row with its own effect column 'Satzanfang' or 'Satzende'; the internal coolant supply is M51 on (p. 4) and M52 off as separate entries, as are M25/M26 and M27/M28 for unclamping and clamping the C and A axes (p. 3).).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D204 Triggering block of a catalog cycle's expansion rule
Question: Machine-config 5a and D63 give every catalog cycle pre, post, requires and restore. The expander turns them into blocks 'around the triggering block', where requires are conditions 'that must hold while the function is written'. Language 4.7 defines a cycle once (modal) and executes it by CYCLE_CALL at each position. Language 4.7.1 puts the Doosan mode code 'before the cycle' (M291 before G83). That is the only example, it uses pre only, and doosan-puma-2600sy.toml carries the same entries commented out. No document names the triggering block. Main (ExpansionRules.RuleOf) fires on the block that names the cycle (CYCLE=name or `CYCLE:<controller>=n`) and never on CYCLE_CALL. So a post, or requires with restore, undoes the mode or the required state directly after the definition, before any hole is drilled (test MachineConfig5a_CatalogCyclePost_StandsDirectlyAfterTheBlockThatNamesTheCycle).
Recommendation: The rule covers the cycle while it is active. @SAVE, requires and pre stand before the block that defines the cycle. Post and @RESTORE stand directly after the CYCLE=OFF that ends the cycle. When another block ends it (the next CYCLE, TOOL or PROGRAM=END; VM 4, cycle row), they stand directly before that block. VM 4 does not end a cycle at SUB=END (it stays active in the caller), but generated blocks stay in their section (language 4.13), so there the rule ends before SUB=END. CYCLE_CALL blocks trigger nothing. The Doosan pre stays where 4.7.1 puts it, and a required state (SPINDLE_MODE=AXIS for C-axis drilling, for example) holds at every hole, as requires demands. Post goes after CYCLE=OFF and not before it because the Fanuc cycle is still modal until G80: a block with a position calls it again unless a G0 cancels it on that control (fanuc.md 6). A post that moves (a RAPID, HOME Z) would then drill, or depend on the control. It is also the programmer's own order: mode on, cycle, holes, G80, mode off. The expander finds the end in the text of the section, without VM state (architecture 5.5). A JUMP out of the range skips post and @RESTORE like any block it jumps over. For a one-shot entry (modal = false, Fanuc G70..G76) the end depends on D224, which asks whether the reader closes it with CYCLE=OFF. Machine-config 5a gets the sentence. Alternative: the rule surrounds every CYCLE_CALL block and not the definition. That needs no lookahead, but the mode code then stands before every hole (between the modal G83 position blocks on Fanuc), and a restore stops and restarts the spindle at every hole.
Where: machine-config 5a (the triggering block of a catalog cycle); language 4.7.1 (mode code sentence); architecture 5.5; VM 4 (cycle row); D224 (end of a one-shot cycle). Code: src/Ncx.Core/Expander/ExpansionRules.cs RuleOf (TODO(question) at line 69, above case "CYCLE"); src/Ncx.Core/Expander/Expander.cs ExpandBlock and BlockExpansion (post and @RESTORE placed at the cycle's end); tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/Expander/ExpansionRuleTests.cs MachineConfig5a_CatalogCyclePre_StandsBeforeTheBlockThatNamesTheCycle and MachineConfig5a_CatalogCyclePost_StandsDirectlyAfterTheBlockThatNamesTheCycle.

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: Keep the recommendation: the Fanuc turning manual writes a catalog cycle in exactly that shape. Its worked C-axis drilling example puts M51 (C-axis index mode on) before the G83 block, then the hole positions, then "G80 M05" to end the cycle, and only then M50 to take the mode off — so pre/@SAVE/requires belong before the block that names the cycle and post/@RESTORE after the block that ends it, never around CYCLE_CALL. The same pages carry the draft's reason for not putting post before the cancel: G83..G85 and G87..G89 are modal and stay in force until G80 or a group-01 G code cancels them, so a post that moves would drill. A state that must be re-established at every hole is what the cycle block's own C-axis clamp M code is: it is named in the G83 block, works modally, and the control emits it before each plunge and its paired release after each retract to R. The Doosan M291/M292 are the two forms of the G83/G88 cycle (clearing versus chip breaking), i.e. a choice made once for the cycle, which is where language 4.7.1 already puts them. Two claims of an earlier draft were struck: the hole blocks of the Fanuc example are not bare, each repeats the clamp M code ("C90.0 M31"), which strengthens rather than weakens the point; and no page ties the Doosan M291/M292 to bit 2 (RTR) of Fanuc parameter 5101, the Doosan sheet being a one-line M list that says neither that the codes are modal nor where they stand, so that identification is control knowledge, not a page. The manuals say nothing about NCX's one-shot cycles (D224) or about a JUMP that leaves the range.
Evidence: FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-B Betriebshandbuch, Drehmaschinensystem (B-64484GE-1/02), p. 101 (The worked example under 4.3.4 (end of cycle) reads M51 ("Indexmodus C-Achse Ein"), M3 S2000, a G00 positioning block, the G83 block with the clamp code M31, three further C positions each repeating M31, then "G80 M05" and last M50 ("Indexmodus C-Achse Aus").); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-B Betriebshandbuch, Drehmaschinensystem (B-64484GE-1/02), p. 93 (G83 to G85 and G87 to G89 are modal G codes that stay in force until cancelled; the drilling data are kept, and the M code used to clamp and release the C axis, once specified, works as a modal code and is cancelled by G80.); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-B Betriebshandbuch, Drehmaschinensystem (B-64484GE-1/02), p. 94 (The control itself outputs the C-axis clamp M code after positioning while the tool moves at rapid to the R plane, and the release code (clamp + 1) after the retract to R; the paragraph "Beenden" adds that a cycle is ended by G80 or by a group-01 G code such as G00 or G01.); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-B Betriebshandbuch, Drehmaschinensystem (B-64484GE-1/02), p. 102 (In the canned cycle with improved M code output, the clamp M code named in the cycle block is output before the tool moves down from the R plane and its paired release code after the retract to R — once per hole, by the control, not by a block around the definition.); M-Funktionen Puma 2600SY (Doosan machine M list), p. 4 (The list gives only "M291 ZYKLUS ENTLEEREN(G83/G88)" and "M292 ZYKLUS SPÄNEBRECHEND (G83/G88)" — the two forms of the same cycle, with no statement of modality or placement.); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-B Betriebshandbuch, Drehmaschinensystem (B-64484GE-1/02), p. 96 (Background only: on Fanuc, whether G83/G87 runs as the peck cycle with chip clearing or as the high-speed peck cycle is a control-side setting, bit 2 (RTR) of parameter 5101, or is chosen per block with G83.5/G83.6. No page connects this to the Doosan M codes.).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D208 Fanuc I J K: absolute CENTER or CENTER:IX
Question: Controller-mapping 2 gives the Fanuc I J K two readings: the CENTER:X row says 'computed from I J K + start' and the CENTER:IX row says 'I J K'. Language 6 and examples/2.5D_FRAESEN.ncx line 41 read N310 G3 X70. Y50. I-.534 J-19.993 as CENTER:X=50 CENTER:Y=50. 13-phase-3 P3-02 (FanucMotion), however, says 'I J K as CENTER:IX', and the paragraph under controller-mapping 2 keeps words 'absolute or incremental ... as written'. Language 2 rule 1 names the arc centre among the meanings NCX fixes once, but it fixes the meaning of each word, not which of the two words a reader writes. Rule 5 ('Numbers untouched') can be read in favour of CENTER:IX as written, but it forbids rounding and formatting, and the reader's sum (50.534 - 0.534 = 50) is exact. Main (FanucMotion.ReadArc) writes the absolute centre when the block has no incremental end-point word (G90, no U W H V) and the start point is known in the plane. It writes CENTER:IX in these cases: under G91 or U/W; from an unknown start (a subprogram's first arc, or after G53 or a frame change); under G12.1; when a diameter-programmed X lies in the plane; and when I or J is an expression. For N310 (Heidenhain H34/H35) both readers write CENTER:X=50 CENTER:Y=50 today, so this arc is not an M6 difference. It is the only I J arc of the three Fanuc mill sources.
Recommendation: Keep main's rule and state it in one sentence under the controller-mapping 2 table. The P3-02 bullet then reads 'I J K as CENTER:X from a known start under G90, else CENTER:IX'. Reasons: (1) Language 6 and the example stay as they are, so the Fanuc and Heidenhain readings of 2.5D_FRAESEN keep the same arc block (CC X50 Y50 is absolute, M6). (2) The centre takes the form of the end point: absolute with an absolute end, incremental with an incremental one. So under G91 the incremental centre keeps an incremental subprogram right at every call position (language 4.13), which a centre computed from one caller's start would not. (3) On a diameter axis the reader does not have to turn a radius I into a diameter CENTER:X (D60). Alternative: always CENTER:IX, as the phase plan says. Language 6 and 2.5D_FRAESEN.ncx line 41 then become CENTER:IX=-0.534 CENTER:IY=-19.993. The two readers then differ on that arc unless the Heidenhain reader also turns CC X Y into CENTER:IX, and P3-04 compiles the changed example. The answer is needed before P3-04.
Where: controller-mapping 2 (CENTER:X and CENTER:IX rows, paragraph under the table); 13-phase-3-readers-compilers.md P3-02 (FanucMotion bullet); language 2 rules 1 and 5, language 6 and examples/2.5D_FRAESEN.ncx line 41 (unchanged under the recommendation); src/Ncx.Readers/Fanuc/FanucMotion.cs ReadArc (TODO(question) at line 361 becomes a comment); tests/Ncx.Readers.Tests/Fanuc/FanucMotionTests.cs G3_WithIJFromAKnownStart_HasTheAbsoluteCentre, G3_UnderG91_KeepsTheIncrementalCentre.

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: Keep main's rule. The manual confirms the recommendation's reason (3) outright and adds one fact the other reasons must be read against: on Fanuc the number after I, J and K is a vector component that refers the centre to the start point and is given "unabhängig von G90 oder G91 immer als Inkrementalwert" — always incremental, whatever the G90/G91 mode — while the end point Xp/Yp/Zp is absolute or incremental according to G90/G91. So an absolute CENTER:X is always the reader's own exact sum (50.534 − 0.534 = 50) and never a form the Fanuc source writes; CENTER:IX under G91, from an unknown start or under G12.1 is the lossless fallback, not a mirror of the control. Reason (3) is the manual's own statement and is the real argument on a lathe: under diameter programming the X-axis command is a diameter value while the "Radiusdefinition bei Kreisinterpolation (R, I, K und etc.)" is a radius value, so a reader that wrote CENTER:X on a diameter axis would have to double the sum (D60, D125), which CENTER:IX avoids.
Evidence: Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 84 (printed 50), §4.4 Kreisinterpolation (Verified word for word. The arc end point is given with Xp, Yp or Zp and is absolute or incremental according to G90/G91. The arc centre is given for Xp, Yp, Zp with the addresses I, J, K; the numeric value after I, J, K is a vector component referring the centre to the start point, "unabhängig von G90 oder G91 immer als Inkrementalwert". I, J, K must carry a sign; I0/J0/K0 may be omitted; if Xp, Yp, Zp are omitted and only the centre is given, the block is a 360° circle); Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 231 (printed 197), Tabelle 8.4 (a) (Verified. Under diameter programming (bit 3 DIA of parameter 1006) the table gives as diameter values: the X-axis command, the incremental X setpoint, the G50 coordinate system setting and the axis position display; as radius values: the X infeed parameter R of a canned cycle and the "Radiusdefinition bei Kreisinterpolation (R, I, K und etc.)". (The table also covers the tool-offset component, switched by bit 1 of parameter 5004, and the feedrate along the axis.)); Programmierhandbuch Grundlagen SINUMERIK 840D sl/828D (03/2013), p. cache p. 170 (printed 170), §8.3.6 (Verified. Under 'Durchmesserwerte (DIAMON/DIAM90)' the list of what diameter values apply to names the interpolation parameters "I, J, K bei G2/G3, falls diese mit AC absolut programmiert sind. Bei inkrementeller Programmierung (IC) von I, J, K wird immer Radius verrechnet." So Siemens knows an absolute arc centre as an explicit written form, which Fanuc does not).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

### Seventh round: needed before the compilers are finished

#### D210 Kind of a Fanuc O section that no block of the file calls
Question: Controller-mapping 1 reads several O programs in one file as several PROGRAMs. Its SUB row, with controller-mapping 6 and fanuc 1, reads Onnnn ... M99 as a SUB, whether it stands after the caller's M30 or in its own file. An O section that nothing in the file calls fits both readings. A file of subprograms only has no NCX form: language 4.13 asks for one or more programs, and VM 5 makes 'a file without a program' an ERROR. VM 3.6 also says that the external program a CALL loads 'must have its own PROGRAM frame'. So a subprogram in its own file is a PROGRAM in NCX either way, and what stays open is its M99: the loop of controller-mapping 6 (JUMP=START), or the return to a caller in another file. Concrete cases: a file holding only O9010 ... M99, which is either a subprogram or a bar-work main program that loops; and a subprogram that holds an M30 (VM 3.6) in a file without its caller. On main both read as a PROGRAM whose M99 is JUMP=START, so in INTERPRETED mode a CALL from another file loops through it until the block cap (VM 3.6).
Recommendation: Keep the rule on main and write it into controller-mapping 1 (SUB row) and fanuc 9. An O section that a block of the file calls is a SUB, and its M30 becomes JUMP=END. An uncalled section is a PROGRAM when it holds an M30 or M2, a skipped one included. Otherwise it is a SUB, which STATIC mode walks once from the default entry state of D99. When no section is a PROGRAM, the first uncalled one becomes it, because a file needs a program (language 4.13, VM 5). An unskipped M99 of such a program is the loop of controller-mapping 6 (LABEL=START, JUMP=START). The reader adds an INFO (D98) that names this reading, since a subprogram called from another file reads the same way. The Fanuc compiler writes a JUMP=START to the label after the header back as M99 (fanuc 10), so such a file compiles to the source's M99 and still returns when the control calls it. Reasons: on the control every O number is a program until something calls it; an M30 marks a main program; bar-work programs end in M99; and an NCX file must hold a program. What PROGRAM=BEGIN, PROGRAM=END and this loop do when an external CALL runs the file is D214. Alternatives: (a) Allow a file of subprograms only (a library file), in which an uncalled Onnnn ... M99 is always a SUB. Language 4.13, VM 5 ('a file without a program') and the external CALL of VM 3.6 then change. (b) The M99 of a program made this way (the first uncalled section, with no M30 or M2) becomes RETURN before PROGRAM=END. A CALL from another file then returns there. Run on its own, it is the VM 3.6 WARNING for RETURN in a program with an empty stack, treated as JUMP=END, so a bar-work program without an M30 stops after one pass instead of looping.
Where: controller-mapping 1 (SUB row) and 6 (M99 paragraph); fanuc 9 rule 4 and fanuc 10 rule 3; language 4.13; VM 3.6 (external program; RETURN with an empty stack); D214; P3-06 (JUMP=START as M99). Code: src/Ncx.Readers/StructurePass.cs DecideKinds (TODO(question) at line 173) and the doc of StructureRole.SectionBegin; src/Ncx.Readers/DiagnosticCodes.Structure.cs (the INFO); tests/Ncx.Readers.Tests/StructurePassTests.cs Sections_UncalledOSectionHoldingM30_IsAProgramWhoseM99Loops (204) and Sections_NoOSectionEndsTheProgram_TheFirstUncalledOneIsTheProgram (226).

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: Keep the rule on main. Fanuc's own table of program-end codes makes M02/M30 the end of a main program and M99 the end of a subprogram, and the manual describes both readings of one and the same Onnnn … M99 section: called, its M99 returns to the calling program; started on its own by searching for its beginning at the keyboard, it runs like a main program and its M99 returns to the beginning of that program, which then repeats — and the way to stop such a program is a /M02 or /M30 block with optional block skip switched off. So an uncalled section holding an M30 or M2, a skipped one included, is a PROGRAM; an uncalled Onnnn … M99 is the bar-work loop (LABEL=START, JUMP=START) when it is the file's program; and the INFO that names this reading is right, because the control itself cannot tell the two apart either — the same stored section is a subprogram or a main program depending only on how it is started.
Evidence: Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 333 (printed 299), Tabelle 13.2 (d) and the VORSICHT (Verified. 'Das Programmende wird durch Programmierung einer der folgenden Codes am Programmende angegeben' — table 13.2 (d): M02 (and M30, printed 'M03' in this volume) for the main program, M99 for the subprogram. When a program-end code is read the CNC ends execution and goes to reset; when the subprogram-end code is read, control returns to the program from which the subprogram was called. VORSICHT: a block containing an optional block skip code such as /M02 ;, /M30 ; or /M99 ; is not regarded as the end of a program); Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 337 (printed 303), §13.3 'Verwendung von M99 im Hauptprogramm' (Verified. If M99 is executed in a main program, control returns to the beginning of the main program and the program is repeated from there; the usual way to write this is a /M99 ; block inserted at a suitable place and run with optional block skip switched off, and the repetition continues as long as that switch stays off. With the switch on, the /M99 block is skipped and execution continues with the next block); Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 337 (printed 303), §13.3 'Nur Unterprogramm' (Verified. Subprograms can be executed like main programs by searching at the MDI keyboard for the beginning of that subprogram. In that case M99 returns control to the beginning of the subprogram and execution repeats; a block with M99 Pn returns to block n inside that subprogram and repeats from there. To end such a program a block containing /M02 ; or /M30 ; is inserted at the right place and the optional block skip switch is turned off); Bedienungshandbuch Serien 16i/18i/160i/180i-MB, MB5 (Band 1 von 2) (FANUC B-63534GE/02), p. cache p. 199 (printed 177), Tabelle 12.2 (b) (Opened to settle the M03/M30 question. The same table in this volume reads 'Code / Bedeutung: M02 Für Hauptprogramm / M30 / M99 Für Unterprogramm'. The 21i-210i-MB, 16i-18i-MA, 16i-18i-TA/TB, 21i-210i-TA/TB and 16i-LB volumes all render it the same way, so the '03' in the 30i-B volume is that manual's own error and not the text cache's).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D211 Missing program end in Fanuc and Siemens sources
Question: Controller-mapping 1 (PROGRAM=END row) and heidenhain 7 rule 4 make a missing M30 before END PGM a WARNING. The Fanuc and Siemens cells name M30 and M2 (and M17 for Siemens), but say nothing of a program that has no end, such as a Fanuc file whose only program runs into the closing %. Code-guidelines 6 lets a stage continue with a WARNING only 'where the specification allows'. On main the shared structure pass (StructurePass.PlanProgram) writes PROGRAM=END after the program's last block, with the WARNING RDR010. The Fanuc and the Heidenhain reader both use it; the Siemens reader is P5-01. A program that ends in an unskipped M99 loop, or has a skipped /M30 (controller-mapping 6), gets no warning. No example is affected. The Fanuc sources end in M2 or M30. None of the three Heidenhain sources has an M30, and all three get RDR010 under controller-mapping 1.
Recommendation: The same WARNING RDR010 for every family, as on main. The reader writes a block the source does not have, which is the case controller-mapping 1 already names for Klartext, and one code keeps one reading. An M99 loop and a /M30 are ends the source writes (controller-mapping 6), so they get no warning. The Fanuc and Siemens cells of the PROGRAM=END row say so. Alternative: no diagnostic for Fanuc and Siemens, where the closing % or the end of the unit ends the program; the WARNING stays for Klartext only.
Where: controller-mapping 1 (PROGRAM=END row); fanuc 9 rule 4; the Siemens reader of P5-01; src/Ncx.Readers/StructurePass.Sections.cs PlanProgram (TODO(question) at line 86); RDR010 in src/Ncx.Readers/DiagnosticCodes.Structure.cs; tests/Ncx.Readers.Tests/StructurePassTests.cs Program_WithoutAnEnd_EndsAfterItsLastBlockWithAWarning (267, assert at 274).

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: Keep RDR010 for every family, and the manuals make the case stronger than the draft assumes. Fanuc defines a program section as beginning with the program number or file name and ending with a program-end code, and shows the file as % / TITEL ; / O0001 ; / … / M30 ; / % — the closing % is the end of the file, not of the program. Siemens says the same in one line: the last block of the execution sequence contains a special word for the program end, M2, M17 or M30. And Fanuc names an alarm for exactly the case the draft asks about: PS5010 DATENSATZENDE is raised when the EOR code is given inside a block, "und der Alarm wird auch erzeugt, wenn das Prozentzeichen am Ende des Programmes gelesen wird". So a Fanuc program that runs into the closing % is not quietly ended by it — the control alarms — and the recommendation's alternative ('the closing % ends the program, so no diagnostic') is wrong about the control. A reader that writes PROGRAM=END with a WARNING is therefore the mild reading, not the generous one.
Evidence: Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 323–324 (printed 289–290), ch. 13, Tabelle 13 (a), Abb. 13 (b) (Verified. The program components are Programmcodeanfang (%), Vorlauf, Programmbeginn, Programmabschnitt, Kommentarabschnitt, Programmcode-Ende (%); figure 13 (b) shows the file as % / TITEL ; / O0001 ; / … / M30 ; / %. Page 290 then says: 'Ein Programmabschnitt beginnt mit einer Programmnummer oder einem Dateinamen und endet mit einem Programmende-Code.'); Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 61 (printed 27), §1.7 (Verified. 'Normalerweise wird hinter dem Satzende-Code (;) am Programmanfang eine Programmnummer spezifiziert und das Programm mit einem Programmende-Code (M02 oder M30) abgeschlossen.'); Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 2412 (printed 2378), Anhang H, alarm 5010 (New, and the strongest page for this question. '5010 DATENSATZENDE — EOR (end of record) Code wurde inmitten eines Satzes angegeben. Der Alarm wird auch erzeugt, wenn das Prozentzeichen am Ende des Programmes gelesen wird.' The 0i-D volume (cache p. 1447) carries the identical wording, and the 16i/21i volumes give it as 'END OF RECORD — The end of record (%) was specified.'); Programmierhandbuch Grundlagen SINUMERIK 840D sl/828D (03/2013), p. cache p. 37 (printed 37), §2.2 (Verified. Under the heading 'Programmende': 'Der letzte Satz in den Abarbeitungsreihenfolgen enthält ein spezielles Wort für das Programmende: M2, M17 bzw. M30.'); Alarm- und Fehlerliste OSP-P200L/P20L (Okuma LG37-005-R4), p. cache p. 342, alarm 2937 (Supplementary, outside the three families of the draft, but it shows the same judgement on a third control: '2937 KEIN PROGRAMMENDE-BEFEHL — Der gewählte Programmendecode ist unzulässig. Code 1: M02 oder M30 wurden nicht am Programmende programmiert.').
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D212 REPEAT without TIMES
Question: Language 4.9 has the REPEAT row repeat the blocks from the label 'TIMES more times', and calls TIMES the 'Repeat count for CALL or REPEAT'. Language 5 rule 5 makes TIMES need CALL or REPEAT but not REPEAT need TIMES. VM 3.6 names only 'REPEAT with TIMES', and VM 5 has no ERROR for a REPEAT without it. So LABEL=1 ... REPEAT=1 parses, and nothing says whether it repeats the blocks once, never, or is an ERROR. STATIC mode only records REPEAT (VM 1), so the answer matters to INTERPRETED mode and to the compilers, which write CALL LBL n REP k, REPEAT label P=k and the Fanuc counter of controller-mapping 6. On main the parser accepts it and INTERPRETED mode repeats the blocks once.
Recommendation: TIMES is optional on REPEAT and defaults to 1, so the blocks run once more. The code does this already (FollowRepeat, TimesOf withoutTimes: 1). A CALL without TIMES also runs once. One more pass is also what a Sinumerik REPEAT label without P does (manual, not in the documents; P5-01 confirms). The compilers write the count 1. The Heidenhain reader never produces this form: it keeps a CALL LBL REP without a count as RAW and reads CALL LBL n without REP as CALL=n (heidenhain.md 7 rule 3). The reference to Heidenhain in the code comment should therefore go. The 4.9 row would read 'TIMES more times, once when TIMES is missing', and VM 3.6 'REPEAT re-executes the section TIMES times, once without TIMES'. Alternative: TIMES is required. A REPEAT without it is then the partner ERROR PAR016 (language 5 rule 5, VM 5), and the Siemens reader writes TIMES=1 (design rule 4: explicit where controllers are implicit).
Where: Language 4.9 (REPEAT and TIMES rows); VM 3.6 (REPEAT bullet); for the alternative, language 5 rule 5 and VM 5. Code: src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/VirtualMachine.Interpreted.cs FollowRepeat (TODO(question) at line 268); tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/VirtualMachine/InterpretedFlowTests.cs Repeat_WithoutTimes_RepeatsTheBlocksOnce; for the alternative, src/Ncx.Core/Parsing/BlockRules.cs s_partners. P5-01 (Siemens REPEAT without P); P3-04 and P3-06 (the count written).

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: Keep the recommendation: TIMES is optional and defaults to 1, so the blocks run once more. The Sinumerik manual states it outright for REPEAT — with no P the program part is repeated exactly once — and its own example comments a REPEATB without P as "execute block N20 once" against P=5 on the line above. The same default holds for a call: Fanuc's M98 with no repeat count calls the subprogram once, and M198 without L takes the count as 1. The reference to Heidenhain in the code comment should indeed go: the TNC dialogue makes REP a number you either enter or skip with NO ENT, and REP is to be used only for program-part repeats, so a CALL LBL without it is the subprogram-call form and a Heidenhain source cannot produce a REPEAT without a count.
Evidence: SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D, Programmierhandbuch NC-Programmierung (06/2019, CNC-SW 4.92), p. 479 (Section 3.1.6, the explanation of the address P: the program part is repeated n times and execution then continues with the line after the REPEAT/REPEATB line, followed by the note "Ist kein P=<n> angegeben, wird der zu wiederholende Programmteil genau einmal wiederholt." The first example comments `N50 REPEATB POSITION2` (no P) as executing block N20 once, against `P=5` five times on the line above); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-MODEL B, Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen (B-64484GE/02), p. 335 (PDF; printed 301) (Note 2 under the M98 subprogram call: when no number of calls is given for a subprogram with a number of at most four digits, it is called only once, and the number then need not be padded to four digits); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-MODEL B, Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen (B-64484GE/02), p. 1108 (PDF; printed 1074) (Section 4.5, external subprogram call M198: if address L is not given, the number of repeat calls is taken as 1. The FS16-compatible format on the same page says the same for its own count field); HEIDENHAIN TNC 640, Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung (892903-18, NC-SW 34059x-10), p. 248, 249 (In the CALL LBL dialogue of the subprogram section the repeat count REP is skipped with NO ENT, and REP is to be used only for program-part repeats. The program-part repeat section then says the control runs the part one time more often than repeats are programmed, because the first repeat starts after the first machining pass — the same counting as NCX's TIMES).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D214 PROGRAM=BEGIN and PROGRAM=END of a called external program
Question: VM 3.6 lets CALL 'load the external program' and push a return pc, and requires that program to 'have its own PROGRAM frame'. The same section says 'PROGRAM=END ends execution of the program: the channel is finished, the run statistics are raised'. VM 2.8 sets channel.finished at PROGRAM=END, and language 4.1 says the control 'stops and rewinds' there. A called program has no SUB=END, so read literally, a CALL of it never returns. VM 3.6 ('A CALL that names a program instead of a subprogram: ERROR'), VM 5 ('CALL of a program') and language 4.13 ('programs are entered from the job only') go further: read literally, they forbid the call. VM 2.1 (program name and number set by PROGRAM=BEGIN), VM 4 (the PROGRAM=END resets) and VM 7 (PROGRAM_BEGIN, and PROGRAM_END with the run statistics) do not name the called case either. Case: CALL="O9010" where O9010.ncx ends with PROGRAM=END. On main the CALL-of-a-program ERROR applies only to a program of the caller's own file (FollowInterpretedCall). The called program runs from the block after its PROGRAM=BEGIN. Its PROGRAM=END returns to the caller, whether the flow, its JUMP=END or a RETURN reaches it. The channel goes on, no VM 4 reset applies, and the caller's program name stays. Neither its PROGRAM=BEGIN nor its PROGRAM=END block executes, and events are raised per block. So it raises no PROGRAM_BEGIN, PROGRAM_END, SUB_BEGIN or SUB_END, and only the CALL event marks it. ExternalProgramTests covers the program name, the single PROGRAM_END and the JUMP=END. The RETURN is handled in RunSection but has no test.
Recommendation: Keep what the code does and write it into VM 3.6. The ERROR 'CALL of a program' names a program of the caller's file. CALL="name" enters the first program of the external file. In a CALL, the called program's PROGRAM=BEGIN block, with NAME, NUMBER and CHANNEL, is its frame and is not executed. Its PROGRAM=END returns to the caller as SUB=END does, and so does a RETURN in it. JUMP=END in it goes to its own PROGRAM=END and so also returns. No program-end effect applies. The channel does not end, the VM 4 resets do not run, and no PROGRAM_BEGIN or PROGRAM_END is raised. The CALL event marks the call, and the called blocks count toward the statistics of the caller's PROGRAM_END (VM 7; D235 asks what those statistics are). Reason: this is how a called program ends on the controls. A Fanuc O program ends with M99 (fanuc.md 1), and a Siemens one with M17 or RET (siemens.md 1, 8). The Sinumerik also treats the M30 or M2 of a main program called as a subprogram as M17 (programming manual, not in the documents; P5-01 confirms). The file also still checks on its own (VM 1). This settles the VM only. The readers and compilers still need to know that a file is called. D210 asks this for Fanuc: there, main reads a lone Onnnn ... M99 file, or an uncalled O section with M30, as a looping PROGRAM. Its answer must reach P3-03, P3-04 and P3-06. A file compiled on its own ends in program_end (M30), which ends the main program when called (VM 3.6 on a Fanuc M30 in a subprogram). A TNC CALL PGM file must hold no M2 or M30 (TNC manual, not in the documents), while heidenhain.md 7 rule 4 warns when M30 is missing. Alternative: PROGRAM=END ends the channel as written, and a called program returns only through a RETURN that its reader writes before PROGRAM=END. Checked on its own, that RETURN is then the VM 3.6 WARNING.
Where: VM 3.6 (CALL, PROGRAM=END, CALL-of-a-program and external-program bullets), VM 2.1 (program row), VM 2.8 (finished), VM 4 (PROGRAM=END resets), VM 5 (CALL of a program), VM 7 (PROGRAM_BEGIN/PROGRAM_END and SUB_BEGIN/SUB_END rows); language 4.1 (PROGRAM=END row), 4.13 (Rules). Code: src/Ncx.Core/VirtualMachine/VirtualMachine.Calls.cs CallExternalProgram (TODO(question) at line 91) and FollowInterpretedCall (CallOfProgram); VirtualMachine.Interpreted.cs RunSection (calledProgram); tests/Ncx.Core.Tests/VirtualMachine/ExternalProgramTests.cs (add a RETURN case). Follow-up: D210 (src/Ncx.Readers/StructurePass.cs DecideKinds) and D235 (run statistics); P3-03, P3-04 and P3-06 (the end of a called program).

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: Keep what the code does and write it into VM 3.6: the called program's PROGRAM=END returns to the caller as SUB=END does, and the ERROR "CALL of a program" stays for a program of the caller's own file. The TNC states this outright — it runs the called NC program to its program end and then continues the calling program with the block after the call — and the Sinumerik states that M2/M30 of a main program called as a subprogram act as M17 (and M17 in a main program as M2/M30). Fanuc is the documented exception the draft already names: M02 and M30 end the main program, reading a program-end code ends execution and resets the CNC, while M99 is the subprogram end that returns, so a Fanuc file meant to be called ends in M99 and a called file ending in M30 does end the caller. The two parentheticals in the draft ("TNC manual, not in the documents" and "Sinumerik programming manual, not in the documents") can now be replaced with these citations. Caveats: The TNC also warns when a called NC program contains M2 or M30 (a warning it clears by itself), and aborts when the END PGM block is missing. That is a different case from heidenhain.md 7 rule 4, whose WARNING is for a missing M30; it belongs with heidenhain 8 rule 6 and D226 (how a file meant for CALL PGM ends), not with rule 4.
Evidence: HEIDENHAIN TNC 640, Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung 892903-18 (NC-SW 34059x-10, 10/2019), p. 252 (8.4 Externes NC-Programm aufrufen, "Arbeitsweise") (The control runs the calling program until CALL PGM, then runs the called NC program to its program end, and then continues the calling program with the block after the call. No labels are needed, the called program must not call back into the caller, and it must contain no M2 or M30 (with FN 9 GOTO LBL 99 named as the substitute); Q parameters act globally across the call.); HEIDENHAIN TNC 640, Benutzerhandbuch Klartextprogrammierung 892903-18 (NC-SW 34059x-10, 10/2019), p. 253 ("Prüfung der gerufenen NC-Programme") (If a called NC program contains M2 or M30 the control issues a warning, which it clears by itself once another program is selected; it also checks called programs for completeness before running them and aborts with an error when the END PGM block is missing.); SINUMERIK 840D sl / 828D, NC-Programmierung, Programmierhandbuch (CNC-SW 4.92, 06/2019), p. 350 (2.13 Hilfsfunktionsausgaben, "Programmende: M2, M17, M30") (A program ends with M2, M17 or M30; when a main program is called from another program as a subprogram, M2 and M30 act like M17, and the other way round M17 in a main program acts like M2/M30.); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-MODEL B, Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fraesen B-64484GE/02, p. PDF 304 (printed 270), 11.1 Hilfsfunktion (M02 and M30 mark the end of the main program: automatic operation is ended and the CNC is reset, with builder-dependent differences, and control returns to the start of the program unless parameter 3404 bits 5 and 4 say otherwise. This is the page that carries the M30 statement.); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-MODEL B, Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fraesen B-64484GE/02, p. PDF 333 (printed 299), table 13.2 (d) "Code für Programmende" (Reading a program-end code ends the program run and puts the CNC into the reset state; reading a subprogram-end code returns to the program that called it, and M99 is that subprogram code. The table's main-program cell prints "M02" and "M03" (a misprint for M30, the same in the English B-64484EN and in the PDF's own text positions), so the M30 half of the rule rests on the caution note below the table (/M02, /M30, /M99) and on page 304, not on the cell.); FANUC Series 30i/31i/32i-MODEL B, Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fraesen B-64484GE/02, p. PDF 337 (printed 303), "Verwendung von M99 im Hauptprogramm" (M99 executed in a main program returns the control to the start of that main program, which then repeats - the looping-PROGRAM reading D210 gives a lone Onnnn ... M99 file.).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D219 Fanuc T word: turret form or preload, by tool holder
Question: Controller-mapping 3 (turret lathes row, ATC row, reader rules) and language 4.4 read a lathe T0656 as TOOL=6 OFFSET=56. They read the Mori Seiki tool spindle's T9001 as PRELOAD=9001, and G361 then gives TOOL=9001 (D91). Fanuc 5 tells the T forms apart by machine kind only. mori-ntx1000-mapps.toml has both four-digit forms on one machine. HEAD 1 is holder H1 (magazine, channel 1, [tool_change] preload = "T{tool:04}"). HEAD 2 is turret H2 (channel 2), which writes T0131 according to a comment in the file. Machine-config 3 has one [tool_change] per machine, and no document says how the reader tells the two forms apart. FanucToolWords reads every T word of a lathe as the turret form, so T9001 becomes TOOL=90 OFFSET=1. It also writes TOOL without a role. VM 3.8 rule 2 sends such a TOOL to default_holder whatever the channel. So Nakamura path 2's G0T0656 (TOOL=6 OFFSET=56) changes the tool of T1, the channel-1 ATC holder of nakamura-ntjx.toml, and not the tool of the lower turret T2.
Recommendation: The tool holder decides; no new key is needed. A program's T words belong to the tool holder whose `channel` is the program's channel, otherwise to default_holder (VM 3.8 rule 2). [tool_change] describes the change of default_holder. (1) A T word on that holder is read through its templates first: on the Mori Seiki, T9001 matches the preload "T{tool:04}", giving PRELOAD=9001. (2) A T word that none of its templates matches, and any T word on another holder of a lathe, is the turret form of fanuc 5: the WY sample's path 1 G0T0101 gives TOOL=1 OFFSET=1, because G340 and G341 do not match it. (3) A T word on a holder other than default_holder carries that holder's role, because a TOOL without a role reaches default_holder (language 4.4; VM 3.8 rules 1 and 2), and OFFSET follows the holder of the last TOOL: Mori Seiki HEAD 2 T0131 gives TOOL:TURRET2=1 OFFSET=31, and Nakamura path 2 G0T0656 gives TOOL:TURRET2=6 OFFSET=56. (4) For such a holder the compiler writes the turret form T{tool:02}{offset:02} (machine-config 3, turret row). This keeps every documented reading and the Nakamura acceptance. It needs one sentence each in machine-config 3 and in the reader rules of controller-mapping 3. It also needs the channel of the file (D223): a HEAD 2 file whose channel is unknown is read as HEAD 1. Alternative 1: VM 3.8 rule 2 sends TOOL and PRELOAD without a role to the holder of the program's channel, so that path 2 keeps TOOL=6 OFFSET=56. Alternative 2: [tool_change.ROLE] tables per holder, like [spindle.ROLE] (VM 3.8 rule 2a), which the Mori Seiki and Nakamura files already sketch in comments. This is more general and costs one schema key.
Where: machine-config 3 (one sentence after the template table); controller-mapping 3 (reader rules paragraph); fanuc 5; VM 3.8 rule 2 and language 4.4 (TOOL with a holder role); the turret-2 comments in docs/spec/examples/machines/mori-ntx1000-mapps.toml:166 and nakamura-ntjx.toml:151; src/Ncx.Readers/Fanuc/FanucToolWords.cs (dispatch at line 135; Turret with its TODO(question) at line 152, which writes TOOL without a role); P3-06 FanucToolWords.

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: The tool holder decides, as recommended, and the manuals show both forms side by side on the machines in question. On the Mori Seiki NTX1000 the tool-spindle T word is a bare four-digit tool number that calls that magazine tool to the tool change position (T9001), with G361 performing the exchange and T0 followed by G361 returning the tool to the magazine; the turret-2 T word is the turret form, the first two digits the tool number, which equals the turret station, the last two the geometry and wear offset number. On the Nakamura every turret and ATC change T word is the turret form (T□□□□, T□□00 cancels the offset), including the ATC cycle's T value, whose last cycle step (12) is 'T-Befehl (Lesen der Werkzeugkorrektur) & M/S-Befehl'; the Nakamura preload is not a T word of this kind at all but the A value of G340, or G341 T with a bare magazine station number. So a T word that matches the holder's own templates is read through them and every other T word of a lathe is the turret form. Two facts to carry into machine-config 3 and fanuc 5: the Nakamura turret form widens to six digits (three plus three) when the offset number exceeds 100, switched by P5040.1, P3032 and P3116.6; and on the NTX1000 the offset base of turret 2 depends on the spindle the tool works against, T0101–T1212 at spindle 1 and T0131–T1242 at spindle 2.
Evidence: Programmieranleitung NTX1000SZM/NT-Baureihe (Mori Seiki PX-NT_4-K0DEEN), p. cache p. 313, §1-1 T-Funktion (Werkzeugspindel) (Verified. The T function calls a specified tool to the tool change position; a four-digit tool number after address T specifies the tool, and the magazine rotates to bring it there. Example: 'T9001;' calls T9001 to the tool change position, then 'G361 B0 D1.;' exchanges the tool presently in the tool spindle for T9001. 'T0; G361;' empties the tool spindle by returning the tool to the magazine. The number carries no offset digits); Programmieranleitung NTX1000SZM/NT-Baureihe (Mori Seiki PX-NT_4-K0DEEN), p. cache p. 314–315, §1-2 T-Funktion (Revolver 2) (Verified. A four-digit number after address T specifies a tool number and a tool offset number; 'Eine Werkzeugnummer ist gleich der Nummer der Revolverstation'; the first two digits are the tool number, the last two the geometry and wear offset number. The NOTE: when machining a workpiece in spindle 2 with a tool in turret 2, the geometry and wear offset numbers are those used for spindle 1 plus 30 — 'T0101 - T1212: Spindel 1 / T0131 - T1242: Spindel 2'. Page 315 adds the example 'G00 T0101;' and the note that the X-axis geometry offset data should be set in diameters); Präzisionsdrehzentrum Programmierhandbuch (1/2) (Nakamura-Tome 4810004ECL-1), p. cache p. 66–67 (printed 6-1/6-2) and cache p. 69 (printed 6-4), ch. 6 (Verified. Turret indexing and tool offset are one word T□□□□: the first two of the four digits are the tool number (turret station number), the last two the tool offset (geometry/wear) number, and T□□00 cancels the offset. Where the offset number exceeds 100 on a 120-tool ATC the T code becomes six digits, three for the tool number (T001□□□ … T120□□□) and three for the offset number; P5040 bit 1, P3032 (max. number of T-code digits) and P3116 bit 6 switch between the four- and six-digit specification. Page 67 adds a second, parameter-selected offset layout (5002.1)); Präzisionsdrehzentrum Programmierhandbuch (1/2) (Nakamura-Tome 4810004ECL-1), p. cache p. 326 (printed 22-1), cache p. 327–328 (printed 22-2/22-3), cache p. 331 (printed 22-6) and cache p. 332 (printed 22-7), ch. 22 (Verified, with the pages corrected. Cache 326 lists the twelve steps of the G340 cycle, of which (12) is 'T-Befehl (Lesen der Werkzeugkorrektur) & M/S-Befehl (nur bei Programmierung des M/S-Werts)'. Cache 327: 'T : Werkzeugwechsel-Nr. (stets anzugeben)', normally four digits and six when the offset number exceeds 100; 'A : Nummer des als nächstes vorzubereitenden Werkzeugs', two digits on a 40- or 80-tool ATC and three on a 120-tool one, 'Der A-Wert muss stets mit Dezimalpunkt programmiert werden'. Cache 328 gives 'G340 T0199. A0299.'; cache 331 gives 'G340 T0101. A02.'; cache 332 (§22-3) gives 'G341 T ;' with T the bare magazine station number of the next tool, two or three digits by ATC size).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D220 CYCLE_CALL of a cycle defined without a position
Question: Language 6 reads Fanuc 'G81 G99 Z-21.732 R5. F565' (no X Y) and Heidenhain 'CYCL CALL' as CYCLE_CALL X=10 Y=10, the point where the tool stands. Language 4.7 (CYCLE_CALL row) calls a CYCLE_CALL without axis words at the current position, and controller-mapping 5 says 'the defining block calls at its own position'. Neither says which form a reader writes. Both readers on main write the bare form, with only the axis words the source block has (FanucCycles.Call, HeidenhainCycles.ReadCall). Expected/BOHREN.ncx, the P3-02 output frozen after review, has the bare form at lines 14, 24, 34, 325 and 344. The choice decides the text both readers write and what P3-04 and P3-06 compile back.
Recommendation: The bare CYCLE_CALL, as main writes it: the reader writes the axis words the source block has. First reason: it round-trips with no extra rule. G81 without X Y compiles back the same way, and so does BOHREN.h's '12 CYCL CALL', which P3-04 must reproduce and which the position form would compile as L X+10 Y+10 FMAX M99. Second reason: both readers already agree on it. Third reason: the position is not implicit, because language 4.7 defines the bare call at the current position. Language 6 then writes CYCLE_CALL, with a comment that the tool stands at X10 Y10 (or a RAPID X=10 Y=10 before it). Alternative: the reader writes the current plane position into every call without axis words (as language 6 does), and the compilers drop words that equal the current position.
Where: language 6 (drilling example), 4.7 (CYCLE_CALL row); controller-mapping 5 (CYCLE_CALL row); src/Ncx.Readers/Fanuc/FanucCycles.cs Call (TODO(question) at lines 757-762); src/Ncx.Readers/Heidenhain/HeidenhainCycles.cs ReadCall; tests/Ncx.Acceptance/Expected/BOHREN.ncx; P3-04, P3-06.

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: The bare CYCLE_CALL, as main writes it. Klartext has three distinct call forms the reader must keep apart: CYCL CALL executes the last defined cycle at the position last programmed before the block and moves nothing; M99 at the end of a positioning block first travels to that position and then calls; CYCL CALL POS calls at the coordinates written in the block, with its own positioning logic, always three axes, and the tool-axis coordinate acting as an extra datum shift. Writing the current plane position into a bare CYCL CALL turns it into one of the other two forms on the way back, so the reader writes only the axis words the source block has, and language 6 gets a comment or a RAPID before the call. The Fanuc half now has a page as well: X and Y of a G8x block are the hole position, and the first step of a canned cycle runs only when a command to position the tool at a hole position is present in the block, so a G81 block without X/Y does no plane positioning and drills where the tool stands.
Evidence: Heidenhain iTNC 530 — Benutzer-Handbuch Zyklenprogrammierung (670 388-12, NC-SW 340490-07, 2011), p. 54 (CYCL CALL executes the last defined machining cycle once; the cycle's start point is the position last programmed before the CYCL CALL block. The dialog asks only for an optional M function, no coordinates. Verified); Heidenhain iTNC 530 — Benutzer-Handbuch Zyklenprogrammierung (670 388-12, NC-SW 340490-07, 2011), p. 55 (M99 is block-wise: the control first travels to the position of the positioning block and then calls the last defined cycle. CYCL CALL POS calls at the position written in that block, with a stated positioning logic; three coordinate axes must always be programmed in it, and its tool-axis coordinate acts "wie eine zusätzliche Nullpunkt-Verschiebung". Three call forms, three texts. Verified); Heidenhain TNC 640 — Benutzerhandbuch Zyklenprogrammierung (892905-18, 10/2019), p. 64 (Same wording on the newer control: the start point of the cycle is the position last programmed before the CYCL CALL block. Pages 64-66 carry CYCL CALL, CYCL CALL PAT, CYCL CALL POS, M99/M89 and SEL CYCLE as separate call forms. Verified); Heidenhain TNC 640 — Benutzerhandbuch Zyklenprogrammierung (892905-18, 10/2019), p. 127 (Heidenhain's own drilling example puts both forms side by side: block 5 CYCL DEF 200, block 6 a positioning block L X+10 Y+10 R0 FMAX M3, block 7 a bare CYCL CALL, then blocks 8-10 with M99 — the shape BOHREN.h has. Verified); Fanuc 0i-D / 0i Mate-D — Anwenderhandbuch Fräsen (B-64304GE-2/01), p. PDF page 73 (printed page 49) (G81's command format is given as G81 X_ Y_ Z_ R_ F_ K_ with "X_ Y_ : Bohrungsposition" — the plane words of the block are the hole position, and every address of the format is optional); Fanuc 0i-D / 0i Mate-D — Anwenderhandbuch Fräsen (B-64304GE-2/01), p. PDF page 65 (printed page 41) (Step 1 of the canned cycle's own operation list: "Wenn ein Befehl zum Positionieren des Werkzeugs an einer Bohrposition existiert, wird die Positionierung ausgeführt." Positioning is conditional on the block carrying it; step 2 then goes to point R and step 3 machines. The same sentence stands in the 0i-D turning manual (PDF page 137)).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.

#### D221 Fanuc M99 P: return to a block of the caller
Question: Controller-mapping 6 (paragraph after the table) reads M99 Pn in a subprogram as 'RETURN plus JUMP in NCX, kept as the two words'. Its CALL row and fanuc 1 say the same: M99 P30 returns to block 30 of the caller. But language 4.9 makes a LABEL unique per program or subprogram. VM 3.6 lets JUMP set pc 'to a LABEL of the current section' and makes a missing target a pre-pass ERROR. RETURN JUMP=30 in the SUB section is therefore that ERROR, whatever the caller holds. Controller-mapping 6 keeps the same construct of Siemens, RET("label", ...), as RAW. The reader keeps M99 P as RAW:FANUC with a WARNING (FanucMacro.ReadCalls), in a main program as well.
Recommendation: Keep RAW, as the code does and as controller-mapping 6 already does for Siemens RET("label"). NCX has no return to a label of the caller. RAW:FANUC keeps the block (D5) and compiles to Fanuc only. Controller-mapping 6 then reads: 'M99 Pn in a subprogram returns to block n of the caller; the reader keeps it as RAW, as Siemens RET("label")'. The documents do not describe M99 Pn in a main program. If the maintainer confirms that it jumps to block Nn of the same program, that case reads as JUMP=n with LABEL=n, which the VM already executes. Alternative: a JUMP in a RETURN block names a LABEL of the section the return goes to. The STATIC walk checks it at every CALL of the subprogram (D99), and a caller without that label is an ERROR at its CALL. Siemens RET("label") would read the same way. A compiler without such a return (Heidenhain LBL 0) reports a CMP ERROR.
Where: controller-mapping 6 (paragraph after the table; CALL, TIMES row; SUB row for RET); fanuc 1; for the alternative, language 4.9 (LABEL, JUMP and RETURN rows) and VM 3.6; src/Ncx.Readers/Fanuc/FanucMacro.cs ReadCalls (TODO(question) at line 214); P3-06 FanucFlow.

ANSWER:
As recommended, confirmed from the manual library: Keep RAW for the subprogram case and answer the open half in the affirmative. Fanuc says that if the address P and a sequence number stand at the end of a subprogram, control returns not to the block after the calling block but to the block with the number given at P — a target NCX cannot name, so RAW:FANUC stands, as for Siemens RET("label"). In a main program, however, M99 returns control to the beginning of the main program, and /M99 Pn returns to the block with number n of that same program (the manual's figure runs N0010 to N0080 M02 with N0060 … M99 P0030 jumping back to N0030); the same holds for a section started on its own by program search, where M99 Pn returns to block n inside that section. So M99 Pn outside a subprogram call is JUMP=n with LABEL=n on the block Nn, which the VM already executes, and only M99 Pn in a called subprogram stays RAW.
Evidence: Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 336 (printed 302), §13.3 'Spezifizieren der Satznummer für Rückkehr zum Hauptprogramm' (Verified. 'Wenn am Ende des Unterprogramms die Adresse P und eine Satznummer stehen, kehrt die Steuerung nicht zu dem Satz nach dem aufrufenden Satz, sondern zu der an P angegebenen Satznummer zurück. P wird allerdings ignoriert, wenn das Hauptprogramm in einem anderen Modus als im Speicherbetrieb ausgeführt wird. Die Verarbeitungszeit ist erheblich länger als bei normaler Rückkehr zum Hauptprogramm.' The figure shows the subprogram ending 'N1060 … M99 P0060 ;' and the caller's N0060 as the target); Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 337 (printed 303), §13.3 'Verwendung von M99 im Hauptprogramm' (Verified. M99 executed in a main program returns control to the beginning of the main program, which is then repeated. 'Wenn /M99Pn ; spezifiziert wird, kehrt die Steuerung nicht zum Anfang des Hauptprogramms, sondern zum Satz mit der Nummer n zurück. Die Rückkehr zum Satz mit der Nummer n dauert dann länger.' The accompanying figure runs N0010 to N0080 M02 with N0060 … M99 P0030 jumping back to N0030 of the same program. No mode restriction is stated here); Betriebshandbuch Drehen/Fräsen 30i/31i/32i-B (FANUC B-64484GE/02), p. cache p. 337 (printed 303), §13.3 'Nur Unterprogramm' (Verified. When a subprogram is started on its own by searching at the keyboard for its beginning, M99 returns control to the beginning of that subprogram and execution repeats; 'Bei einem Satz mit M99Pn kehrt die Steuerung auf den Satz im Unterprogramm mit der Nummer n zurück, und die Ausführung wird wiederholt.' The example ends N1040 … M02 ; / N1050 M99 P1020 ;, with the /M02 block skipped while optional block skip is on).
Settled 2026-10-01: the maintainer let the manual-confirmed answers that agree with their recommendation be applied without reviewing each one.
